title: Hyperbolic lattices with mass disorder: Phases and phase transitions
comment: 6 Pages and 6 Figures (Supplemental Materials as Ancillary File)
summary: Nearest-neighbor (NN) tight-binding models (TBMs) on plaquette-centered $\{ 10,3\}$ (Schläfli symbol), $\{ 8,3\}$, and $\{ 8,4\}$ hyperbolic lattices on a Poincaré disk with open boundary conditions display a vanishing, a finite, and a diverging density of states (DOS) near zero energy (band center), respectively, yielding a Dirac liquid, a Fermi liquid, and a flat band. Emergent bipartite nature of these lattices within the framework of NN-TBMs, allows us to scrutinize the impact of mass disorder on the electronic states and DOS therein. From extensive numerical calculations of the average and typical DOS using the kernel polynomial method, we show that hyperbolic Dirac liquid remains stable against weak mass disorder, undergoing a semimetal-to-metal quantum phase transition at moderate disorder, followed by an Anderson metal-to-insulator transition at even stronger disorder. The remaining two systems display only the latter transition. Critical exponents near all these transitions are found to be close to the ones mediated by on-site potential disorder.

AI.tldr: Nearest-neighbor tight-binding models on three hyperbolic lattices ({10,3}, {8,3}, {8,4}) show vanishing, finite, and diverging zero-energy DOS respectively (Dirac liquid, Fermi liquid, flat band). Under mass disorder studied via the kernel polynomial method, the Dirac liquid undergoes a semimetal-to-metal transition then an Anderson transition, while the other two only show the Anderson transition; critical exponents resemble those from on-site potential disorder.
AI.motivation: Hyperbolic lattices realize nontrivial flat-band and Dirac physics, but how mass disorder affects their electronic states and DOS (beyond the well-studied on-site potential disorder) is unknown.
AI.method: Construct NN tight-binding models on plaquette-centered {10,3}, {8,3}, and {8,4} hyperbolic lattices on a Poincaré disk with open boundary conditions. Exploit emergent bipartite nature to introduce mass disorder, and compute average and typical DOS numerically via the kernel polynomial method.
AI.result: Zero-energy DOS is vanishing, finite, and diverging for {10,3}, {8,3}, {8,4}, corresponding to a Dirac liquid, Fermi liquid, and flat band. The Dirac liquid is stable against weak mass disorder, undergoes a semimetal-to-metal transition at moderate disorder, and an Anderson metal-to-insulator transition at stronger disorder; the other two systems exhibit only the Anderson transition. Critical exponents near all transitions are close to those mediated by on-site potential disorder.
AI.conclusion: Mass disorder induces distinct disorder-driven quantum phase transitions in hyperbolic lattices, with universality classes resembling on-site potential disorder.

title: Walshness: an intrinsic neural-network representability metric for quantum states
summary: Neural quantum states (NQS) have emerged as powerful representations of quantum states with rapidly expanding applications across quantum many-body physics. Yet our understanding of when neural networks can efficiently represent physical quantum states remains limited, in part due to the nonlinear parameterization of NQS, the intricate sign structure of quantum states, and the sensitive dependence on basis choice. We introduce Walshness, a complexity metric of a quantum state which quantifies whether it admits a compact neural-network representation. We rigorously prove that a general quantum many-body state admits an efficient NQS representation if and only if it has bounded Walshness for various NQS architectures. We provide an algorithm for finding the optimal basis by minimizing the energy of a corresponding classical spin model. This allows us to empirically improve the learnability of various physical quantum states, including ground states of the transverse-field Ising model and mixed-field toric code, often reducing infidelity by orders of magnitude, and recovers and generalizes the basis choice given by the well-known Marshall sign rule in frustrated antiferromagnets. Our results provide an intrinsic complexity metric for quantum states with provable connections to their neural-network representability.

AI.tldr: Walshness is introduced as a basis-dependent complexity metric characterizing when quantum many-body states admit compact neural quantum state (NQS) representations, with an efficient-iff-bounded-Walshness theorem and an algorithm to find the optimal basis.
AI.motivation: Understanding of when neural networks can efficiently represent physical quantum states remains limited, owing to the nonlinear parameterization of NQS, the intricate sign structure of quantum states, and the sensitive dependence on basis choice.
AI.method: Define Walshness, a complexity metric quantifying whether a state admits a compact neural-network representation. Prove an equivalence between efficient NQS representability and bounded Walshness for various NQS architectures. Develop an algorithm that finds the optimal basis by minimizing the energy of a corresponding classical spin model.
AI.result: The basis-search algorithm empirically improves learnability of physical states, including ground states of the transverse-field Ising model and mixed-field toric code, often reducing infidelity by orders of magnitude, and recovers and generalizes the basis choice given by the Marshall sign rule in frustrated antiferromagnets.
AI.conclusion: Walshness provides an intrinsic complexity metric for quantum states with provable connections to their neural-network representability, linking NQS representation theory to a classical spin-model optimization.

title: Beyond Light Cones: State Preparation Complexity in Quantum Spin Glasses
summary:
We introduce a method for studying state preparation complexity in dense quantum $p$-spin Hamiltonians on $n$ qubits, going beyond bounds based only on circuit lightcones. The key input is the class's effective profile complexity, which is derived from the metric entropy of its Pauli profiles. These profiles record expectations of all Pauli operators supported on exactly $p$ qubits. Classes with uniformly bounded quadratic effective profile complexity remain separated from the ground-state energy by a positive multiple of $\sqrt n$ for sufficiently large fixed $p$. At subquadratic effective profile complexity, the class cannot outperform a suitable benchmark class at leading order, with product states providing a universal benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem of Berta et al. (arXiv:1810.12197) with Gaussian process entropy bounds.
  Applying this framework, we show that attaining near-ground-state energy requires $Ω(n^2/\log n)$ one- and two-qubit gates, even with arbitrary discardable ancillas. We also obtain depth-width tradeoffs, entanglement-depth and matrix product state bond-dimension lower bounds, and obstructions for both orientations at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966), with total circuit width $O(n)$. In first-level reverse magic, a shallow circuit is followed by an unrestricted Clifford circuit. The latter can spread local observables across the system, preventing a direct application of small-lightcone bounds. For this first-level class, our bounds also allow arbitrarily many clean ancillas at fixed shallow-circuit depth. A sharper benchmark shows that Clifford+$T$ circuits with $o(n)$ $T$-gates have no leading-order energy advantage over product stabilizer states, even with unrestricted Clifford operations and arbitrary discardable ancillas.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces effective profile complexity, derived from metric entropy of Pauli profiles, to bound state preparation complexity in dense quantum p-spin Hamiltonians beyond lightcone arguments.
AI.motivation: Existing state preparation complexity bounds for quantum p-spin Hamiltonians rely only on circuit lightcones, which become ineffective when unrestricted Clifford layers or clean ancillas spread observables globally. A finer, lightcone-independent complexity measure is needed.
AI.method: Effective profile complexity is defined via metric entropy of Pauli profiles (expectations of Pauli operators on exactly p qubits). The proof combines an adaptation of the nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem of Berta et al. with Gaussian process entropy bounds, comparing classes against product-state benchmarks.
AI.result: Reaching near-ground-state energy requires Omega(n^2/log n) one- and two-qubit gates even with arbitrary discardable ancillas. The framework also yields depth-width tradeoffs, entanglement-depth and MPS bond-dimension lower bounds, and obstructions at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy with total circuit width O(n). Clifford+T circuits with o(n) T-gates show no leading-order energy advantage over product stabilizer states.
AI.conclusion: Effective profile complexity provides a lightcone-independent tool for state preparation lower bounds, handling reverse magic (shallow circuit plus unrestricted Clifford) and clean ancillas, and unifying several circuit-complexity and entanglement resource lower bounds.

title: Beyond Lie Algebras: Lie-Wedge Stratification and Pure-State Stabilizability in Single-Channel Qubit Control
summary: Lie algebras describe how control generators combine, but in open systems they erase the distinction between reversible control and irreversible dissipation. Lie wedges retain this information. We study drift-free single-qubit systems with bidirectional Hamiltonian controls and at most one independently actuated dissipator generated by a traceless jump operator. In this work, we prove that they fall into thirteen structural strata defined by the generated algebra and its Lie-wedge geometry. The control algebra and four channel properties determine the stratum; in each wedge, the reversible directions are precisely the coherent controls. We then use the stratification to determine whether a wedge contains a generator with a unique globally attractive pure state. In five strata, stabilizability depends on additional channel data. In one exceptional stratum, no single control-rotated dissipative direction suffices, but averaging two such directions in the wedge yields stabilization. Lie wedges therefore reveal control capabilities that the generated Lie algebra misses.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies drift-free single-qubit open quantum systems with bidirectional Hamiltonian controls and at most one independently actuated dissipator into thirteen structural strata based on generated Lie algebra and Lie-wedge geometry, and uses this stratification to determine stabilizability to a unique globally attractive pure state.
AI.motivation: Standard Lie algebras capture how control generators combine, but in open systems they fail to distinguish reversible coherent control from irreversible dissipation. Lie wedges are introduced/used to retain this distinction, since control capabilities relevant to stabilization depend on the reversible vs. irreversible structure, not just the generated algebra.
AI.method: The authors study drift-free single-qubit systems with bidirectional Hamiltonian controls and at most one independently actuated dissipator generated by a traceless jump operator. They analyze the generated Lie algebra together with the Lie-wedge geometry and classify the systems according to the control algebra and four channel properties. Within each wedge, they identify the reversible directions with the coherent controls, and then use the resulting stratification to test for the existence of a generator with a unique globally attractive pure state.
AI.result: The systems fall into thirteen structural strata defined by the generated algebra and Lie-wedge geometry. The control algebra and four channel properties determine the stratum, and in each wedge the reversible directions are exactly the coherent controls. In five strata, stabilizability depends on additional channel data. One exceptional stratum admits no single control-rotated dissipative direction sufficient for stabilization, but averaging two such directions in the wedge yields stabilization.
AI.conclusion: Lie-wedge geometry provides a finer and more informative description of open-system control than the generated Lie algebra alone, revealing stabilizability properties that the Lie algebra misses, including cases where stabilization requires convex/combined use of multiple dissipative directions.

title: Sharp Target-Domain Certificates for Quantum-Kernel Advantage under Distribution Shift
comment: 42 pages, 7 figures; 16-page Supplementary Information available as ancillary material. Submitted to EPJ Quantum Technology
summary: Quantum predictive advantage under shift usually requires known target labels. We derive the assumption-free sharp identified interval for the finite-batch advantage of a fixed candidate over the best member of a prespecified fixed classical-kernel family under any bounded loss and unrestricted completions of the unaudited labels; zero-one accuracy has exact closed-form partial-label updates. Across eight security shifts, zero-label upper endpoints against 115 classical kernels span 0.002-0.088. Retrospective auditing reduces every endpoint to 0.010 with 0-33 of 500 labels, including entangling-ZZ models. Prospective corroboration on two eligible tasks met predefined criteria: four task-classifier medians require 0-3 labels (overall median 0; maximum 76), and all 20 realized effects are negative; a third task fails its feature gate. Protocol controls reverse an apparent advantage, while finite-shot noise can increase predictive distinctness without useful advantage. The framework separates protocol validity, target predictive indispensability, and quantum relevance.

AI.tldr: The paper derives an assumption-free sharp identified interval for finite-batch quantum predictive advantage and uses it to audit claims that quantum models outperform classical kernels under distribution shift, showing most apparent advantages collapse to near-zero after small amounts of label supervision.
AI.motivation: Claims of quantum predictive advantage under shift often rely on known target labels, which makes the evaluation assumption-laden and potentially circular. The authors aim to remove that dependence and obtain a clean, assumption-free bound on the advantage of a quantum candidate over the best member of a fixed classical-kernel family.
AI.method: They construct a sharp identified interval for the finite-batch advantage under bounded loss and unrestricted completions of unaudited labels, with exact closed-form partial-label updates for zero-one accuracy. They evaluate across eight security shifts against 115 classical kernels, add retrospective auditing with a small number of inspected labels, and run prospective corroboration on eligible tasks using a feature gate.
AI.result: Zero-label upper endpoints span 0.002-0.088 across the eight shifts. Retrospective auditing reduces every endpoint to 0.010 using only 0-33 of 500 labels, including entangling-ZZ models. In prospective tests, four task-classifier medians require 0-3 labels (overall median 0; maximum 76), all 20 realized effects are negative, and a third task fails its feature gate. Protocol controls reverse an apparent advantage, and finite-shot noise can raise predictive distinctness without yielding useful advantage.
AI.conclusion: The framework cleanly separates protocol validity, target predictive indispensability, and quantum relevance, providing a rigorous way to evaluate quantum predictive advantage under shift and preventing overstatement from label-informed or noisy evaluations.

title: Exact Posterior Prediction from Product Haar Measurements and a Randomized-Mesh Maximum-Likelihood Bridge
summary: We study prediction of one unmeasured copy of an unknown finite-dimensional pure quantum state after independently measuring the observed copies with the one-copy Haar POVM. For the resulting fixed separable observation, the Bayes predictive state under quantum relative-entropy loss is the full-rank posterior mean. We evaluate it exactly through permanents of minors of the outcome Gram matrix, prove positivity and normalization of the permanent representation, and establish minimaxity among decision rules based on these fixed outcomes. Using Hilbert--Schmidt projection of the posterior mean and an exactly analyzed linear-inversion competitor, we prove a finite-sample posterior-purity bound and an explicit relative-entropy guarantee with sample count $O((d^2/ε)\log(d/ε))$. Using the exact collective benchmarks proved in a companion paper, we also obtain entropy and posterior-purity comparisons. To connect the fine product data to a regular ray-valued experiment without assuming deterministic finite-sample uniqueness, we draw one random orientation for a finite projective mesh, retain it for the entire sample, and apply a selected finite-alphabet MLE in the resulting reference experiment. A nested recovering mesh uniformly recovers the fine Fisher information. Consequently every sufficiently fine fixed mesh gives a regular finite-alphabet model. Its selected MLE has Haar-averaged inverse-Fisher coefficient $\overline a_k$, and refining the mesh after the fixed-mesh large-sample limit makes $\overline a_k$ approach $d-1$. This yields epsilon-optimal leading relative-entropy and posterior-overlap bounds for the fine posterior and the sharper fixed-dimensional asymptotic scale $(d/ε)\log(d/ε)$. The latter is not asserted as a uniform finite-sample guarantee. No deterministic finite-sample MLE uniqueness or triangular mesh schedule is used.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Bayes prediction of an unmeasured copy of a pure quantum state given independent one-copy Haar POVM measurements, computing the posterior mean exactly via permanents, proving minimaxity, and deriving relative-entropy guarantees with refined finite-sample and asymptotic rates.
AI.motivation: Predicting an unmeasured copy of an unknown pure quantum state from independently measured copies is central to quantum state estimation and prediction. The one-copy Haar POVM produces fixed separable observations, and understanding the Bayes-optimal predictive behavior under relative-entropy loss, along with finite-sample guarantees and asymptotic efficiency, is important for both theoretical foundations and practical benchmarking against collective measurement strategies.
AI.method: The authors study one-copy Haar POVM measurements and derive the Bayes predictive state under quantum relative-entropy loss as the full-rank posterior mean. They evaluate it exactly through permanents of minors of the outcome Gram matrix, prove positivity and normalization, and establish minimaxity among decision rules for fixed outcomes. They use Hilbert-Schmidt projection of the posterior mean and an exactly analyzed linear-inversion competitor. For the ray-valued experiment, they draw a random orientation for a finite projective mesh held fixed across the sample and apply a selected finite-alphabet MLE, using a nested recovering mesh and Fisher-information analysis with the Haar-averaged inverse-Fisher coefficient.
AI.result: The permanent representation of the posterior mean is proven positive and normalized, with minimaxity among fixed-outcome decision rules. A finite-sample posterior-purity bound and an explicit relative-entropy guarantee with sample count O((d^2/ε)log(d/ε)) are established. Comparisons of entropy and posterior purity against exact collective benchmarks are obtained. The refined model yields epsilon-optimal leading relative-entropy and posterior-overlap bounds for the fine posterior and the sharper asymptotic scale (d/ε)log(d/ε), with the inverse-Fisher coefficient approaching d-1 as the mesh is refined.
AI.conclusion: The fixed separable one-copy Haar POVM experiment admits an exact permanent-based posterior mean that is minimax and yields finite-sample relative-entropy guarantees. By connecting product data to a regular ray-valued experiment via a fixed random mesh and a selected finite-alphabet MLE, the authors obtain epsilon-optimal asymptotic relative-entropy and posterior-overlap bounds with leading scale (d/ε)log(d/ε), approaching the optimal coefficient d-1. No deterministic finite-sample MLE uniqueness or triangular mesh schedule is required, and the sharper asymptotic scale is not asserted as a uniform finite-sample guarantee.

title: Global and nonlocal magic of quantum many-body scars
summary: Nonergodic features of chaotic quantum many-body systems are commonly characterized through local observables, fidelity, and entanglement entropy. Here, using global and nonlocal measures of nonstabilizerness (magic), we study quantum many-body scars near infinite temperature in $(1+1)$-dimensional Abelian $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and U$(1)$ lattice gauge theories, both analytically and numerically. We derive an exact closed-form expression for the nonlocal trace distance magic solely from the Schmidt spectrum, reducing the optimization over local unitaries to a finite maximization over stabilizer-compatible Schmidt ranks. We find that scar eigenstates can exhibit extensive global magic despite their anomalously low entanglement, while retaining anomalously large nonlocal magic compared with ergodic states. We further show that constrained Hilbert spaces can generate irreducible nonlocal magic through stabilizer-incompatible Schmidt ranks, even for a flat entanglement spectrum.

AI.tldr: Using global and nonlocal measures of nonstabilizerness (magic), this work analytically and numerically characterizes quantum many-body scars in (1+1)D Abelian Z2 and U(1) lattice gauge theories, deriving an exact closed-form expression for nonlocal trace-distance magic from the Schmidt spectrum.
AI.motivation: Nonergodic features of chaotic quantum many-body systems are typically probed via local observables, fidelity, and entanglement entropy. The paper aims to introduce global and nonlocal measures of nonstabilizerness as complementary diagnostics of scar physics in lattice gauge theories.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical study of quantum many-body scars near infinite temperature in (1+1)-dimensional Abelian Z2 and U(1) lattice gauge theories. An exact closed-form expression for the nonlocal trace-distance magic is derived from the Schmidt spectrum, reducing the optimization over local unitaries to a finite maximization over stabilizer-compatible Schmidt ranks.
AI.result: Scar eigenstates exhibit extensive global magic despite anomalously low entanglement, while retaining anomalously large nonlocal magic compared with ergodic states. Constrained Hilbert spaces can generate irreducible nonlocal magic through stabilizer-incompatible Schmidt ranks, even for a flat entanglement spectrum.
AI.conclusion: Nonstabilizerness, in both global and nonlocal forms, serves as a sharp diagnostic of nonergodicity in gauge-theoretic scar states, with constrained Hilbert spaces acting as a source of irreducible nonlocal magic independent of entanglement.

title: Stellar rank under the contraction of SU(1,1) to the Heisenberg-Weyl group
summary: Under the contraction of $SU(1,1)$ to the Heisenberg-Weyl group, the zeros of the Husimi function of a state redistribute according to a single scale, and we determine which of them survive. The stellar rank of a single-mode bosonic pure state, the number of these zeros, characterises the Gaussian states on the plane through the vanishing of the rank. On the Poincaré disk, where the same construction applies to the discrete series of $SU(1,1)$, it does not, because the zero set leaves a zero-free factor undetermined. We therefore ask how the zero structure behaves in the contraction limit rather than how it should be classified at fixed Bargmann index. The entire difference between the two Hilbert spaces reduces to one weight sequence $w_k(m)=(2k)^m/(2k)_m$, whose monotonicity in $k$ drives every estimate below. The rescaled states form a normal family, every nonzero limit point lies in the Segal-Bargmann space, and those with finitely many zeros are exactly the finite-rank Fock states. The rank is upper semicontinuous, with equality precisely when all zeros scale as $O(1/\sqrt{2k})$, the scale of the coherent-state labels. A two-sided Harnack estimate pins the profile on compact sets. Separately, a family of rank $r$ degenerates if and only if the amplitudes on the lowest $r+1$ weight vectors tend to zero. Mass escapes at the edge of the rescaled disk instead, by a first-order transition of the semiclassical Husimi potential at an explicit critical coupling. Finally, the contraction limit retains exactly the lowest $2r+3$ amplitudes, and this number cannot be lowered.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how the zero structure of the Husimi function of single-mode bosonic pure states behaves under the contraction of SU(1,1) to the Heisenberg-Weyl group, showing the behaviour is governed by one weight sequence and characterized by a semiclassical first-order transition.
AI.motivation: On the plane, stellar rank (number of Husimi zeros) characterizes Gaussian states via vanishing rank, but on the Poincaré disk the same construction fails because the zero set leaves a zero-free factor undetermined. Thus the fixed-Bargmann-index classification is inadequate, motivating study of the zero structure in the contraction limit instead.
AI.method: The analysis reduces the difference between the two Hilbert spaces to a single weight sequence w_k(m)=(2k)^m/(2k)_m, whose monotonicity in k drives all estimates. Tools include normal-family compactness of rescaled states, the Segal-Bargmann space, a two-sided Harnack estimate pinning the profile on compact sets, and a semiclassical Husimi potential analysis.
AI.result: Rescaled states form a normal family; every nonzero limit point lies in the Segal-Bargmann space; finitely-zero limits are exactly finite-rank Fock states. The rank is upper semicontinuous, with equality precisely when all zeros scale as O(1/sqrt(2k)). A rank-r family degenerates iff amplitudes on the lowest r+1 weight vectors vanish. Mass escapes at the disk edge via a first-order transition of the semiclassical Husimi potential at an explicit critical coupling. The contraction limit retains exactly the lowest 2r+3 amplitudes, a bound that cannot be lowered.
AI.conclusion: The contraction limit provides the correct framework for understanding Husimi zero structure, with the stellar rank being upper semicontinuous and characterized by the scaling of zeros. The sharp retention of the lowest 2r+3 amplitudes and the first-order mass-escape transition give precise, non-improvable quantitative results.

title: Symmetry Discovery in Quantum Learning: Observable-Level and Task-Level Inference from Finite Measurements
summary: Symmetry reduces the capacity of a quantum learning model, but the imposed group must match both the measured information and the label transformation. We establish a finite-measurement theory for inferring this group from candidate transformations. The central structural result identifies observable-invisible transformations with the stabilizer of a projected state whenever the probe span is invariant. It turns recovered generators into a valid subgroup and identifies the continuous invisible space with its Lie algebra. For finite dictionaries, an unbiased shadow statistic distinguishes zero from positive squared expectation discrepancies with an inverse-gap measurement rate, improving the inverse-square-gap rate of uniform discrepancy estimation. A commuting qubit lower bound proves the gap dependence optimal at fixed snapshot scale, and simultaneous intervals support data-dependent tolerances. Task validation then tests either the joint distribution through a characteristic kernel or its encoded mean through a classical--quantum discrepancy. An exact group-average identity relates the latter to joint-state asymmetry and specifies its conversion to binary task breaking mass. Projection bias quantifies the cost of excessive symmetry, while an $\ell_1$ readout bound quantifies the capacity gained by relaxing it. At an invariant pure-state backbone, retained and nontrivial breaking sectors are Fisher-orthogonal. Ising-chain calculations connect finite-shot recovery, label-dependent symmetry, and physical sector drift. These results determine which symmetry the measurements support and provide the statistical and geometric basis for a subsequent release decision.

AI.tldr: This work develops a finite-measurement theory for inferring the correct symmetry group of a quantum learning model from candidate transformations, establishing statistical, algebraic, and geometric foundations for deciding which symmetry the measurements support.
AI.motivation: Symmetry constrains the capacity of a quantum learning model, but an imposed group must simultaneously match the measured information and the label transformation. A mismatch is costly, so one needs a principled, finite-measurement method to infer the correct group from candidate transformations.
AI.method: The paper identifies observable-invisible transformations with the stabilizer of a projected state when the probe span is invariant, turning recovered generators into a valid subgroup and matching the continuous invisible space to its Lie algebra. For finite dictionaries it uses an unbiased shadow statistic separating zero from positive squared expectation discrepancies with an inverse-gap measurement rate. Task validation uses a characteristic kernel on the joint distribution or a classical-quantum discrepancy on the encoded mean, with a group-average identity linking the latter to joint-state asymmetry. Projection bias and an l1 readout bound quantify the cost of excessive symmetry and the capacity gained by relaxing it.
AI.result: An unbiased shadow statistic achieves inverse-gap measurement rate, improving on the inverse-square-gap rate of uniform discrepancy estimation; a commuting qubit lower bound proves the gap dependence optimal at fixed snapshot scale, and simultaneous intervals support data-dependent tolerances. An exact group-average identity relates the encoded-mean discrepancy to joint-state asymmetry and specifies its conversion to binary task breaking mass. At an invariant pure-state backbone, retained and nontrivial breaking sectors are Fisher-orthogonal. Ising-chain calculations connect finite-shot recovery, label-dependent symmetry, and physical sector drift.
AI.conclusion: The results determine which symmetry the measurements support and provide the statistical and geometric basis for a subsequent release decision.

title: Projector Form of the Quantum Brachistochrone and Its Relation to Two-Boundary Quantum Algorithm Design
summary: We clarify the relation between the time-optimal quantum evolution of Carlini et al. and the coherent two-boundary optimal-control formulation recently proposed for quantum algorithm design.

AI.tldr: This work establishes a connection between the time-optimal quantum evolution approach and the coherent two-boundary optimal-control framework used for quantum algorithm design.
AI.motivation: Two distinct formalisms—the time-optimal quantum evolution of Carlini et al. and the coherent two-boundary optimal-control formulation—have been developed for quantum control and algorithm design, but their mutual relation remained unclear.
AI.method: A theoretical/comparative analysis is performed to relate the two formulations, drawing out the correspondence between them.
AI.result: The relation between the time-optimal quantum evolution of Carlini et al. and the coherent two-boundary optimal-control formulation is clarified.
AI.conclusion: The two approaches are shown to be connected, providing a unified understanding relevant to quantum algorithm design.

title: Entanglement cost of quantum depolarization
summary: Entanglement cost is the asymptotic rate of Bell pairs required to prepare a quantum state. Its regularized definition has made exact evaluation difficult, even for isotropic states (i.e., depolarized maximally entangled states). In this work, we determine the entanglement cost of every qubit isotropic state and, more generally, every two-qubit Bell-diagonal state. Our proof uses a family of suitably tuned qubit semigroups to transform a general log-Sobolev entropy bound into supporting lines of Wootters' function. A recent exact tensorization theorem of Dong et al. [arXiv:2606.17729] extends these bounds to arbitrarily many copies, yielding a general lower bound on entanglement cost. Matching this bound with the entanglement of formation also determines the exact cost for a broader class of two-qubit states. For qudit isotropic states, we derive another general lower bound from the full depolarizing $2\to 3$ norm. This bound substantially improves on the PPT-relative entropy of entanglement and nearly matches the entanglement of formation, leaving a gap of at most $2\%$ of $\log d$ that vanishes as $d$ grows. Finally, the exact qubit results and qudit bounds extend to the entanglement cost of preparing quantum depolarizing channels under both parallel and sequential strategies.

AI.tldr: This work exactly determines the entanglement cost of all two-qubit isotropic and Bell-diagonal states, and derives strong lower bounds for qudit isotropic states and quantum depolarizing channels.
AI.motivation: Entanglement cost is defined asymptotically via regularization, making exact evaluation notoriously difficult, even for the well-studied family of isotropic states. The paper aims to resolve this longstanding gap and provide exact or near-exact characterizations for qubit and qudit settings, including channel preparation costs.
AI.method: The proof employs a family of suitably tuned qubit semigroups to convert a general log-Sobolev entropy bound into supporting lines of Wootters' function, giving lower bounds on entanglement cost. A recent exact tensorization theorem of Dong et al. extends these bounds to arbitrarily many copies. For qudit isotropic states, a general lower bound is derived from the full depolarizing 2-to-3 norm. Matching with entanglement of formation yields exact costs for a broader class of two-qubit states.
AI.result: Exact entanglement cost is established for every qubit isotropic state and every two-qubit Bell-diagonal state, and for a broader class of two-qubit states. For qudit isotropic states, the new bound substantially improves on the PPT-relative entropy of entanglement and nearly matches the entanglement of formation, leaving a gap of at most 2% of log d that vanishes as d grows.
AI.conclusion: The exact qubit results and qudit bounds also extend to the entanglement cost of preparing quantum depolarizing channels under both parallel and sequential strategies, providing new insights into channel simulation costs.

title: Simultaneous Perturbation as a Spectral Filter
summary: Parameterized quantum circuits require repeated measurements to estimate objective gradients, making the number of circuit evaluations a central resource. Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) is widely used because it obtains a full gradient estimate from only two cost evaluations, independently of the number of parameters. We analyze the random perturbation for the structured Fourier landscapes generated by quantum circuits. For a finite update width, we derive the exact mode-by-mode response of the mean Rademacher estimator and show that it selectively suppresses modes involving many parameters. For general generators, the filtered mean field need not be conservative. We derive its sampling variance, compare it with Gaussian random-direction smoothing, and formulate the resulting stochastic dynamics through a Fokker--Planck equation. The non-conservative field generates acceleration to the steady state and the global minimum of the cost function by gradually decreasing the parameters in SPSA.

AI.tldr: This paper provides an analytical, spectral characterization of SPSA's Rademacher gradient estimator on structured Fourier quantum landscapes, deriving the exact mode-by-mode response, the estimator's variance, its non-conservative mean field, and a Fokker--Planck description of the training dynamics.
AI.motivation: Parameterized quantum circuits need repeated measurements to estimate objective gradients, so the number of circuit evaluations is a central resource. SPSA is attractive because it delivers a full gradient estimate from only two cost evaluations regardless of parameter count, yet its behavior on the structured Fourier landscapes produced by quantum circuits is not well understood.
AI.method: The authors analyze the random perturbation underlying SPSA on structured Fourier landscapes. For a finite update width they derive the exact mode-by-mode response of the mean Rademacher estimator, showing selective suppression of modes that involve many parameters. They then treat general generators, show the filtered mean field need not be conservative, derive its sampling variance, compare it with Gaussian random-direction smoothing, and cast the resulting stochastic dynamics as a Fokker--Planck equation.
AI.result: The mean Rademacher estimator exhibits a mode-dependent filtering effect that attenuates high-order Fourier modes coupling many parameters. For general generators the induced mean field is non-conservative. Explicit sampling-variance expressions are obtained and compared against Gaussian random-direction smoothing, and the stochastic dynamics admit a Fokker--Planck formulation.
AI.conclusion: The non-conservative field arising from Rademacher perturbation generates acceleration toward the steady state and toward the global minimum of the cost function as SPSA progressively decreases the parameters, clarifying why SPSA is effective on Fourier-structured quantum landscapes.

title: Minimax Quantum State Tomography with Periodic Clifford Measurements
summary: Quantum state tomography provides a foundation for characterizing state preparation and predicting measurement outcomes. We characterize the minimax expected trace norm risk of quantum state tomography over classes with polynomial spectral decay under randomized nonadaptive single copy measurements. Under an explicit sufficient block size condition for the two layer periodic Clifford ensemble, we establish statewise expected trace norm oracle inequalities for operator norm minimum distance and measurement weighted projected least squares, with bounds that depend on each state's actual spectral tail, while the estimators require no prior knowledge of the state's structural characteristics, including its rank, eigenbasis, or spectral structure. Over these polynomial spectral decay classes, both estimators attain the minimax expected trace norm rates up to constants. As a direct consequence, the same estimators attain the minimax rate over every fixed rank constrained class, while remaining adaptive to the unknown structural characteristics of the state. For admissible logarithmic block sizes, the periodic Clifford measurements attain these guarantees with logarithmic elementary gate depth. The main technical ingredient is a uniform bound on the fourth moment of projectors for the periodic Clifford ensemble. The bound is sharp in dimension and holds for arbitrary test states, including those entangled across blocks. Covariance concentration and positivity yield adaptive oracle bounds, while a shared rotation information argument on spectral tail packings establishes matching lower bounds. We also provide polynomial time reconstruction algorithms, numerical comparisons, and Lean formalizations of all labeled theoretical results.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the minimax expected trace norm risk of quantum state tomography over polynomial spectral decay classes using randomized nonadaptive single-copy measurements, showing that operator-norm minimum-distance and measurement-weighted projected least squares estimators achieve adaptive, statewise oracle inequalities and matching minimax rates, with efficient periodic Clifford measurements and supporting algorithms, numerics, and Lean formalizations.
AI.motivation: Quantum state tomography underlies state-prep characterization and outcome prediction, yet optimal risk behavior over structured state classes—especially with structured, experimentally feasible measurements—remains incompletely understood. The work seeks minimax optimal, adaptive estimation over polynomial spectral decay classes under single-copy randomized measurements.
AI.method: It studies randomized nonadaptive single-copy measurements, specifically a two-layer periodic Clifford ensemble under an explicit sufficient block-size condition. It proves a uniform fourth-moment bound on projectors for this ensemble (sharp in dimension, valid for arbitrary test states including block-entangled ones). Using covariance concentration and positivity, it derives statewise expected trace norm oracle inequalities for operator-norm minimum distance and measurement-weighted projected least squares, and establishes lower bounds via a shared-rotation information argument on spectral tail packings. Polynomial-time reconstruction algorithms are also provided.
AI.result: Statewise expected trace norm oracle inequalities hold with bounds depending on each state's actual spectral tail, without prior knowledge of rank, eigenbasis, or spectral structure. Both estimators attain the minimax expected trace norm rates up to constants over polynomial spectral decay classes, and consequently attain the minimax rate over every fixed rank-constrained class while remaining adaptive. For admissible logarithmic block sizes, the periodic Clifford measurements achieve these guarantees with logarithmic elementary gate depth.
AI.conclusion: The estimators are minimax optimal and adaptive over polynomial spectral decay and fixed-rank classes, realizable with logarithmic-depth periodic Clifford measurements. The key technical bound is sharp and general, and the results are supported by polynomial-time algorithms, numerical comparisons, and Lean formalizations of all labeled theoretical results.

title: Physical-Work Fluctuation Relations from Accessible Quantum Macrostates
summary: Jarzynski's equality recovers an equilibrium free-energy difference from nonequilibrium work trajectories, but its exponential average can converge very slowly because rare trajectories carry large weight. We show that coarse thermodynamic information measured at the nonequilibrium endpoint can reduce this sampling burden while keeping the same microscopic trajectories and the same free-energy target. The endpoint mean energy and a coarse spatial record define a maximum-entropy state and select one member of an exact family of fluctuation relations. That physically selected member provides an exact statistical control for the ordinary Jarzynski estimator, even when the final energy and retained record do not commute. In a finite Bose--Hubbard system, this control substantially lowers the finite-confidence sampling cost, while a small controlled departure from exact endpoint matching produces a square-root information--sampling tradeoff.

AI.tldr: Endpoint coarse thermodynamic information defines a maximum-entropy state that selects one member of an exact family of fluctuation relations, providing statistical control for the Jarzynski estimator and lowering sampling cost.
AI.motivation: Jarzynski's equality extracts equilibrium free-energy differences from nonequilibrium work trajectories, but its exponential average converges slowly because rare trajectories carry large weight. A method is needed to reduce this sampling burden while preserving the microscopic trajectories and free-energy target.
AI.method: Coarse thermodynamic information measured at the nonequilibrium endpoint (endpoint mean energy and a coarse spatial record) is used to define a maximum-entropy state, selecting one member of an exact family of fluctuation relations. This physically selected member serves as an exact statistical control for the ordinary Jarzynski estimator, even when final energy and retained record do not commute.
AI.result: In a finite Bose-Hubbard system, the control substantially lowers the finite-confidence sampling cost. A small controlled departure from exact endpoint matching yields a square-root information-sampling tradeoff.
AI.conclusion: Coarse endpoint thermodynamic information can be leveraged to reduce the sampling cost of Jarzynski's equality without changing trajectories or the free-energy target, with a square-root tradeoff emerging from controlled deviations.

title: Exact replica-sector hierarchy of multi-resolvent correlations in random free fermions
summary: The spectral weight with which a many-body eigenstate contributes to a given channel is not fixed by the smooth one-point ETH envelope, and its higher-order correlations---the connected cumulants of three and more channel-resolved spectral functions---have lacked a systematic organization. We construct one. In random free fermions, where every channel overlap is a squared Slater minor of a Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrix, the $r$-resolvent moment admits an exact replica-sector decomposition: a sum over the double-coset sectors of the orthogonal Weingarten algebra, in which the permutation sectors are the replica contraction classes and each sector value is determined by the overlap pattern of the channels and of the eigenstates. The sector coefficients follow from an exact occupancy-matrix assembly---a signed convolution over the slot permutations, a decomposition into connected blocks, and a finite-state chain transfer matrix whose local transition rules are independent of $r$ and $k$---so the sector theorem holds at arbitrary finite multiplicity, realized exactly at $r=3$ ($k=2,3,4$), $r=4$ and $r=5$ ($k=2$). The structure carries the physical hierarchy: the fully coincident sector is the projection that yields the Selberg moment ratios $q_r$, the levels are nested by exact marginalization, and the sectors are the multi-energy spectral cumulants behind the resolvent cumulants, with the irreducible self-energy vertices of the Feshbach ladder as the connected kernel. The multi-resolvent correlations of random free fermions are therefore organized, level by level, by one replica-sector algebra---an exact microscopic benchmark for the higher-order fluctuation sector of eigenstate thermalization, with its microscopic sector geometry made explicit.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a systematic replica-sector algebra that organizes higher-order spectral cumulants (channel-resolved connected correlators) in random free fermions, with an exact decomposition valid at arbitrary finite replica multiplicity and a physical hierarchy tied to Selberg moment ratios and Feshbach self-energy vertices.
AI.motivation: The spectral weight of a many-body eigenstate in a given channel is not governed by the smooth one-point ETH envelope, and the higher-order correlations of these channel-resolved spectral functions (connected cumulants of three or more) had no systematic organization. The work aims to supply such an organizing framework and an exact microscopic benchmark for the higher-order fluctuation sector of eigenstate thermalization.
AI.method: In random free fermions, where each channel overlap is a squared Slater minor of a Haar-orthogonal one-body eigenvector matrix, the r-resolvent moment is given an exact replica-sector decomposition: a sum over double-coset sectors of the orthogonal Weingarten algebra, with permutation sectors as replica contraction classes and each sector value fixed by the overlap pattern of channels and eigenstates. Sector coefficients are computed via an exact occupancy-matrix assembly: a signed convolution over slot permutations, decomposition into connected blocks, and a finite-state chain transfer matrix whose local transition rules are independent of r and k.
AI.result: The sector theorem holds at arbitrary finite multiplicity, realized exactly at r=3 (k=2,3,4), r=4 and r=5 (k=2). A physical hierarchy emerges: the fully coincident sector is the projection yielding the Selberg moment ratios q_r; levels are nested by exact marginalization; sectors are the multi-energy spectral cumulants behind the resolvent cumulants, with the irreducible self-energy vertices of the Feshbach ladder as the connected kernel.
AI.conclusion: The multi-resolvent correlations of random free fermions are organized, level by level, by a single replica-sector algebra, providing an exact microscopic benchmark for the higher-order fluctuation sector of eigenstate thermalization with its microscopic sector geometry made explicit.

title: Exact Critical Curve for Uniform Stabilizer-State Identification
comment: Related arXiv paper: arXiv:2609.13923,"Partial Stabilizer Learning under Fixed Commuting Constraints and the Absence of a Copy-Rate Discount,"establishes the first-order copy threshold for unrestricted stabilizer-state identification, but leaves the fixed-offset regime k=n+c untreated. This submission resolves that regime by determining the limiting optimal success probability
summary: The sample complexity of identifying an unknown pure stabilizer state has been a longstanding problem in quantum information. In this paper, we resolve the entire exact critical crossover for the uniform ensemble of pure $n$-qubit stabilizer states under arbitrary collective measurements and without side information. For $k=n+c$, with fixed integer $c$, the optimal success probability converges to an explicit positive series $P_{\infty}(c)$. In particular, $P_{\infty}(0)=0.1760837896\ldots$, while its two tails obey a quadratic-exponential law below threshold and $1-P_{\infty}(c)\sim2^{-c}$ above threshold. The pretty-good measurement is exactly optimal for every finite $n$ and $k$. The proof diagonalizes the stabilizer Gram operator through Clifford tensor-power duality and a defect filtration, including the exceptional binary sectors. The resulting integer-scale law quantifies the $n+O(1)$ copy threshold.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the exact critical crossover for identifying an unknown pure n-qubit stabilizer state from a uniform ensemble under arbitrary collective measurements, showing the optimal success probability converges to an explicit positive series P_∞(c) at k=n+c copies, with pretty-good measurement exactly optimal for all finite n and k.
AI.motivation: The sample complexity of identifying an unknown pure stabilizer state has been a longstanding open problem in quantum information. Prior work lacked a complete characterization of the exact critical crossover (the precise number of copies around n where success becomes achievable) under the most general collective measurements and without side information.
AI.method: The authors analyze the uniform ensemble of pure n-qubit stabilizer states under arbitrary collective measurements with no side information. The proof diagonalizes the stabilizer Gram operator using Clifford tensor-power duality together with a defect filtration, handling the exceptional binary sectors. They also establish exact optimality of the pretty-good measurement.
AI.result: For k = n + c with fixed integer c, the optimal success probability converges to an explicit positive series P_∞(c). Specifically, P_∞(0) = 0.1760837896..., with the two tails obeying a quadratic-exponential law below threshold and 1 − P_∞(c) ∼ 2^{−c} above threshold. The pretty-good measurement is exactly optimal for every finite n and k. The resulting integer-scale law quantifies the n + O(1) copy threshold.
AI.conclusion: The paper fully resolves the exact critical crossover for stabilizer-state identification from a uniform ensemble under collective measurements, yielding an explicit limiting success-probability series, sharp tail behaviors on both sides of threshold, and exact optimality of the pretty-good measurement, thereby characterizing the n + O(1) sample-complexity threshold.

title: A Frame-Spread Lower Bound for Quantum Entropy Estimation under Fixed Rank-One Measurements
summary: We study estimation of the von Neumann entropy of a $d$-dimensional quantum state from independent outcomes of a fixed rank-one measurement. Let $κ_ν\in[1,d+1]$ denote the normalized trace-zero frame spread; $κ_ν=1$ for exact complex projective $2$-designs. For any fixed rank-one measurement and $n\le c_2d^2/κ_ν$, the minimax mean-squared error is at least $c_1\log^2\{d^2/(κ_νn)\}$. For bounded frame spread and every fixed $0<a<2$, the minimax risk is of order $\log^2 d$ throughout $n\lesssim d^{2-a}$; hence fixed uniform accuracy requires $Ω(d^2)$ observations. Existing tomography bounds give bounded risk from $O(d^3\log^3 d)$ observations for finite equal-weight exact designs and the Haar covariant measurement, while the intermediate minimax regime remains open. The results concern a fixed measurement repeated independently across copies; adaptive and collective protocols, and protocols that reuse common randomness across copies, are not covered.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes minimax lower bounds for estimating von Neumann entropy from independent outcomes of a fixed rank-one measurement, showing that Ω(d²)—and more precisely order log²d risk up to n ≲ d^{2-a}—is unavoidable for bounded frame spread.
AI.motivation: Estimating the von Neumann entropy of a d-dimensional quantum state is a central problem in quantum information, but prior work has mostly addressed achievability (upper bounds) via tomography and special measurements. The minimax behavior for a fixed, generic rank-one measurement across a wide sample-size regime was not established, motivating sharp lower bounds that characterize the fundamental difficulty.
AI.method: The analysis uses the normalized trace-zero frame spread κ_ν ∈ [1, d+1]—equal to 1 for exact complex projective 2-designs—as the key parameter of a fixed rank-one measurement. Minimax mean-squared error lower bounds are derived for n ≤ c₂d²/κ_ν, and the bounded-frame-spread regime is analyzed to pin the order of the risk across sample sizes up to n ≲ d^{2-a} for every fixed 0 < a < 2.
AI.result: For any fixed rank-one measurement and n ≤ c₂d²/κ_ν, the minimax MSE is at least c₁ log²{d²/(κ_ν n)}. For bounded frame spread and every fixed 0 < a < 2, the minimax risk is of order log²d throughout n ≲ d^{2-a}, implying that fixed uniform accuracy requires Ω(d²) observations. This contrasts with existing tomography upper bounds that achieve bounded risk from O(d³ log³ d) observations for finite equal-weight exact designs and the Haar covariant measurement.
AI.conclusion: Fixed rank-one measurements exhibit an intrinsic Ω(d²) sample-complexity barrier for uniformly accurate von Neumann entropy estimation when frame spread is bounded, with minimax risk order log²d over a broad sample-size range. The intermediate regime between Ω(d²) and O(d³ log³ d) remains open. The results apply to a fixed measurement repeated independently; adaptive and collective protocols, and protocols reusing common randomness across copies, are not covered.

title: Frame dependence of Kochen-Specker contextuality for relativistic spin systems
summary: We ask whether Kochen-Specker contextuality is Lorentz invariant. On the full Hilbert space, it is, since boosts act unitarily. Restricted to spin, it is not: momentum acts as an environment applying momentum-dependent Wigner rotations, leaving spin observables unsharp and breaking the operator identities behind state-independent contextuality. For spin $1/2$ one scalar governs the loss, the packet average $Δ$ of $\sin^2(θ_W/2)$ (where $θ_W$ is the Wigner angle); for any spin, a ray degrades at a rate set by its spin variance transverse to the boost. In the spin-only account, the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom fails for every $Δ>0$; the Yu-Oh set loses contextuality between $Δ\approx0.008$ and $0.016$, with state independence going first; the Peres-Mermin square loses contextuality at $Δ\approx0.059$ or $0.074$ by orientation; singlet CHSH loses nonlocality for $Δ\geq0.159$; and a GHZ-state OR gate loses Raussendorf's contextuality certificate at $Δ\approx0.206$. A $q$-plate implements the channel exactly on photon polarisation, with a retardation in place of the rapidity, so the nonlocality, GHZ and aimed-source results are testable without motion.

AI.tldr: Kochen-Specker contextuality is Lorentz invariant on the full Hilbert space but not for spin alone: boosts induce momentum-dependent Wigner rotations that unsharpen spin observables, breaking the operator identities behind state-independent contextuality. A single scalar controls the loss for spin-1/2, and thresholds are computed for several contextuality/nonlocality tests, with an experimental realization via a q-plate.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether Kochen-Specker contextuality survives Lorentz boosts. While boosts act unitarily (and thus preserve contextuality) on the full Hilbert space, restricting attention to the spin degree of freedom traces out momentum, which may degrade contextuality. The goal is to quantify how relativistic motion affects foundational quantum-information resources.
AI.method: Treat momentum as an environment applying momentum-dependent Wigner rotations to spin, yielding unsharp spin observables and breaking the operator identities underlying state-independent contextuality. For spin-1/2, characterize the degradation by one scalar: the packet average Δ of sin²(θ_W/2), where θ_W is the Wigner angle. For general spin, the degradation rate of a ray is set by its spin variance transverse to the boost. Analyze implications for the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom, the Yu-Oh set, the Peres-Mermin square, singlet CHSH, and a GHZ-state OR gate. Propose a q-plate, which implements the channel exactly on photon polarisation with retardation replacing rapidity.
AI.result: In the spin-only account: the Free Will Theorem's SPIN axiom fails for every Δ>0; the Yu-Oh set loses contextuality between Δ≈0.008 and 0.016, with state independence lost first; the Peres-Mermin square loses contextuality at Δ≈0.059 or 0.074 depending on orientation; singlet CHSH loses nonlocality for Δ≥0.159; and a GHZ-state OR gate loses Raussendorf's contextuality certificate at Δ≈0.206.
AI.conclusion: Kochen-Specker contextuality is Lorentz invariant only on the full Hilbert space; restricted to spin it is not, due to momentum-induced Wigner rotations. The degradation is governed by Δ (spin-1/2) or transverse spin variance (general spin), producing concrete thresholds for several contextuality and nonlocality tests. A q-plate reproduces the channel exactly on photon polarisation, making the nonlocality, GHZ, and aimed-source predictions testable without actual motion.

title: Nonlinear collective-spin dynamics for quantum-enhanced sensing in solid-state platforms
summary: Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising platforms for quantum-enhanced sensing. In systems such as nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, donor spins in silicon, and magnetic materials, interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that improve measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. This tutorial develops an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding these effects through nonlinear collective-spin dynamics. We show how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states. We then connect these ideal collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, discussing how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations. The tutorial focuses on a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing, rather than a comprehensive comparison of experimental platforms or a practical guide to sensing experiments.

AI.tldr: This tutorial presents an intuitive, materials-oriented framework for understanding quantum-enhanced sensing in collective spin systems via nonlinear collective-spin dynamics, linking idealized phase-space descriptions to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state platforms.
AI.motivation: Collective spin systems in solid-state materials are promising for quantum-enhanced sensing, where interactions among many spins can generate collective quantum correlations that push measurement precision beyond the standard quantum limit. There is a need for an accessible, materials-focused understanding of how nonlinear collective-spin dynamics underpin these enhancements.
AI.method: The authors develop a tutorial-level framework centered on nonlinear collective-spin dynamics, showing how nonlinear interactions reshape collective spin states in phase space, redistribute quantum fluctuations, and generate metrologically useful states such as spin-squeezed and entangled states.
AI.result: The tutorial connects idealized collective dynamics to microscopic interactions and realistic solid-state systems, and discusses how interaction strength, disorder, decoherence, and experimental control affect sensing performance. Different platforms and experiments are compared to highlight key material properties, advantages, and limitations.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a materials-oriented understanding of nonlinear collective-spin sensing rather than a comprehensive platform comparison or practical sensing guide.

title: Quantum gates from the middle convolution of twisted Burau representations
summary:
We study braid representations obtained from character-twisted Burau inputs by the Katz-Long-Moody (KLM) construction, which corresponds to multiplicative middle convolution for KZ-type equations. For $n\ge2$, let $q=e^{2πia}$, $τ=e^{2πic}$, where $a,c>0$ and $nc+(n+1)a<1$. Known form and signature results give a positive-definite invariant form for $λ=e^{2πil}$, $0<l<1-nc-(n+1)a$. For fixed input, unitary realizations are unique up to simultaneous unitary conjugation. We address two questions.
  First, we determine spectra and invariant summands of the $M=n(n+1)$-dimensional output. The generator spectrum recovers $(q,τ)$. The output decomposes into two trivial and two reduced Burau summands, and an $n(n-1)$-dimensional summand isomorphic to Long's reduced construction, generically irreducible for $n=3,4$. If $a$ or $c$ is irrational, every generator is non-Clifford in every finite-dimensional Weyl-Heisenberg frame; if $1,a,c$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$, every generator is entangling for every nontrivial bipartition. The full braid image is not projectively dense. For general positive-definite unitary inputs, irreducibility of the full braid output at a nonexceptional parameter forces the free-group input operators to commute.
  Second, we construct one orthonormal basis giving each generator one block of size $2(n+1)$, $n-2$ blocks of size two, and identity elsewhere. Each generator is a product of $2n$ rank-one phase reflections and, in a fixed binary encoding, an $O(M)$-length word in one-qubit unitaries and CNOTs, without auxiliary qubits and including direction preparation and its inverse. We give finite-alphabet approximation, conditioning and error bounds, and a matched-resource comparison with a Quantum Shannon reference compiler. The gate bound is exponential in the encoded qubit count and excludes classical preprocessing.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes character-twisted Burau braid representations built via the Katz-Long-Moody construction, determining their spectra, invariant summands, and entanglement/Clifford properties, and constructs an explicit orthonormal basis giving a structured block decomposition with explicit gate-count and error bounds for a binary-encoded quantum circuit implementation.
AI.motivation: Character-twisted Burau inputs under the KLM construction correspond to multiplicative middle convolution for KZ-type equations, and understanding the resulting unitary braid representations is important both for representation theory and for quantum computation (entangling gates, non-Clifford resources, circuit synthesis). Prior forms and signature results gave positive-definite invariant forms but left open the spectral decomposition, reducibility, and explicit gate-level realization of the output representations.
AI.method: Fix q=e^{2πia}, τ=e^{2πic} with a,c>0 and nc+(n+1)a<1, and λ=e^{2πil} with 0<l<1-nc-(n+1)a, giving a positive-definite invariant form and unitary realizations unique up to simultaneous unitary conjugation. The authors compute the spectra and invariant summands of the M=n(n+1)-dimensional output, decompose it into trivial and reduced Burau summands plus an n(n-1)-dimensional Long-type summand, and analyze non-Clifford behavior in Weyl-Heisenberg frames, entangling properties across bipartitions, and density of the braid image. They then construct an orthonormal basis yielding a block decomposition (one 2(n+1) block, n-2 size-two blocks, identity elsewhere), express each generator as a product of 2n rank-one phase reflections, and give an O(M)-length one-qubit-unitary-plus-CNOT word using a fixed binary encoding, with finite-alphabet approximation, conditioning, and error bounds and a matched-resource comparison to a Quantum Shannon reference compiler.
AI.result: The generator spectrum recovers (q,τ). The M=n(n+1)-dimensional output splits into two trivial and two reduced Burau summands plus an n(n-1)-dimensional summand isomorphic to Long's reduced construction, generically irreducible for n=3,4. If a or c is irrational, every generator is non-Clifford in every finite-dimensional Weyl-Heisenberg frame; if 1,a,c are Q-linearly independent, every generator is entangling for every nontrivial bipartition. The full braid image is not projectively dense. For general positive-definite unitary inputs, irreducibility of the full braid output at a nonexceptional parameter forces the free-group input operators to commute. In the constructed basis, each generator is a product of 2n rank-one phase reflections and an O(M)-length word in one-qubit unitaries and CNOTs without auxiliary qubits; finite-alphabet approximation, conditioning, and error bounds are given, with the gate bound exponential in the encoded qubit count and excluding classical preprocessing.
AI.conclusion: The KLM output from character-twisted Burau inputs has an explicit, rigid structure—spectrum determined by (q,τ), a fixed decomposition into trivial, reduced Burau, and Long-type summands, and strong non-Clifford and entangling guarantees—while its braid image is never projectively dense and irreducibility imposes commutativity on the input operators. A concrete orthonormal basis yields a simple block form and an O(M)-length one-qubit-unitary-plus-CNOT circuit (no ancillas), with rigorous approximation/error bounds, though the gate bound grows exponentially in the encoded qubit count.

title: Hidden-State Updates and observable-record composition in retrocausal models
summary: A hidden-variable model can reproduce context-independent individual readouts while failing to preserve observable records when devices are connected or reused. We distinguish two composition requirements. For a finite family of nonnegative instrument matrices, an invariant space generated by normalization defects characterizes unit continuation mass under every finite adaptive policy. Its annihilator defines the maximal admissible positive cone closed under outcome-conditioned updates. A separate observation space characterizes indistinguishability of context-dependent hidden preparations under joint readout. A finite-state example passes every fixed sequence but fails under outcome-dependent stopping. For a wrapped-Cauchy spin source with an explicitly stipulated unchanged-source passive extension, two individually fair probes acquire a setting-dependent agreement probability with contrast $ε^2\operatorname{sech}(2g)/4$. More generally, protection under one and two identical uses forces a continuous binary passive response to be constant; measurable two-valued exceptions remain possible. Exact rational calculations, exhaustive finite-policy experiments, continuous source sampling, and quadrature test the stated examples. The criteria apply to specified instrument families and accessible records; they do not construct a microscopic detector or establish consistency under unrestricted network composition.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes when hidden-variable models that reproduce context-independent individual readouts fail to preserve observable records under device composition/reuse, via two composition requirements characterized by an invariant space (normalization defects) and an observation space (indistinguishability), with examples and numerical tests.
AI.motivation: Hidden-variable models can match context-independent individual readouts yet fail to preserve observable records once devices are connected or reused; a precise account of such composition-induced failures is needed.
AI.method: For a finite family of nonnegative instrument matrices, an invariant space generated by normalization defects characterizes unit continuation mass under every finite adaptive policy, and its annihilator defines the maximal admissible positive cone closed under outcome-conditioned updates. A separate observation space characterizes indistinguishability of context-dependent hidden preparations under joint readout. Verification uses exact rational calculations, exhaustive finite-policy experiments, continuous source sampling, and quadrature; a wrapped-Cauchy spin source with a stipulated unchanged-source passive extension is analyzed.
AI.result: A finite-state example passes every fixed sequence but fails under outcome-dependent stopping. For the wrapped-Cauchy spin source, two individually fair probes acquire a setting-dependent agreement probability with contrast ε²·sech(2g)/4. Protection under one and two identical uses forces a continuous binary passive response to be constant, while measurable two-valued exceptions remain possible.
AI.conclusion: The criteria apply to specified instrument families and accessible records only; they do not construct a microscopic detector or establish consistency under unrestricted network composition.

title: Finite-blocklength classical communication over the quantum erasure channel with and without classical feedback
summary: We determine the optimal success probability for transmitting a fixed number of classical messages through a finite number of uses of the quantum erasure channel, assisted by noiseless classical feedback and without initial shared entanglement. For an input dimension $d$, an erasure probability $p$, a blocklength $n$, and $M$ equiprobable messages, the optimal success probability is equal to $E[\min\{1,d^K/M\}]$, where $K$ is binomial with parameters $n$ and $1-p$. The converse allows arbitrary adaptive quantum encoders, quantum memories, and receiver instruments. Its main ingredient is an elementary dimension bound for noiseless quantum communication with classical feedback, proved by fixing the classical controls without conditioning the sender's state on the observed transcript. A classical protocol that transmits the base-$d$ digits of an integer representing the message, repeating each digit until the receiver acknowledges its reception or the prescribed blocklength is reached, attains the bound for every integer $M$. We also establish a relative-majorization property of erasure-channel outputs and exactly evaluate a hypothesis-testing converse, recovering the same numerical bound without feedback. That converse need not be achievable without feedback: four uses of the qubit erasure channel and four messages give a strict gap. A product-state code employing tetrahedral qubit states nevertheless outperforms every classical binary erasure code with these parameters. We give an explicit message-size formula and show that the bounded-remainder normal approximation and the average-success strong-converse exponent are unchanged without feedback. We also determine the feedback-assisted error exponent below capacity, prove that it agrees with the no-feedback exponent above a critical rate, and give no-feedback bounds at lower rates.

AI.tldr: The optimal success probability for transmitting M classical messages through n uses of a quantum erasure channel with classical feedback and no shared entanglement is E[min{1,d^K/M}], where K ~ Binomial(n, 1-p), and is achieved by a digit-repetition-with-acknowledgment protocol.
AI.motivation: The paper seeks a fully general, exact characterization of the best achievable success probability for classical communication over the quantum erasure channel when noiseless classical feedback is available but no shared entanglement is pre-shared, covering arbitrary adaptive quantum encoders and receivers.
AI.method: The converse relies on an elementary dimension bound for noiseless quantum communication with classical feedback, proved by fixing the classical controls without conditioning the sender's state on the observed transcript. Achievability uses a classical protocol transmitting base-d digits, repeating each digit until acknowledged or blocklength is exhausted. The authors also prove a relative-majorization property of erasure-channel outputs and exactly evaluate a hypothesis-testing converse.
AI.result: For input dimension d, erasure probability p, blocklength n, and M equiprobable messages, the optimal success probability is E[min{1, d^K/M}] with K ~ Binomial(n, 1-p). The bound is attainable for every integer M. A strict feedback/no-feedback gap exists: four uses of the qubit erasure channel with four messages. A product-state tetrahedral qubit code beats all classical binary erasure codes with those parameters. An explicit message-size formula is given; bounded-remainder normal approximation and the average-success strong-converse exponent are unchanged without feedback.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers an exact, closed-form optimal success probability for feedback-assisted classical communication over the quantum erasure channel, resolves achievability with a simple digit-repetition-acknowledgment scheme, exposes a strict advantage of feedback in the finite-blocklength regime, and characterizes the feedback-assisted error exponent below capacity, showing it coincides with the no-feedback exponent above a critical rate while providing no-feedback bounds at lower rates.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing and Error Correction vs No-Cloning
summary:
Secret sharing is ubiquitous throughout cryptography. All possible access structures are classically feasible, and in the case of threshold access structures, the protocols are even very efficient. However, when moving to the quantum setting, the no-cloning theorem shows that many access structures are impossible. In fact, no-cloning exactly characterizes feasibility: for thresholds, quantum secret sharing is possible if and only if the threshold $t$ is strictly more than $n/2$.
  In this work, we propose a variant of quantum secret sharing (QSS) where two or more identical copies of the input state are provided, but the output is only required to recover one copy. This notion circumvents the simple one-copy no-cloning obstruction, though the natural $k$-copy generalization still gives much milder obstructions. For thresholds using $k$ copies, no-cloning implies that QSS is impossible whenever $t\leq n/(k+1)$.
  It is tempting to hypothesize that no-cloning continues to exactly characterize the many-copy case. However, we show that this is not the case. We give positive results showing that multiple copies allow for going slightly beyond the single-copy obstruction: for thresholds, we construct QSS whenever $t>(n-k+1)/2$. On the other hand, we give a novel obstruction we call the Clique Path obstruction, which applies to arbitrary access structures. For thresholds, it shows that QSS is impossible whenever $t\leq (n-1)/k$. Our upper and lower bounds exactly match for $k=2$. Both our results leverage connections to the $k$-colorability of certain graphs derived from the access structure. We leave closing the gap for $k\geq 3$ copies as a fascinating direction for future work.
  Secret sharing is closely related to error correction, which can also be considered in the many-copy setting. Our results imply similar obstructions for quantum error correction for erasure channels.

AI.tldr: This work studies a many-copy variant of quantum secret sharing (QSS) and quantum error correction, where multiple identical copies of the input state are provided but only one copy must be recovered. It constructs protocols achieving thresholds $t>(n-k+1)/2$ and proves a new "Clique Path" obstruction making QSS impossible for $t\leq(n-1)/k$, with the bounds matching exactly for $k=2$.
AI.motivation: Classical secret sharing supports all access structures, but in the quantum setting the no-cloning theorem makes many access structures impossible—for threshold structures, one-copy QSS is feasible iff $t>n/2$. The natural question is whether no-cloning continues to exactly characterize feasibility when multiple copies of the input state are available, or whether additional obstructions arise.
AI.method: The authors introduce a $k$-copy variant of QSS where $k$ identical copies of the input state are given but only one copy need be reconstructed, which circumvents the simple one-copy no-cloning obstruction. They derive feasibility and impossibility results for threshold and arbitrary access structures by connecting these questions to the $k$-colorability of certain graphs derived from the access structure.
AI.result: For threshold structures with $k$ copies, no-cloning gives an impossibility for $t\leq n/(k+1)$, while the authors construct QSS whenever $t>(n-k+1)/2$. They further prove a new Clique Path obstruction applying to arbitrary access structures, which for thresholds shows impossibility when $t\leq(n-1)/k$. The upper and lower bounds exactly match for $k=2$. These results also imply analogous obstructions for quantum error correction over erasure channels.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to the tempting hypothesis, no-cloning does not exactly characterize the many-copy case. Multiple copies allow slightly surpassing the single-copy obstruction, but new obstructions (Clique Path) emerge. The threshold bounds coincide for $k=2$, and closing the gap for $k\geq3$ copies is left as an open problem.

title: Robust classical and quantum communication over almost-iid channels
summary: The independent and identically distributed (iid) paradigm for asymptotic communication through quantum channels describes $n$ uses of a channel $Φ$ by $Φ^{\otimes n}$. Since exact tensor-power behaviour is an idealization, we ask whether the asymptotic capacities of $Φ$ remain achievable for channel sequences that are almost-iid along $Φ$. We consider sequences of Choi-almost-iid channels whose normalized Choi states are Mazzola-Sutter-Renner (MSR) almost-iid along the normalized Choi state of $Φ$, with defect parameters $r_n=o(n)$. In Renner's exponential de Finetti theorem for quantum states, almost-iid states appear in the approximating mixture and motivate the MSR almost-iid class.
