Choi-almost-iid channels play the corresponding role in an exponential de Finetti theorem for quantum channels established in a companion paper. In this paper, we prove that the universal unassisted classical and quantum capacities of the class of Choi-almost-iid channels along $Φ$ equal those of the channel $Φ$. Here universality is within this class: for each rate below the relevant capacity, a code sequence depending on $Φ$ and the rate, but not on the particular channel sequence, achieves vanishing error for every sequence in the class.

AI.tldr: The asymptotic capacities of a quantum channel Φ, defined under the idealized iid tensor-power model Φ^⊗n, remain achievable for channel sequences that are "almost-iid" along Φ (Choi-almost-iid channels with MSR almost-iid normalized Choi states, defect r_n = o(n)). The universal unassisted classical and quantum capacities of this whole class equal those of Φ itself, with a single Φ-dependent code sequence achieving vanishing error for every sequence in the class.
AI.motivation: The standard iid paradigm treats n uses of a channel Φ as the exact tensor power Φ^⊗n, which is an idealization since realistic channels are never exactly iid. The paper asks whether the asymptotic classical and quantum capacities of Φ—defined via this idealization—persist for channel sequences that are only approximately iid along Φ, addressing the robustness of iid-based capacity results to realistic perturbations.
AI.method: The authors define sequences of Choi-almost-iid channels: channels whose normalized Choi states are Mazzola-Sutter-Renner (MSR) almost-iid along the normalized Choi state of Φ, with defect parameters r_n = o(n). This class is motivated by Renner's exponential de Finetti theorem for quantum states, where almost-iid states appear in the approximating mixture, and by a companion paper's exponential de Finetti theorem for quantum channels. The proof establishes that a single code sequence, depending only on Φ and the target rate (not on the specific channel sequence), achieves vanishing error uniformly over the class.
AI.result: The universal unassisted classical and quantum capacities of the class of Choi-almost-iid channels along Φ are equal to the corresponding capacities of Φ. Universality holds within the class: for every rate below the relevant capacity, one Φ-dependent, rate-dependent code sequence achieves vanishing error for every channel sequence in the class.
AI.conclusion: The idealization of exact tensor-power channel use can be relaxed to defect parameters r_n = o(n) without loss of the unassisted classical or quantum capacity: asymptotic iid-based capacities are robust and achievable universally across the almost-iid channel class, mirroring the role of almost-iid states in de Finetti-type approximations for channels.

title: Flexible rigidity: Compiling generic trusted-preparation protocols into sequential device-independent protocols
summary:
We give a generic compiler for turning a wide class of device-dependent protocols with trusted state preparation into sequential device-independent protocols. In order for our compiler to apply, the trusted-preparation protocol needs to satisfy certain minimal conditions: having an entanglement-based realization in the first place, and the entanglement-based realization corresponding to the optimal strategy of any non-local game that satisfies a fairly weak rigidity condition. We apply our generic compiler to give sequential device-independent protocols for uncloneable encryption, copy-protection of point functions, and blind randomness expansion.
  Our technical contribution is a new class of rigidity theorems based on Rényi divergences, with flexible cryptographic applications. They allow our compiler to achieve a constant rate (i.e., the ratio of trusted states prepared to device uses), while tolerating a constant level of noise per device usage. This overcomes a fundamental scaling obstacle faced by previous rigidity theorems for trace distance or fidelity. For the generic sequential case, our proof is based on the sharp-divergence chain rule by Fawzi and Fawzi (2021), which suffices for a constant but fairly low rate. In the special case when the devices retain no memory, we improve the rates by deriving a novel subadditivity property for a modified channel sandwiched divergence, which may be of independent interest. Finally, as a prospect for future improvements, we also prove a chain rule for the iterated-mean divergences from Brown, Fawzi and Fawzi (2021).

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generic compiler transforming device-dependent protocols (with trusted state preparation) into sequential device-independent protocols for uncloneable encryption, copy-protection of point functions, and blind randomness expansion, enabled by new Rényi-divergence-based rigidity theorems achieving constant rate under constant noise.
AI.motivation: Existing rigidity theorems based on trace distance or fidelity face a fundamental scaling obstacle: they cannot simultaneously achieve a constant rate of trusted states to device uses while tolerating constant noise. This limits the efficiency of sequential device-independent protocols built from device-dependent trusted-preparation schemes.
AI.method: The authors define a generic compiler applicable when the trusted-preparation protocol admits an entanglement-based realization that matches the optimal strategy of any non-local game satisfying a weak rigidity condition. Technically, they introduce a new class of rigidity theorems based on Rényi divergences; for the generic sequential case the proof uses the sharp-divergence chain rule (Fawzi and Fawzi, 2021). For memoryless devices, rates are improved via a novel subadditivity property of a modified channel sandwiched divergence. They also prove a chain rule for iterated-mean divergences (Brown, Fawzi, Fawzi, 2021).
AI.result: The compiler yields sequential device-independent protocols for uncloneable encryption, copy-protection of point functions, and blind randomness expansion. The new rigidity theorems achieve a constant rate (trusted states prepared to device uses) while tolerating a constant noise level per device usage, overcoming the scaling obstacle of prior trace-distance/fidelity rigidity results. Reduced rates apply in the generic case, with improved rates for memoryless devices.
AI.conclusion: Rényi-divergence-based rigidity theorems enable a generic compiler from device-dependent (trusted-preparation) protocols to sequential device-independent protocols with constant-rate and constant-noise tolerance. The subadditivity property for a modified channel sandwiched divergence and the chain rule for iterated-mean divergences are of independent interest and point toward future rate improvements.

title: Learning Local Fermionic Lindbladians under Parity Superselection
summary: Parity superselection forbids direct measurement of odd Majorana observables. We learn time-independent, parity-covariant, $k$-mode-local Lindbladians on $m$ modes using even preparations and measurements with uninterrupted short-time evolution. Internal markers turn odd probes into even observables, and pair measurements among three separated markers calibrate their dynamical contributions. Signed Fierz inversion recovers canonical coefficients, while semidefinite fitting yields a valid generator. For finite-range models on known bounded-degree graphs with suitable marker access and a supplied weighted-strength bound $\barα$, entrywise error $\varepsilon$ is achieved using $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\barα^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(m/δ))$ samples, without external modes or known nonzero coefficient locations. Recovery to diamond-norm error $\varepsilon$ costs an additional factor $m^2$, matching lower bounds for short-time experiments on fresh systems up to logarithmic and fixed geometric factors. Without a supplied graph, one idle ancillary mode per system mode and potentially nonlocal pair operations give total absolute coefficient error at most $\varepsilon$ per mode using $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_k(\barα^2\mathsf d^2m^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(m/δ))$ samples, under a supplied approximate coefficient-degree bound $\mathsf d$ and controlled weak-coefficient tails. All guarantees hold with probability at least $1-δ$. For geometric models, fixed-support even observables can be predicted with logarithmic system-size sample complexity at fixed time and accuracy. We also give finite-volume and exponential-tail extensions.

AI.tldr: This paper develops sample-efficient protocols for learning parity-covariant, k-mode-local Lindbladians on m fermionic modes despite parity superselection, using even preparations/measurements, internal markers, signed Fierz inversion, and semidefinite fitting, with rigorous sample-complexity and diamond-norm guarantees.
AI.motivation: Parity superselection forbids direct measurement of odd Majorana observables, obstructing standard tomography of fermionic Lindbladians. The goal is to learn physically valid generators (time-independent, parity-covariant, k-mode-local Lindbladians) using only even preparations and measurements, without external modes or prior knowledge of nonzero coefficient locations.
AI.method: Internal markers convert odd probes into even observables; pair measurements among three separated markers calibrate marker dynamical contributions. Signed Fierz inversion recovers canonical coefficients, while semidefinite fitting enforces a valid (completely positive) generator. Learning proceeds via uninterrupted short-time evolution. For unknown graphs, one idle ancillary mode per system mode plus potentially nonlocal pair operations are used, under a supplied approximate coefficient-degree bound and controlled weak-coefficient tails.
AI.result: On known bounded-degree finite-range graphs with suitable marker access and weighted-strength bound ᾱ, entrywise error ε requires Õ(ᾱ²ε⁻²log(m/δ)) samples; diamond-norm error ε costs an extra m² factor, matching lower bounds for short-time experiments up to logarithmic/fixed geometric factors. Without a known graph, total absolute coefficient error ≤ ε per mode is achieved with Õ_k(ᾱ²d²m^⌊k/2⌋ε⁻²log(m/δ)) samples. Guarantees hold with probability ≥ 1−δ; geometric models allow logarithmic-size prediction of fixed-support even observables.
AI.conclusion: Parity-covariant k-local Lindbladian learning is achievable under superselection with near-optimal sample complexity, both graph-aware and graph-agnostic, and extends to finite-volume and exponential-tail settings. Geometric locality further enables system-size-independent prediction of fixed observables.

title: Clifford-hierarchy stabilizer formalism with applications to twisted quantum doubles
summary: Recent work has shown that quantum double models can be used to circumvent the Bravyi-Koenig bound. In particular, this is achieved through code-switching protocols in which non-Pauli stabilizer phases appear as intermediate codes. We introduce the $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer formalism, which generalizes the Pauli stabilizer formalism by combining Pauli-$X$ operators with diagonal operators drawn from a fixed level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy on prime-dimensional qudits. This yields a natural class of beyond-Pauli stabilizer models, including many twisted quantum double phases. We classify a large class of these $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer states, showing that they are uniform superpositions over affine-linear subspaces with diagonal phases. In particular, when the stabilizers of a state require operators from level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy, we show that the diagonal gates required to produce the phases in the wavefunction sit one level higher. We further show that every 2D twisted quantum double ${\cal D}^ω(\mathbb{Z}_p^n)$ with $ω$ a product of type-III cocycles and $p$ an odd prime admits a realization using only Clifford ($k=2$) stabilizers, and we conjecture that phases where $ω$ contains a type-I or type-II cocycle require level-$p$ Clifford-hierarchy stabilizers for $p$-dimensional qudits. Finally, we demonstrate that a pair of qudit toric codes may be deterministically prepared in a logical magic state by measuring $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizers. Together, these results provide a concrete stabilizer framework for topological codes beyond Pauli stabilizer models and their logical gates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer formalism, a beyond-Pauli stabilizer framework combining Pauli-$X$ operators with diagonal gates from level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy, providing a concrete approach to topological codes and logical gates that circumvent the Bravyi-Koenig bound.
AI.motivation: Quantum double models can circumvent the Bravyi-Koenig bound via code-switching protocols where non-Pauli stabilizer phases appear as intermediate codes, but a concrete and general stabilizer framework for such beyond-Pauli topological codes was lacking.
AI.method: The authors introduce the $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer formalism on prime-dimensional qudits, which generalizes the Pauli stabilizer formalism by combining Pauli-$X$ operators with diagonal operators from a fixed level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy. They then classify a large class of these stabilizer states.
AI.result: The $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizer states are classified as uniform superpositions over affine-linear subspaces with diagonal phases; when stabilizers require level-$k$ Clifford-hierarchy operators, the diagonal gates producing the wavefunction phases sit one level higher. Every 2D twisted quantum double ${\cal D}^\omega(\mathbb{Z}_p^n)$ with $\omega$ a product of type-III cocycles and $p$ an odd prime admits a realization using only Clifford ($k=2$) stabilizers, while phases with type-I or type-II cocycles are conjectured to require level-$p$ stabilizers for $p$-dimensional qudits. A pair of qudit toric codes can be deterministically prepared in a logical magic state by measuring $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ stabilizers.
AI.conclusion: The $X\mathcal C^{(k)}_d$ framework offers a concrete stabilizer formalism for topological codes beyond Pauli stabilizer models and their logical gates, and enables deterministic preparation of logical magic states in qudit toric codes.

title: Factor Code Networks
summary:
For a quantum code defined by an isometry $T:H_{\rm code} \to H_{\rm phys}$, an operator map is a *-homomorphism $\varphi: B(H_{\rm code}) \to B(H_{\rm phys})$ from the space of operators on the logical Hilbert space to the space of operators on the physical Hilbert space satisfying $\varphi({\cal O}) T = T {\cal O}$ for every operator ${\cal O}$ on $H_{\rm code}$. This can additionally be taken to be unital $\varphi(I_{code}) = I_{phys}$ if and only if $\dim H_{\rm code}$ divides $\dim H_{\rm phys}$. In this case, $\varphi(B(H_{\rm code})$ is a von Neumann factor subalgebra of $B(H_{\rm phys})$ and we call the pair $(T,\varphi)$ a {\it factor code}.
  A code network is a family of Hilbert spaces $\{{\cal H}_i\}$ indexed by a partially ordered set with isometries $T_{ji}:{\cal H}_i \to {\cal H}_j$ for $i < j$ satisfying $T_{kj} T_{ji} = T_{ki}$ for $i < j < k$. In this paper, we ask when this can be promoted to a {\it factor code network} by defining unital operator maps $\varphi_{ji}$ so that $(T_{ji}, \varphi_{ji})$ is a factor code and $\varphi_{kj} \varphi_{ji} = \varphi_{ki}$. We show that the divisibility conditions on Hilbert space dimensions are sufficient for any code network with a tree structure but not in general. For a diamond-shaped network, we show that promotion is possible if and only if the principle angles between $T_{42} H_2$ and $T_{43} H_3$ all have multiplicity divisible by $H_1$.
  For incomparable $i_1,i_2 < j$, we characterize when $\varphi_{j i_1} (B(H_{i_1}))$ and $\varphi_{j i_2} (B(H_{i_2}))$ commute, when they generate all of $B(H_j)$, and when they intersect only on multiples of the identity. For $i < j_1,j_2 < k$, we characterize when $\varphi_{k j_1} (B(H_{j_1})) \cap \varphi_{k j_2} (B(H_{j_2})) = \varphi_{k i} (B(H_{i}))$ and when these algebras together with $B(H_k)$ form a nondegenerate commuting square.

AI.tldr: This paper studies when a quantum code network can be promoted to a "factor code network" by defining unital *-homomorphisms satisfying consistency, characterizing this for tree and diamond structures and analyzing algebra commutativity, generation, and commuting-square relations for incomparable nodes.
AI.motivation: Operator maps φ satisfying φ(O)T = TO connect logical and physical operator algebras; the paper asks when such maps can be consistently assigned across a whole network of nested codes so that the family forms factor codes, generalizing single-code results to networks and clarifying which dimension-divisibility conditions suffice.
AI.method: Define factor codes via unital *-homomorphisms φ: B(H_code) → B(H_phys) with φ(O)T = TO, existing iff dim H_code divides dim H_phys. Introduce code networks over partially ordered sets with isometries T_{ji} obeying T_{kj}T_{ji}=T_{ki}, and ask for unital φ_{ji} making (T_{ji},φ_{ji}) factor codes with φ_{kj}φ_{ji}=φ_{ki}. Analyze tree networks, diamond networks via principal-angle multiplicities, and the algebra relations for incomparable and intermediate nodes.
AI.result: Hilbert-space dimension divisibility is sufficient for any tree-structured code network, but not in general. For a diamond network, promotion is possible iff all principal angles between T_{42}H_2 and T_{43}H_3 have multiplicities divisible by dim H_1. For incomparable i_1,i_2<j, the paper characterizes when φ_{ji_1}(B(H_{i_1})) and φ_{ji_2}(B(H_{i_2})) commute, generate all of B(H_j), or intersect only in scalar multiples of the identity; for i<j_1,j_2<k it characterizes when φ_{kj_1}(B(H_{j_1})) ∩ φ_{kj_2}(B(H_{j_2})) = φ_{ki}(B(H_i)) and when these algebras with B(H_k) form a nondegenerate commuting square.
AI.conclusion: Dimension divisibility alone guarantees promotion for tree structures but fails in general; the diamond case reveals principal-angle multiplicity conditions as the precise obstruction. The paper further provides algebraic criteria for commutativity, generation, trivial intersection, and commuting-square structure among the image algebras at incomparable and intermediate nodes, clarifying the operator-algebraic geometry of factor code networks.

title: Mixed-state phases induced by power-law quantum channels
summary: Open quantum systems can exhibit inherently mixed quantum orders, such as strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB), which have no analogue in pure states. It is generally expected that a finite-depth local quantum channel cannot induce a phase transition to SW-SSB in one spatial dimension. We circumvent this obstruction by introducing a long-range quantum channel, which implements two-body dephasing on pairs of sites with probability falling off according to a power-law in the site separation. Applying this channel to a one-parameter family of matrix product states interpolating between trivial and symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases, we construct a phase diagram that hosts trivial, mixed SPT, and SW-SSB phases with respect to Rényi-2 diagnostics. Notably, the mixed SPT phase is distinct from previously studied decohered SPT phases: it hosts two logical qubits and exhibits nonvanishing Rényi-2 string order, despite vanishing conventional string order. Through a series of mappings to a classical statistical mechanics model, we establish a direct connection between the loss of logical information and the onset of SW-SSB in this model. Finally, we consider the feasibility of experimental realization of the phenomena we have studied. We emphasize that our family of mixed states can be tuned to regimes of high purity, substantially reducing measurement overhead and enabling their experimental realization and detection on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: A long-range two-body dephasing channel induces a phase transition to strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SW-SSB) in 1D, yielding a phase diagram with trivial, mixed SPT, and SW-SSB phases.
AI.motivation: Finite-depth local quantum channels are generally expected to be unable to induce SW-SSB phase transitions in one spatial dimension, leaving a fundamental obstruction to realizing mixed quantum orders. The authors aim to circumvent this obstruction and explore inherently mixed quantum orders that have no pure-state analogue.
AI.method: The authors introduce a long-range quantum channel that implements two-body dephasing on site pairs with probability decaying as a power-law in separation. They apply it to a one-parameter family of matrix product states interpolating between trivial and SPT phases, diagnosing phases via Rényi-2 quantities, and map the model to a classical statistical mechanics model.
AI.result: The constructed phase diagram hosts trivial, mixed SPT, and SW-SSB phases with respect to Rényi-2 diagnostics. The mixed SPT phase differs from previously studied decohered SPT phases: it hosts two logical qubits and exhibits nonvanishing Rényi-2 string order despite vanishing conventional string order. The mapping establishes a direct connection between loss of logical information and the onset of SW-SSB.
AI.conclusion: Long-range dephasing overcomes the obstruction to SW-SSB in 1D, revealing a distinct mixed SPT phase and linking logical information loss to SW-SSB onset. The states can be tuned to high-purity regimes, reducing measurement overhead and enabling experimental realization and detection on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Causal Trade-Offs in Superluminal Extensions of Relativity. A no-go theorem
summary: Extensions of relativity that include superluminal reference frames have recently been proposed by Dragan and Ekert as a way to reconcile relativistic symmetry with quantum uncertainty. In this work, we develop a causal modelling framework to formally study this proposal and prove a no-go theorem demonstrating that a theory permitting superluminal reference frames can avoid superluminal signalling only if it severely constrains which spacetime regions are accessible to operational protocols, if the choice of reference frame has observable consequences or if free variables do not exist or their existence depends on the reference frame. Crucially, our result goes beyond the familiar intuition that superluminal transformations may lead to superluminal signalling; our no-go result shows that Dragan and Ekert's proposal of introducing objective uncertainty does not, by itself, eliminate this conflict. In fact, because superluminal signalling might instead be avoided by relaxing other fundamental assumptions in the presence of superluminal reference frames, the proposed objective uncertainty may not be necessary at all. Our results clarify the limitations of uncertainty-based resolutions and the causal trade-offs faced by superluminal extensions of relativity.

AI.tldr: A causal-modelling no-go theorem shows that Dragan and Ekert's superluminal reference-frame proposal avoids superluminal signalling only at the cost of severely restricting accessible spacetime regions, making frame choice observable, or eliminating frame-independent free variables; hence objective uncertainty alone does not resolve the conflict.
AI.motivation: Dragan and Ekert proposed extending relativity with superluminal reference frames and objective quantum uncertainty to reconcile relativistic symmetry with quantum theory, but whether such frames necessarily imply superluminal signalling was unclear. The paper aims to formalize and test this proposal rigorously.
AI.method: The authors develop a causal modelling framework to formally analyze theories admitting superluminal reference frames and derive a no-go theorem characterizing the conditions under which superluminal signalling is avoided.
AI.result: A theory permitting superluminal reference frames can avoid superluminal signalling only if it severely constrains which spacetime regions operational protocols can access, if the choice of reference frame has observable consequences, or if free variables do not exist or depend on the reference frame. The result goes beyond the standard intuition that superluminal transformations yield signalling: introducing objective uncertainty does not by itself eliminate the conflict.
AI.conclusion: Because superluminal signalling could instead be avoided by relaxing other fundamental assumptions, the proposed objective uncertainty may be unnecessary. The work clarifies the limits of uncertainty-based resolutions and the causal trade-offs facing superluminal extensions of relativity.

title: Quantum Algorithms for OPI Variants Beyond Locality and Classical Decodability
summary:
Regev's reduction is a quantum algorithmic framework for finding codewords satisfying nonlinear constraints by decoding the dual code. To date, applications that have not been dequantized have relied on efficient classical decoders and coordinate-wise constraints specifying a set of allowed values for each coordinate. We push past these two restrictions separately via two separate contributions.
  Our first contribution uses a quantum decoder to find solutions $\mathbf{y}\in(\mathbb{F}_q\setminus\{0\})^m$ to $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{y}=0$, where $\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{F}_q^{n\times m}$. For fixed prime $q>2$, Chen, Liu, and Zhandry (Eurocrypt 2022) solve this problem for random matrices with $m=Ω(n^2)$, a regime now covered by classical algorithms. We adapt their template to codes (spanned by the rows of $\mathbf{B}$) with a ``two-fold multiplication property'': the coordinate-wise products of pairs of codewords span a space of dimension much smaller than $m$.
  Our second contribution retains classical decoding but allows global constraints on symbol frequencies. We study ``histogram-local'' constraints, which specify the allowed numbers of occurrences of each symbol. For broad families of these constraints, we show that a uniformly random satisfying vector remains satisfying with constant probability after resampling a uniformly random coordinate. This stability provides sufficient Fourier mass at decodable Hamming weights, yielding efficient quantum algorithms for variants of optimal polynomial intersection (OPI).

AI.tldr: This paper extends Regev's reduction for quantum decoding by removing two key restrictions: it introduces a quantum decoder for codes with a two-fold multiplication property, and it enables classical decoding with global histogram-local constraints, yielding quantum algorithms for optimal polynomial intersection variants.
AI.motivation: Regev's reduction finds codewords satisfying nonlinear constraints via dual-code decoding, but prior non-dequantized applications relied on (i) efficient classical decoders and (ii) coordinate-wise constraints. The authors aim to overcome both limitations to broaden the framework's applicability.
AI.method: First contribution: adapt the Chen–Liu–Zhandry quantum decoder to solve B y = 0 over (F_q\{0})^m for codes with a two-fold multiplication property, where coordinate-wise products of codeword pairs span a much smaller space than m. Second contribution: retain classical decoding while allowing global histogram-local constraints on symbol frequencies; prove stability under uniformly resampling one coordinate, giving Fourier mass at decodable Hamming weights.
AI.result: A quantum decoder works for structured codes beyond the prior random-matrix regime m=Ω(n^2) (which is now classically solvable), and histogram-local constraints yield efficient quantum algorithms for variants of optimal polynomial intersection (OPI).
AI.conclusion: Regev's reduction can be pushed past both the classical-decoder and coordinate-wise-constraint restrictions separately, expanding the set of problems amenable to quantum speedups.

title: Graph Neural Post-selection for Quantum Error Correction
summary: Post-selection improves the logical reliability of quantum computation by rejecting shots which are likely to result in logical failure. We introduce graph neural networks that predict decoder failure without additional decoder executions, using only syndromes, and for high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, existing belief-propagation posteriors. We evaluate rotated surface and bivariate bicycle (BB) code memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise. Retaining 90% of shots gives approximately 3700x and 740x reductions in logical error rates for [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] BB codes at realistic physical error rates. For the distance 5 surface code at physical noise p=0.003, our neural post-selector achieves logical error suppression comparable to the leading complementary gap method without running the decoder.

AI.tldr: Graph neural networks predict decoder failure from syndromes alone (and BP posteriors for qLDPC codes), enabling post-selection that suppresses logical errors without extra decoder runs.
AI.motivation: Post-selection improves logical reliability by rejecting failure-prone shots, but existing methods (e.g., complementary gap) require running the decoder, adding cost.
AI.method: GNNs predict decoder failure using only syndromes (plus existing belief-propagation posteriors for high-rate qLDPC codes), avoiding additional decoder executions. Evaluated on rotated surface and bivariate bicycle (BB) code memories under uniform depolarising circuit-level noise.
AI.result: Retaining 90% of shots yields ~3700x and ~740x logical error rate reductions for [[72,12,6]] and [[144,12,12]] BB codes at realistic physical error rates. For the distance-5 surface code at p=0.003, the neural post-selector matches the leading complementary gap method's logical error suppression without running the decoder.
AI.conclusion: Learning-based, decoder-free post-selection is effective across surface and high-rate qLDPC codes, achieving strong logical error suppression at modest shot rejection.

title: Noisy Quantum Query Complexity via Fractional Block Sensitivity
summary:
We study quantum query complexity under several models of imperfect oracle access, and develop lower bounds through a common framework based on fractional block sensitivity (\(\fbs\)).
  For a negligent oracle that applies the correct query with probability \(1-p\), we prove a lower bound in terms of \(\fbs(f,0^n)\). We also show, perhaps surprisingly, that negligence need not destroy quantum speedups: any function \(f\) can be transformed into a partial function \(f'\) whose negligent query complexity essentially preserves the quantum query complexity of \(f\). This gives partial functions with exponential quantum speedups even under negligent queries, and in particular rules out a general lower bound in terms of \(\fbs(f)\) for partial functions in this model.
  For two other models, we obtain general lower bounds in terms of \(\fbs(f)\) for all Boolean functions. For hybrid algorithms using \(Q\) coherent and \(C\) classical queries, we prove the tradeoff \(C+Q^2=Ω(\fbs(f))\). For an IID dephasing noisy model where each query dephases the query-index register at rate \(p\) independently, we prove \(Ω\!\left(p\,\fbs(f)\right)\) queries are necessary.
  Finally, we introduce a broader family of time-varying dephasing models and identify a variational resource that is always lower bounded by \(\fbs(f)\). Computing this resource reduces to a convex optimization problem, providing a simple way to derive lower bounds for new noise schedules. As applications, we recover the hybrid and IID dephasing bounds and determine the query complexity of unstructured search when the dephasing rate grows over time.

AI.tldr: This work establishes quantum query lower bounds under imperfect oracle access via a fractional block sensitivity (fbs) framework, covering negligent oracles, hybrid coherent/classical algorithms, and IID dephasing noise, while showing that negligence can preserve exponential quantum speedups.
AI.motivation: Real quantum oracles are imperfect—queries may fail, dephase, or be classically simulated. Existing lower-bound techniques (e.g., based on block sensitivity) do not directly handle such noisy oracle models, and it is unclear whether standard adversarial bounds still hold. The paper aims to develop a unified framework for proving query lower bounds across several imperfect-oracle models and to clarify when noise destroys or preserves quantum speedups.
AI.method: The authors use fractional block sensitivity (fbs) as a common lower-bound measure. They analyze three imperfect-oracle models: (1) a negligent oracle applying the correct query with probability 1-p, proving bounds via fbs(f,0^n) and constructing a partial-function transformation f' preserving quantum query complexity; (2) hybrid algorithms with Q coherent and C classical queries, proving C + Q^2 = Ω(fbs(f)); (3) an IID dephasing model where each query dephases the index register at rate p independently, proving Ω(p·fbs(f)) queries are needed. They further introduce time-varying dephasing models and identify a variational resource lower-bounded by fbs(f), computable via convex optimization.
AI.result: For negligent oracles, a lower bound in terms of fbs(f,0^n) is proven, and a partial-function transformation shows exponential quantum speedups can survive negligence, ruling out a general fbs(f) lower bound for partial functions. For hybrid algorithms, the tradeoff C + Q^2 = Ω(fbs(f)) is established for all Boolean functions. For IID dephasing, Ω(p·fbs(f)) queries are necessary. The variational resource yields a convex optimization that recovers the hybrid and IID bounds and determines the query complexity of unstructured search under time-growing dephasing rates.
AI.conclusion: Fractional block sensitivity provides a unified framework for quantum query lower bounds under imperfect oracle access. While noise generally incurs fbs-based penalties in hybrid and dephasing models, negligence does not necessarily eliminate quantum speedups. The time-varying dephasing framework offers a general, computationally tractable method for deriving bounds under new noise schedules.

title: Blind Unforgeability implies Plus-One Unforgeability
summary:
We prove that quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, settling an open question in the literature. Since plus-one unforgeability is known not to imply blind-unforgeability, our result establishes that blind-unforgeability is \emph{strictly stronger} than plus-one unforgeability in the quantum setting.
  The implication is proven using a new \emph{smoothing} technique that coherently rescales the query histories of a quantum-query algorithm in a black-box manner. This enables us to transform any successful plus-one attacker into a blind-unforgeability attacker with only inverse-polynomial loss. Our proof represents a conceptual shift from merely extracting a useful query history as in earlier attempts, which we show inevitably fails in general, to first coherently reshaping how query histories interfere.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that quantum blind-unforgeability strictly implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, resolving an open problem via a new coherent smoothing technique.
AI.motivation: Establishing the precise relationship between two quantum unforgeability notions—blind-unforgeability and plus-one unforgeability—was an open question; since the converse implication is known to fail, proving this direction would show strict separation.
AI.method: A new smoothing technique that coherently rescales the query histories of a quantum-query algorithm in a black-box manner, transforming any successful plus-one attacker into a blind-unforgeability attacker with only inverse-polynomial loss.
AI.result: Quantum blind-unforgeability implies quantum plus-one unforgeability, and combined with the known non-implication in the other direction, blind-unforgeability is strictly stronger than plus-one unforgeability in the quantum setting.
AI.conclusion: The work resolves the open question and introduces a conceptual shift from extracting a useful query history (which provably fails in general) to coherently reshaping how query histories interfere.

title: Near-Optimal Ground-State Preparation without Controlled Hamiltonian Evolutions
comment: The authors acknowledge the use of ChatGPT 5.6 and 6 for help with writing and reviewing the manuscript, including identifying technical errors and inconsistencies in earlier versions
summary: Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental tasks in quantum simulation. Existing ground-state preparation algorithms achieve near-optimal complexity using block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, raising a natural question: is controlled Hamiltonian evolution necessary, or can the same scaling be attained in the weaker access model that provides access to only uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution? We resolve this question by giving two algorithms that access the input Hamiltonian $H$ only through queries to $U_H$ and its inverse $U_H^\dagger$, where $\|H\|\leα_H$ and $τ=Θ(1/α_H)$. Given an input state with ground-state weight at least $η$ and a spectral gap of $H$ of at least $γ$, our first algorithm uses fresh copies of the input state and requires $\widetilde O(α_H/(γη))$ queries to $U_H$ and $U_H^\dagger$, while our second algorithm uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse to improve this complexity to $\widetilde O(α_H/(γ\sqrtη))$. The latter bound matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors, showing that algorithms with additional access to controlled Hamiltonian evolution cannot improve the query complexity for ground-state preparation beyond logarithmic factors. Both algorithms are based on a simple mechanism that we call the spectral descent principle, in which the algorithm starts from the input state $|ψ\rangle$ and progressively descends through the energy spectrum, moving closer to the ground state until the desired fidelity is reached. We also extend this framework to ground-state property and energy estimation and give explicit complexity guarantees for both tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that uncontrolled Hamiltonian evolution suffices for near-optimal ground-state preparation, matching known lower bounds and proving controlled Hamiltonian evolution offers no asymptotic advantage beyond logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: Ground-state preparation, energy estimation, and property estimation are fundamental quantum simulation tasks. Existing near-optimal algorithms rely on block encodings or controlled Hamiltonian evolution, leaving open whether controlled evolution is actually necessary or whether the same scaling is achievable with weaker access to only uncontrolled evolution.
AI.method: The authors introduce the spectral descent principle and give two algorithms accessing H only via U_H and U_H^dagger (with ||H|| <= alpha_H, tau = Theta(1/alpha_H)). The first uses fresh copies of the input state; the second uses coherent access to the input-state preparation unitary and its inverse. Both progressively descend the energy spectrum from the input state toward the ground state.
AI.result: For an input state with ground-state weight >= eta and spectral gap >= gamma, the first algorithm needs Otilde(alpha_H/(gamma*eta)) queries; the second achieves Otilde(alpha_H/(gamma*sqrt(eta))). The latter matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors. The framework is also extended to ground-state property and energy estimation with explicit complexity guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Controlled Hamiltonian evolution is not necessary: uncontrolled evolution attains near-optimal ground-state preparation complexity, and additional access to controlled evolution cannot improve query complexity beyond logarithmic factors.

title: First-quantized quantum simulation with non-local potentials by matrix-product-state encoding
summary: Quantum simulations based on first-quantized approaches can offer lower space and gate complexities than second-quantized approaches. The gate requirements for these simulations can be further reduced by employing pseudopotentials, a technique widely used in classical quantum chemistry calculations to decrease the number of simulated electrons. However, implementing pseudopotentials in quantum circuits remains challenging due to their non-local nature. In this study, we proposed a method to efficiently implement non-local potentials using matrix product state (MPS) encoding. MPS encoding allows us to efficiently implement a Trotter step operator with a circuit depth of $O(\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}}) n^{\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}})} + 8Lnn_{\mathrm{atom}}χ^2 + 2n^2)$, where $\mathrm{deg}(V_{\mathrm{loc}})$ is the degree of the polynomial local potential, $n_{\mathrm{atom}}$ is the number of atoms in the system, $L$ is the maximum number of projector functions across all atoms, and $n$ is the number of qubits used to represent the binary-encoded wave function in one-dimensional space. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a model of the ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse. Our results showed that MPS encoding significantly reduces the required circuit depth compared to a direct unitary decomposition, providing a pathway for practical first-quantized simulations.

AI.tldr: This work implements non-local pseudopotentials in first-quantized quantum simulation using matrix product state (MPS) encoding, achieving reduced circuit depth demonstrated on a 1D hydrogen ionization model.
AI.motivation: First-quantized quantum simulations have lower space and gate complexity than second-quantized approaches, and pseudopotentials can further reduce gate requirements by decreasing simulated electrons. However, pseudopotentials are non-local, making them difficult to implement on quantum circuits.
AI.method: The authors encode non-local potentials via matrix product state (MPS) encoding, enabling efficient implementation of a Trotter step operator with circuit depth O(deg(V_loc) n^{deg(V_loc)} + 8L n n_atom χ² + 2n²), where deg(V_loc) is the local potential polynomial degree, n_atom the atom count, L the max number of projector functions per atom, and n the qubits for the binary-encoded 1D wave function.
AI.result: Applied to a model of ionization of a one-dimensional hydrogen atom driven by an ultrashort laser pulse, MPS encoding significantly reduced the required circuit depth compared to direct unitary decomposition.
AI.conclusion: MPS encoding provides a practical pathway for first-quantized quantum simulations incorporating pseudopotentials, reducing circuit depth and enabling feasible implementations.

title: Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes
summary:
Sipser and Spielman constructed LDPC codes from either bipartite \emph{spectral} expanders or one-sided \emph{lossless} expanders. In higher dimensions, \emph{spectral} expansion similarly played a central role in the constructions of asymptotically good classical LTCs and qLDPC codes by Dinur, Evra, Livne, Lubotzky, and Mozes and by Panteleev and Kalachev. Alternatively, Lin and Hsieh constructed classical LTCs and qLDPC codes from two-dimensional \emph{lossless} cubical complexes.
  In this work we develop the higher-dimensional \emph{lossless} approach. We do not construct the required high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes; rather, we investigate what their existence would imply. We associate with a high-dimensional cubical complex a \emph{level chain complex}, whose chain groups are supported on the level sets of the Boolean cube rather than on its cells. Our main technical contribution is a clean local-to-global theorem for this structure: suitable one-dimensional lossless expansion in the directional graphs implies small-set coboundary expansion of the global level complex. As a consequence, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes give rise to asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes. We expect the local-to-global principle developed here to have further applications.

AI.tldr: This work develops a higher-dimensional lossless expansion approach, showing that directional one-dimensional lossless expansion in high-dimensional cubical complexes implies small-set coboundary expansion of a "level chain complex," which would yield asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs).
AI.motivation: Prior constructions of good LDPC codes, classical LTCs, and qLDPC codes relied on spectral expansion (Sipser–Spielman; Dinur–Evra–Livne–Lubotzky–Mozes; Panteleev–Kalachev) or two-dimensional lossless cubical complexes (Lin–Hsieh). The paper aims to extend the lossless approach to higher dimensions, sidestepping the difficulty of explicitly constructing high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes by instead studying the consequences of their hypothetical existence.
AI.method: The authors associate to a high-dimensional cubical complex a level chain complex, whose chain groups are supported on the level sets of the Boolean cube rather than on its cells. They prove a local-to-global theorem for this structure: suitable one-dimensional lossless expansion in the directional graphs implies small-set coboundary expansion of the global level complex.
AI.result: The local-to-global principle yields that sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes would give rise to asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes.
AI.conclusion: The paper advances the higher-dimensional lossless program by providing a clean local-to-global theorem, connecting directional lossless expansion to small-set coboundary expansion. The authors anticipate further applications of this local-to-global principle beyond the qLTC consequence established here.

title: Polynomial-time local-unitary equivalence of graph states
summary: Local-unitary (LU) equivalence asks whether two quantum states differ only by independent changes of basis on their qubits. For graph states, whether this relation can be decided in polynomial time has remained open for over a decade. We give a deterministic algorithm that decides LU equivalence for graphs on $n$ labelled vertices in $\widetilde O(n^{6.38})$ bit operations and constructs exact single-qubit unitaries whenever the states are equivalent. Building on Claudet and Perdrix's quasipolynomial algorithm, we replace the enumeration of vertex subsets by a compact system of constraints generated from pairs and triples. The remaining graph transformation is found by solving linear equations over the binary field. These new steps cost $\widetilde O(n^5)$ bit operations; the inherited graph preprocessing sets the overall bound. We also count the local-Clifford (LC) classes of graph states within any LU class: their number is a power of two, computable within the same bound. For any given graph state, this decides whether single-qubit Clifford gates reach every graph state in its LU class, and supplies a counterexample when they do not. The method also decides LU equivalence of stabilizer codes encoding one logical qubit.

AI.tldr: This paper gives the first deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for deciding local-unitary (LU) equivalence of graph states, running in O~(n^{6.38}) bit operations, constructively producing the single-qubit unitaries. It also counts local-Clifford classes within an LU class and decides LU equivalence of one-qubit stabilizer codes.
AI.motivation: Local-unitary equivalence—whether two quantum states differ only by independent per-qubit basis changes—had an open complexity status for graph states for over a decade. Resolving whether this relation is decidable in polynomial time is a fundamental problem, with consequences for classifying and transforming graph states and stabilizer codes.
AI.method: Building on Claudet and Perdrix's quasipolynomial algorithm, the authors replace enumeration of vertex subsets with a compact constraint system generated from pairs and triples of vertices; the remaining graph transformation is found by solving linear equations over the binary field. These new steps cost O~(n^5), with inherited graph preprocessing determining the overall O~(n^{6.38}) bound. The algorithm is deterministic and constructs exact single-qubit unitaries when equivalence holds.
AI.result: Decides LU equivalence for graphs on n labelled vertices in O~(n^{6.38}) bit operations, with constructive single-qubit unitaries. The number of local-Clifford classes within any LU class is a power of two, computable within the same bound. This determines whether single-qubit Clifford gates reach every graph state in an LU class and provides a counterexample otherwise. It also decides LU equivalence of stabilizer codes encoding one logical qubit.
AI.conclusion: LU equivalence of graph states is decidable in polynomial time, resolving a decade-old open question, with the algorithm additionally yielding LC-class counts, reachability questions for Clifford gates, and a solution for one-logical-qubit stabilizer codes.

title: Quantum Krylov Learning
summary: The Hamiltonian of a natural quantum system is usually determined indirectly, by proposing microscopic models and comparing their predicted observables with experiment. A more direct approach is to extract information about the Hamiltonian from measurements on the system itself. In many settings, however, direct access to the full system is unavailable and measurements can be performed only through controllable probes, as in quantum sensing and boundary spectroscopy. Existing Hamiltonian learning protocols under such restricted access typically require a special symmetry, a known parametric form, or controlled operations beyond free evolution. We introduce Quantum Krylov Learning (QKL), a restricted-access framework that avoids these requirements. QKL uses single temperature probe autocorrelators and their operator Krylov structure to extract model-independent spectral information about the unknown system. Rather than fitting a parametrized Hamiltonian, it reconstructs the operator Krylov Jacobi matrix representing the dynamical modes accessible to the probe. The method assumes that the unobserved system is at, or near, infinite temperature. Under this condition, the Jacobi matrix can be reconstructed directly from the autocorrelation of a probe observable, without oracle access to the Hamiltonian. The required operations are free evolution under the unknown $H$, together with probe state preparation and measurement. The learning core therefore requires no symmetry, no parametric model, and no controlled-unitary gates. We show a Lieb--Robinson bound for the operator Krylov chain and derive a data-driven criterion for the required observation window. We also establish an end-to-end sample complexity guarantee: under generic conditions on the spectral gaps and weights, the number of measurement shots required to achieve spectral precision $\varepsilon$ is polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Quantum Krylov Learning (QKL), a restricted-access framework that reconstructs model-independent spectral information about an unknown Hamiltonian from single-temperature probe autocorrelators, requiring no symmetry, parametric form, or controlled operations.
AI.motivation: The Hamiltonian of natural quantum systems is usually inferred indirectly via microscopic models. Direct extraction from measurements is preferable, but in settings like quantum sensing and boundary spectroscopy only controllable probes have access to the system, not the full system. Existing Hamiltonian learning protocols under such restricted access typically demand a special symmetry, a known parametric form, or controlled operations beyond free evolution—limitations QKL aims to remove.
AI.method: QKL uses single temperature probe autocorrelators and their operator Krylov structure to extract model-independent spectral information. Instead of fitting a parametrized Hamiltonian, it reconstructs the operator Krylov Jacobi matrix representing the dynamical modes accessible to the probe. It assumes the unobserved system is at or near infinite temperature, under which the Jacobi matrix is reconstructed directly from the autocorrelation of a probe observable without oracle access to the Hamiltonian. Required operations are free evolution under the unknown H plus probe state preparation and measurement. A Lieb–Robinson bound for the operator Krylov chain and a data-driven criterion for the required observation window are derived.
AI.result: The learning core requires no symmetry, no parametric model, and no controlled-unitary gates. An end-to-end sample complexity guarantee is established: under generic conditions on spectral gaps and weights, the number of measurement shots required to achieve spectral precision ε is polynomial in 1/ε. A Lieb–Robinson bound for the operator Krylov chain and a data-driven observation-window criterion are also provided.
AI.conclusion: QKL enables model-independent Hamiltonian spectral learning under restricted access using only free evolution and probe preparation/measurement, achieving polynomial sample complexity and removing common requirements of symmetry, parametric models, and controlled gates.

title: Unifying and Extending Strong Simulation of Quantum Circuits
summary:
We establish functional aggregate queries (FAQs) as a unifying language for exact classical simulation of quantum circuits. A circuit becomes a sum-product query: factors encode gates, internal wire variables are aggregated, and free boundary variables index transition amplitudes. The central insight is that distinct sources of simulation tractability can be exploited within the same InsideOut evaluation scheme. The query specifies what is computed; the evaluation plan, semiring, and representation of intermediate factors determine the cost.
  This view unifies structural and algebraic simulation guarantees. With explicit factor representations, FAQ evaluation recovers the treewidth bound for tensor-network contraction and yields finer sparsity-sensitive bounds via fractional covers. Over a formal phase semiring, compressed intermediate factors recover rank-width-based simulation for compatible quadratic phase representations. For Clifford circuits, affine-quadratic factors are closed under multiplication and marginalization and remain polynomial in size, yielding polynomial-time exact amplitude computation without any bounded-width assumption.
  Beyond these recoveries, the framework yields a new tractability criterion: tensor layout symmetry width. This parameter combines local cut-rank with separator symmetry through exact tree-tensor representations. We give a constructive evaluation bound and exhibit a circuit family with bounded tensor layout symmetry width but unbounded phase-graph rank-width and circuit line-graph treewidth. These results establish representation-aware FAQ evaluation as a common algorithmic foundation for classical simulation and a systematic route to new tractable regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes functional aggregate queries (FAQs) as a unifying language for exact classical quantum circuit simulation, where circuits become sum-product queries, and shows that structural and algebraic tractability sources can be exploited within a single InsideOut evaluation scheme.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits has produced many disparate tractability results—treewidth bounds for tensor-network contraction, rank-width-based methods for quadratic phase representations, and polynomial-time Clifford simulation—but these guarantees come from different formalisms and are hard to compare or combine. The paper seeks a common algorithmic foundation that unifies these guarantees and exposes how evaluation choices (plan, semiring, factor representation) drive simulation cost.
AI.method: The authors cast quantum circuits as functional aggregate queries: gates become factors, internal wire variables are aggregated out, and free boundary variables index transition amplitudes. Simulation is performed via InsideOut evaluation, parameterized by the evaluation plan, the semiring, and the representation of intermediate factors. They instantiate this scheme with explicit factor representations (recovering treewidth and refinement via sparsity-sensitive fractional covers), with compressed factors over a formal phase semiring (recovering rank-width-based simulation for compatible quadratic phase representations), and with affine-quadratic factors closed under multiplication and marginalization (yielding polynomial-time Clifford amplitude computation).
AI.result: FAQ evaluation recovers the treewidth bound for tensor-network contraction and gives finer sparsity-sensitive bounds via fractional covers; compressed intermediate factors over a formal phase semiring recover rank-width-based simulation for compatible quadratic phase representations; affine-quadratic factors for Clifford circuits remain polynomial in size under multiplication and marginalization, giving polynomial-time exact amplitude computation without bounded-width assumptions. The framework also yields a new criterion—tensor layout symmetry width—combining local cut-rank with separator symmetry via exact tree-tensor representations, with a constructive evaluation bound and a circuit family exhibiting bounded tensor layout symmetry width but unbounded phase-graph rank-width and circuit line-graph treewidth.
AI.conclusion: Representation-aware FAQ evaluation provides a common algorithmic foundation for classical quantum circuit simulation, unifying existing structural and algebraic tractability results and offering a systematic route to identifying new tractable regimes.

title: A polynomial-time classical sampler for noisy quantum circuits from statistical mechanics
summary: Developing classical simulation algorithms for noisy quantum circuits is essential to delineating the limits of quantum advantage. Existing classical sampling approaches for general circuits require circuit depths to grow logarithmically with system size, so that noise drives the global output state close to a trivial state. Here we show that local accumulation of noise at a depth independent of system size is already sufficient. Specifically, we prove that any geometrically local circuit composed of unital operations and interspersed with single-qubit depolarizing noise of strength $p$ after $Ω(p^{-1} \log p^{-1})$ depth can be approximately sampled from a polynomial-time classical computer. Our proof maps the output state of the circuit to a polymer model in statistical mechanics, and combines a convergent cluster expansion with hypercontractivity of the depolarizing channel.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a local accumulation of noise at a depth independent of system size suffices for classical simulability. It shows that any geometrically local circuit of unital operations interspersed with single-qubit depolarizing noise of strength $p$ can be approximately sampled classically in polynomial time after depth $\Omega(p^{-1}\log p^{-1})$.
AI.motivation: Classical simulation algorithms for noisy quantum circuits are essential for delineating the limits of quantum advantage. Existing classical sampling approaches for general circuits require circuit depths growing logarithmically with system size, relying on noise driving the global output state close to a trivial state. This work aims to relax that requirement and show that noise acting only locally, at depth independent of system size, is already sufficient for classical simulability.
AI.method: The proof maps the output state of the circuit to a polymer model in statistical mechanics, then combines a convergent cluster expansion with the hypercontractivity of the depolarizing channel to establish the classical samplability.
AI.result: It is proved that any geometrically local circuit composed of unital operations and interspersed with single-qubit depolarizing noise of strength $p$ after $\Omega(p^{-1}\log p^{-1})$ depth can be approximately sampled from a polynomial-time classical computer.
AI.conclusion: Local noise accumulation at depth independent of system size already suffices to make geometrically local unital circuits classically simulable in polynomial time, thereby tightening the boundary of quantum advantage.

title: Optimal two-mode bosonic loss codes from finite group symmetry
comment: 7-page Letter and 65-page Supplemental Material; 3 main figures and 28 supplementary figures
summary: Photon loss is a dominant noise process in bosonic quantum hardware, including superconducting cavities. Fixed-total-photon-number qubit encodings in two bosonic modes retain the loss-detection advantage of dual-rail qubits while supporting photon loss correction. Optimizing entanglement fidelity in this setting for $4\leq n\leq25$ over arbitrary encoders and decoders reveals finite-group structure in every best-found code: 11 correspond to two-dimensional irreducible representations and 11 to reducible ones. Motivated by this emergence, we derive the necessary-and-sufficient Knill-Laflamme conditions for arbitrary finite-group-invariant codes, reducing their construction to equations on representation multiplicity spaces. For every finite subgroup of $SU(2)$ and every tensor rank, we explicitly construct the minimum number of operators required to impose all corresponding loss-correction constraints. These results produce analytic counterparts to most numerical codes and predict constructions missed by the initial search. Exact MacWilliams-Farkas certificates show that our codes achieve the maximum possible loss distance in 21 of the 22 sectors, and we prove that the resulting distance bound is monotone in total photon number. Beyond the scan, we identify a binary-polyhedral sequence with photon number $n_d=\lceil(3d^2+1)/4\rceil$ and construct each corresponding code through distance $d=10$. To our knowledge, the constructed $(n,d)=(28,6),(49,8),(76,10)$ codes give the smallest reported $n$ for their respective distances; all members through $d=9$ attain the fixed-$n$ LP distance bound. Together, these constructions, certificates, and a symmetry-reduced constraint count provide evidence for an infinite code family conjectured to attain every distance at the minimum photon number.

AI.tldr: Photon loss in bosonic quantum hardware is addressed via fixed-total-photon-number qubit encodings in two modes; a numerical search over encoders/decoders for 4≤n≤25 reveals finite-group structure in every best-found code, motivating a general finite-group-invariant Knill-Laflamme framework that yields analytic codes, optimal loss distances, and a conjectured infinite family attaining every distance at minimal photon number.
AI.motivation: Photon loss is a dominant noise process in bosonic quantum hardware such as superconducting cavities. Fixed-total-photon-number encodings in two bosonic modes preserve the loss-detection advantage of dual-rail qubits while enabling photon loss correction. However, optimal constructions of such codes were not well characterized, motivating a systematic search and a principled algebraic theory.
AI.method: Entanglement fidelity was optimized over arbitrary encoders and decoders for total photon numbers 4≤n≤25, revealing finite-group structure in every best-found code (11 two-dimensional irreducible representations, 11 reducible). Necessary-and-sufficient Knill-Laflamme conditions were derived for arbitrary finite-group-invariant codes, reducing construction to equations on representation multiplicity spaces. For every finite subgroup of SU(2) and every tensor rank, the minimum number of operators needed to impose all loss-correction constraints was explicitly constructed. Exact MacWilliams-Farkas certificates were computed, and a symmetry-reduced constraint count was used.
AI.result: Analytic counterparts to most numerical codes were produced, predicting constructions missed by the initial search. Codes achieve maximum possible loss distance in 21 of 22 sectors; the distance bound is proven monotone in total photon number. A binary-polyhedral sequence with n_d=⌈(3d²+1)/4⌉ was identified and codes constructed through distance d=10. Constructed (n,d)=(28,6),(49,8),(76,10) codes give the smallest reported n for their distances; all members through d=9 attain the fixed-n LP distance bound.
AI.conclusion: The constructions, certificates, and symmetry-reduced constraint count provide evidence for an infinite code family conjectured to attain every distance at the minimum photon number, offering a unified algebraic framework for loss-correcting bosonic encodings.

title: Characterizing unitaries via quasi-process functions
summary: It is well-known that every n-qubit unitary can be decomposed into a product of controlled single-qubit unitaries. We show that the control conditions in such a decomposition naturally define a quasi-process function, an object that originally came up in the study of indefinite causal order. Here quasi-process functions yield a representation of every n-qubit unitary in a canonical form, namely, as a quasi-process function unitary (qPFU). We use this representation to show how quantum nonlocality without entanglement (QNLWE) can be understood in terms of unitaries that encode the trade-off between causal order and locality noted in R. Kunjwal and Ä. Baumeler, arXiv:2202.00440. Specifically, we obtain two sufficient (but not necessary) criteria---mutual exclusivity of control conditions (MECC) and Unambiguity---for a unitary to be a process function unitary (PFU), i.e., it admits a qPFU representation where the quasi-process function is a process function, an object that can model paradox-free classical causal loops. We also show the inequivalence of these criteria, neither implying the other. We then show that the circuit depth of MECC unitaries admits a characterization in terms of clique-partitioning problems on Hamming graphs and use this correspondence to provide bounds on the circuit depth of n-qubit MECC unitaries. Finally, we show how MECC unitaries provide a recipe for constructing a unitary purification of the associated process function, thereby providing a large class of unitary processes of interest in quantum causality. The generality of this causality-inspired representation of unitaries makes it a versatile tool for analyzing the structure of quantum circuits in other domains.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that every n-qubit unitary can be canonically represented via a quasi-process function arising from the control conditions of its controlled-single-qubit decomposition, yielding a quasi-process function unitary (qPFU) representation. This framework connects quantum nonlocality without entanglement (QNLWE) to causal order, produces two sufficient criteria (MECC and Unambiguity) for process function unitaries, analyzes circuit depth via Hamming graph clique-partitioning, and constructs unitary purifications of process functions.
AI.motivation: Quantum nonlocality without entanglement (QNLWE) and the trade-off between causal order and locality (Kunjwal & Baumeler) lack a unified unitary-based account. The authors seek a canonical representation of arbitrary n-qubit unitaries that bridges indefinite causal order, process functions, and quantum circuit structure.
AI.method: Starting from the standard decomposition of any n-qubit unitary into controlled single-qubit unitaries, the control conditions are interpreted as defining a quasi-process function, giving a canonical qPFU representation. From this, the authors derive two sufficient criteria—mutual exclusivity of control conditions (MECC) and Unambiguity—for a unitary to be a process function unitary (PFU), prove their inequivalence, characterize MECC circuit depth through clique-partitioning on Hamming graphs, and construct unitary purifications of associated process functions.
AI.result: A canonical qPFU representation exists for every n-qubit unitary. Two sufficient (not necessary) criteria, MECC and Unambiguity, identify PFUs, and neither implies the other. MECC unitary circuit depth is characterized via clique-partitioning of Hamming graphs, yielding depth bounds for n-qubit MECC unitaries. MECC unitaries also supply a recipe for unitary purification of the associated process function.
AI.conclusion: QNLWE can be understood through unitaries encoding the causal-order/locality trade-off. The causality-inspired quasi-process function representation is general and versatile, offering a tool for analyzing quantum circuit structure, providing a large class of unitary processes relevant to quantum causality, and potentially applicable across other domains.

title: Quantum key distribution using generalized contextuality against post-quantum eavesdroppers
summary: Bell nonlocality allows secret key to be certified without trusting the internal operation of the devices, and even against eavesdroppers constrained only by the no-signaling principle. We ask whether generalized contextuality, a notion of nonclassicality available in prepare-and-measure experiments on a single system, can play an analogous role. In our approach, Alice and Bob first establish operational equivalences among their local preparation and measurement procedures, which are then treated as theory-independent constraints that any physical intervention on the communication channel, including that of an adversary, must respect. Eve is otherwise unrestricted, that is, her intervention on the transmitted system is not assumed to be described by quantum theory. Within this adversarial model, we show that Eve's optimal guessing probability against individual attacks is the solution of a finite linear program, and hence that a worst-case asymptotic key rate follows from the observed statistics and the operational equivalences alone. We prove that contextuality is necessary for a positive key rate. However, we also show that it is not sufficient. Concretely, the (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code, known to yield secret key against a quantum eavesdropper, yields none certifiable key rate against a post-quantum one. Conversely, operational equivalences with no analogue among no-signaling constraints can strictly increase the asymptotic key rate. We illustrate this with the prepare-and-measure version of the standard CHSH protocol with an aligned key-generating setting.

AI.tldr: The paper asks whether generalized contextuality in prepare-and-measure experiments can certify secret key-like Bell nonlocality. Under a post-quantum adversarial model constrained only by operational equivalences, the authors show Eve's optimal guessing probability for individual attacks is a finite linear program, giving a worst-case asymptotic key rate from observed statistics alone. Contextuality is necessary but not sufficient for a positive rate; some protocols (e.g., the (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code) certify key against quantum but not post-quantum eavesdroppers, while certain operational equivalences without no-signaling analogues can strictly increase the asymptotic key rate.
AI.motivation: Bell nonlocality enables device-independent key certification even against no-signaling-constrained eavesdroppers. The authors ask whether generalized contextuality, a weaker notion of nonclassicality accessible in single-system prepare-and-measure experiments, can play an analogous role in certifying secret key.
AI.method: Alice and Bob establish operational equivalences among their local preparation and measurement procedures, treated as theory-independent constraints that any physical intervention on the communication channel, including an adversary's, must respect. Eve is otherwise unrestricted (not assumed quantum). The authors formulate Eve's optimal guessing probability against individual attacks as a finite linear program, and derive a worst-case asymptotic key rate from observed statistics and operational equivalences alone.
AI.result: Contextuality is proven necessary for a positive key rate but not sufficient. The (3,2)-parity-oblivious random access code, which yields secret key against a quantum eavesdropper, yields no certifiable key rate against a post-quantum one. Conversely, operational equivalences with no analogue among no-signaling constraints can strictly increase the asymptotic key rate, illustrated with the prepare-and-measure version of the standard CHSH protocol with an aligned key-generating setting.
AI.conclusion: Generalized contextuality can serve as a resource for certifying secret key in a post-quantum adversarial model, but it is strictly weaker than Bell nonlocality: it is necessary yet insufficient for a positive key rate, and specific operational equivalences beyond no-signaling constraints can enhance the achievable asymptotic key rate.

title: Late-Time Power Laws in Fluorescence Decays: Quantum Decay or Alternative Mechanisms?
summary: In quantum mechanics, the properties of an unstable system are closely related to its corresponding energy distribution. One of the predictions of the theory is the emergence of a late-time power law in the survival probability $P(t)$ of the unstable state. However, in complex systems, similar effects may emerge due to other phenomena. This is the case for nonextensive statistical models, for some continuous lifetime distribution models, and also for certain energy-migration models applied to fluorescence. In this work, these alternative interpretations are confronted with data from time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy experiments with erythrosine B and eosine Y as fluorophores. It turns out that some of the features expected within the quantum-mechanical description, such as the sharp transition from the exponential to the power-law regime, cannot be reproduced by the specific statistical and energy-migration parametrizations fitted in the analysis.

AI.tldr: Time-resolved fluorescence data (erythrosine B, eosine Y) are used to test alternative origins of late-time power-law decays in survival probability, and only the quantum-mechanical description accounts for the observed sharp exponential-to-power-law transition.
AI.motivation: The late-time power law in the survival probability of an unstable quantum state is a standard quantum-mechanical prediction, but similar power-law tails can arise from unrelated mechanisms in complex systems, notably nonextensive statistical models, certain continuous lifetime distribution models, and energy-migration models used in fluorescence. This ambiguity motivates discriminating experimentally between the quantum-mechanical and alternative interpretations.
AI.method: Time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy experiments are performed with erythrosine B and eosine Y as fluorophores. The measured decay data are fitted with specific parametrizations of the competing descriptions: nonextensive statistical models, continuous lifetime distribution models, and energy-migration models, and compared with the quantum-mechanical prediction.
AI.result: The alternative statistical and energy-migration parametrizations that were fitted cannot reproduce certain features expected within the quantum-mechanical description, in particular the sharp transition from the exponential regime to the power-law regime.
AI.conclusion: Among the considered interpretations tested against time-resolved fluorescence data, the quantum-mechanical description is the one whose characteristic signature, a sharp exponential-to-power-law crossover, is consistent with the data, whereas the examined nonextensive, lifetime-distribution, and energy-migration parametrizations fail to capture it.

title: Engineering non-ergodic properties in two dimensional quantum many-body systems
summary: Non-ergodic quantum many-body dynamics offers a route to persistent quantum coherence far from equilibrium, beyond the conventional expectations of thermalizing statistical mechanics. Most known examples have been identified through intuition, analogy, or numerical search, rather than by systematic Hamiltonian design. This leaves few general methods for engineering robust non-ergodic dynamics in disorder-free interacting quantum many-body systems, especially in higher dimensions where enhanced connectivity generally disfavors ergodicity breaking. Here, we use an eigenstate-to-Hamiltonian construction approach to systematically engineer two-dimensional quantum spin Hamiltonians with tunable non-ergodic properties. Starting from a common parent model and input eigenstate, we construct two target Hamiltonians on the square lattice that differ in their interaction geometry: axial versus diagonal. We show that the resulting interaction geometry and coupling pattern control the Hilbert-space structure and dynamics. The axial model forms a connected Hilbert-space network and exhibits an anisotropy-driven crossover from ergodic to non-ergodic behavior through the suppression of resonances. In contrast, the diagonal model exhibits Hilbert-space fragmentation and, within its largest irreducible sector, signatures of quantum many-body scar dynamics including towers of highly localized, low-entanglement eigenstates, and long-lived coherent revivals. These results establish a direct link between Hamiltonian design, Hilbert-space network structure, and emergent non-ergodic dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors use an eigenstate-to-Hamiltonian construction to engineer 2D square-lattice spin Hamiltonians with tunable non-ergodic dynamics, showing that interaction geometry (axial vs. diagonal) controls Hilbert-space network structure, yielding an ergodic-to-non-ergodic crossover in the axial case and fragmentation with scar-like dynamics in the diagonal case.
AI.motivation: Most known non-ergodic quantum many-body dynamics are found via intuition, analogy, or numerical search rather than systematic design. General methods for engineering robust non-ergodic dynamics in disorder-free interacting systems remain scarce, especially in higher dimensions where enhanced connectivity typically disfavors ergodicity breaking.
AI.method: An eigenstate-to-Hamiltonian construction approach is applied. Starting from a common parent model and input eigenstate, two target Hamiltonians on the square lattice are constructed with differing interaction geometry—axial versus diagonal—so that interaction geometry and coupling pattern determine the Hilbert-space structure and dynamics.
AI.result: The axial model produces a connected Hilbert-space network and an anisotropy-driven crossover from ergodic to non-ergodic behavior via resonance suppression. The diagonal model exhibits Hilbert-space fragmentation and, in its largest irreducible sector, quantum many-body scar signatures: towers of highly localized, low-entanglement eigenstates and long-lived coherent revivals.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a direct link between Hamiltonian design, Hilbert-space network structure, and emergent non-ergodic dynamics, offering a systematic route to engineer tunable non-ergodic behavior in disorder-free higher-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

title: Operator-language Feynman rules for driven-dissipative quantum systems: from mean field to non-Gaussian photon correlations
