summary: We construct Feynman rules for Lindblad master equations in the operator language of quantum optics: a fixed algebra of elementary operator moves and closed-form propagators for perturbation theory about an exactly solvable, in most cases Gaussian, generator. The expansion separates into a kinematic part (the shift algebra on the Wick-ordered eigenoperators $O_{mn}=:(c^\dagger)^m c^n:$, from which the vertex table for a specified interaction is assembled) and a dynamical part that enters only through the resolvent of the unperturbed generator, diagonal and additive for any stable, diagonalizable Gaussian $L_0$, including thermal and squeezed reservoirs and correlated decay, and equally available for a two-level emitter, driven or undriven. In the driven Kerr cavity the loop expansion is the semiclassical expansion and the series is asymptotic. In a strongly driven two-level atom, dressed lines replace a series of finite radius by one accurate deep into saturation, one line per Mollow component. For Kerr rings and chains the cost is polynomial in the number of sites at fixed perturbative order. On a three-site ring the diagrams recover the non-Gaussian part of the three-photon correlation that the Gaussian cumulant closure lacks; carried to tenth order they give the smallest $g^{(3)}$ error of the methods compared for $U\leq0.25κ$ at a cost below that of a fourth-order closure, and third- and fourth-order closures are more accurate at moderate coupling. The same rules, extended to the counting-field-tilted generator, give the photon-counting cumulants of a disordered eight-site chain beyond direct diagonalization; quantum-jump trajectories at three couplings agree with them to within $1.6$ standard errors, within one at the strongest coupling, where they place the third cumulant six standard errors above the Gaussian value.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs Feynman rules for Lindblad master equations in quantum optics, using an algebra of elementary operator moves and closed-form propagators to enable a systematically improvable perturbative diagrammatic expansion.
AI.motivation: Non-Gaussian dynamics and higher-order photon correlations in open quantum systems (Kerr cavities, driven two-level atoms, Kerr rings/chains, disordered chains) are not captured by Gaussian cumulant closures, and direct diagonalization is prohibitively costly. A systematic diagrammatic perturbation theory in the operator language is needed.
AI.method: Constructs Feynman rules for Lindblad master equations with a fixed algebra of elementary operator moves and closed-form propagators around an exactly solvable (mostly Gaussian) generator. The expansion splits into a kinematic part (shift algebra on Wick-ordered eigenoperators O_mn=:(c†)^m c^n:, yielding vertex tables for a given interaction) and a dynamical part entering only via the resolvent of the unperturbed generator, which is diagonal and additive for any stable, diagonalizable Gaussian L_0 (thermal, squeezed reservoirs, correlated decay) and also for driven/undriven two-level emitters. Extended to a counting-field-tilted generator for photon-counting cumulants.
AI.result: In the driven Kerr cavity the loop expansion coincides with the semiclassical expansion and is asymptotic. In a strongly driven two-level atom, dressed lines replace a finite-radius series with one accurate deep into saturation, one line per Mollow component. For Kerr rings and chains the cost is polynomial in the number of sites at fixed perturbative order. On a three-site ring, diagrams recover the non-Gaussian part of the three-photon correlation missed by Gaussian cumulant closure; to tenth order they yield the smallest g^(3) error among compared methods for U≤0.25κ at a cost below a fourth-order closure, while third- and fourth-order closures are more accurate at moderate coupling. The tilted-generator rules give photon-counting cumulants of a disordered eight-site chain beyond direct diagonalization; quantum-jump trajectories at three couplings agree within 1.6 standard errors (within one at strongest coupling), where they place the third cumulant six standard errors above the Gaussian value.
AI.conclusion: The Feynman rules provide a systematic, systematically improvable perturbative framework for Lindblad dynamics that captures non-Gaussian correlations and photon-counting statistics beyond Gaussian closures, with favorable polynomial scaling in system size and cost competitive with or below cumulant closures, and validated against quantum-jump trajectories.

title: Quantum Circuit Pruning: From NISQ Architectures to Fault-Tolerant Operations
summary: We present a routing-aware pruning strategy for quantum circuits that selectively removes parametric two-qubit gates whose computational contribution is outweighed by the fidelity cost of their execution, and assess it across both Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) and fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) architectures. Each two-qubit gate of a circuit is evaluated by comparing an architecture-independent lower bound on the fidelity cost of omitting the gate against a hardware-specific model for the routing execution cost in each setting. We additionally provide an analytical characterization of the pruning boundary as a function of rotation angle, qubit distance, and hardware noise. Simulations on benchmark circuits demonstrate gate count reductions of up to 48.6% and fidelity improvements of up to 47.7% in the NISQ regime, while a feasibility analysis on FT hardware indicates that pruning is expected to remain relevant across a range of code distances and physical error rates. These results establish routing-aware pruning as a practical and unified compilation strategy across the quantum computing stack.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a routing-aware pruning strategy that removes parametric two-qubit gates when their computational value is lower than the fidelity cost of executing (including routing), evaluated across NISQ and FTQC settings.
AI.motivation: Two-qubit gates, especially with routing overhead and noise, impose significant fidelity costs; some parametric gates contribute little computationally but still incur these costs, motivating a principled criterion for selective removal spanning both NISQ and fault-tolerant architectures.
AI.method: Each two-qubit gate is assessed by comparing an architecture-independent lower bound on the fidelity cost of omitting it against a hardware-specific routing execution cost model. An analytical characterization of the pruning boundary is derived as a function of rotation angle, qubit distance, and hardware noise. The approach is evaluated via simulations on benchmark circuits and a feasibility analysis on fault-tolerant hardware.
AI.result: NISQ simulations show gate count reductions up to 48.6% and fidelity improvements up to 47.7%. The FTQC feasibility analysis indicates pruning remains relevant across a range of code distances and physical error rates.
AI.conclusion: Routing-aware pruning is presented as a practical, unified compilation strategy applicable across the quantum computing stack, from NISQ to fault-tolerant regimes.

title: Beyond Feasibility: Finite-Depth Accessibility in Constrained QAOA
summary:
Constraint-preserving mixers keep QAOA within a feasible subspace, but feasibility and global mixer connectivity do not determine which feasible configurations are available to a particular shallow circuit. We study constrained QAOA at the level of the circuit actually executed: a specified feasible initial state, finite depth, and finite schedule of mixer interactions. We define the finite-depth accessible set $R_p(M,x_0)$ and show that the computational-basis support of the ideal QAOA circuit is contained within it. This gives a parameter-independent objective ceiling $f_R^\star=\max_{x\in R_p}f(x)$ and a normalized reachable-quality diagnostic $Q_R$, separating accessible volume from the objective quality contained within it.
  We evaluate this framework using resource-matched block-local XY mixer schedules for constrained portfolio optimization and synthetic block-constrained quadratic problems. Across 207 favorable-tail CVaR QAOA configurations, $Q_R$ shows the strongest association with realized shallow-QAOA performance among the structural diagnostics considered, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of $0.7003$ and $0.8057$; the relationship remains positive under controlled and dependence-aware analyses. The distinction persists across changes in feasible initialization, portfolio size, and objective family.
  A compilation-only study further shows that, for the dense portfolio Hamiltonians considered here, phase-separator routing dominates the compiled two-qubit resource scale, while mixer schedules with comparable compiled two-qubit cost can exhibit markedly different finite-depth accessible quality. These results motivate objective-relevant finite-depth accessibility as a complementary diagnostic for resource-bounded constrained QAOA.

AI.tldr: This paper defines a finite-depth accessible set R_p(M,x_0) for constrained QAOA and a normalized reachable-quality diagnostic Q_R, showing it best predicts shallow-QAOA performance among structural diagnostics across 207 CVaR configurations.
AI.motivation: Constraint-preserving mixers keep QAOA within a feasible subspace, but feasibility and global mixer connectivity alone do not determine which feasible configurations a particular shallow circuit can actually reach. The paper argues that constrained QAOA should be analyzed at the level of the executed circuit.
AI.method: The authors define the finite-depth accessible set R_p(M,x_0) for a specified feasible initial state, finite depth, and finite mixer schedule, showing the ideal QAOA circuit's computational-basis support is contained within it. They derive a parameter-independent objective ceiling f_R^star and a normalized reachable-quality diagnostic Q_R separating accessible volume from objective quality. They evaluate this on resource-matched block-local XY mixer schedules for constrained portfolio optimization and synthetic block-constrained quadratic problems.
AI.result: Across 207 favorable-tail CVaR QAOA configurations, Q_R shows the strongest association with realized shallow-QAOA performance (Pearson 0.7003, Spearman 0.8057), remaining positive under controlled and dependence-aware analyses and across changes in feasible initialization, portfolio size, and objective family. A compilation-only study shows phase-separator routing dominates compiled two-qubit resource scale for dense portfolio Hamiltonians, while mixer schedules with comparable compiled cost can yield markedly different accessible quality.
AI.conclusion: Objective-relevant finite-depth accessibility is proposed as a complementary diagnostic for resource-bounded constrained QAOA.

title: Negative quasiprobabilities redistribute (and complex ones reduce) the information in unabsorbed photons
summary: Negative Kirkwood--Dirac quasiprobabilities are credited with the quantum advantage of interaction-free measurement and postselected metrology. We test that claim on the task interaction-free measurement was designed for: learning about a sample letting it absorb as little light as possible. The Kirkwood--Dirac distribution of path and output gives the linear response to a weak sample: its real part responds to absorption, its imaginary part to a phase. For a pure single photon passing once through any interferometer, the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon is the direct-transmission value minus a sum of squared imaginary parts: no interferometer or readout beats direct transmission. Negativity plays no role beyond concentrating information in weakly lit outputs. The imaginary parts of the Kirkwood-Dirac distribution depend on the output basis here, not on the sample, so a basis exists in which every term is real, which is optimal. A single photon gains information per absorbed photon only through a phase response, which for an optical line needs a thick or inhomogeneously broadened sample, or through many passes when absorptions go uncounted, as shown by a critically coupled resonator. For detecting a weak absorber, negativity gives a single-shot advantage that does not accumulate over multiple trials; advantage instead accumulates when there are outputs which are dark without the object, a case which needs no negativity.

AI.tldr: Negative Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities do not provide a fundamental advantage for interaction-free measurement or postselected metrology; the Fisher information per absorbed photon never exceeds the direct-transmission value, and negativity only concentrates information in weakly lit outputs.
AI.motivation: Negative Kirkwood-Dirac quasiprobabilities are widely credited with enabling the quantum advantage of interaction-free measurement and postselected metrology. This paper tests that claim on the task interaction-free measurement was designed for: learning about a sample while letting it absorb as little light as possible.
AI.method: The authors analyze the Kirkwood-Dirac distribution of path and output for a pure single photon passing once through an arbitrary interferometer. They decompose its real part (response to absorption) and imaginary part (response to phase) and compute the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon, comparing it to the direct-transmission value. They also examine a critically coupled resonator and the case of uncounted absorptions with many passes.
AI.result: For a pure single photon through any interferometer, the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon equals the direct-transmission value minus a sum of squared imaginary parts, so no interferometer or readout beats direct transmission. The imaginary parts of the Kirkwood-Dirac distribution depend on the output basis, not the sample, so a basis exists in which every term is real, which is optimal. Negativity gives only a single-shot advantage for detecting a weak absorber that does not accumulate over multiple trials.
AI.conclusion: Negativity plays no role beyond concentrating information in weakly lit outputs. A single photon gains information per absorbed photon only through a phase response (requiring a thick or inhomogeneously broadened sample, or many passes when absorptions go uncounted). Advantage instead accumulates when there are outputs that are dark without the object, a case that needs no negativity.

title: esQueranto: Differentiable Structured Quantum Light for Automated Scientific Discovery
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures. Software and examples available at https://github.com/artificial-scientist-lab/esQueranto
summary: Uncovering new phenomena in nature requires experiments. For centuries, their design has been exclusively a human endeavor. Today, a new paradigm is emerging in which artificial intelligence and computational methods can design experiments themselves. Realizing this form of automated scientific discovery requires simulators that are sufficiently expressive to represent the diverse physical processes and couplings from which new experiments can be constructed. In this direction, we introduce \textsc{esQueranto}, a differentiable software that brings photon-number quantum optics and structured-light propagation into a common description, allowing the spatial evolution of light to directly influence non-classical quantum states and their interference. \textsc{esQueranto} is implemented in JAX, providing automatic differentiation and hardware-accelerated evaluation for optimization and automated search. We demonstrate the framework across a broad range of quantum-optical applications that exercise complementary aspects of its physical description. By combining quantum and structured-light physics within a single differentiable simulator, \textsc{esQueranto} takes an important step towards the dream of a foundational simulator in physics.

AI.tldr: esQueranto is a differentiable JAX-based simulator unifying photon-number quantum optics with structured-light propagation, enabling gradient-based optimization and automated experiment design across quantum-optical applications.
AI.motivation: Experiment design has historically been exclusively human-driven, but AI and computational methods are enabling automated scientific discovery. This paradigm requires simulators expressive enough to capture diverse physical processes and couplings, yet no simulator unifies photon-number quantum optics with structured-light propagation to support automated experiment construction.
AI.method: The authors introduce esQueranto, a differentiable software implemented in JAX that brings photon-number quantum optics and structured-light propagation into a common description. This allows spatial evolution of light to directly influence non-classical quantum states and their interference. JAX provides automatic differentiation and hardware-accelerated evaluation for optimization and automated search.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated across a broad range of quantum-optical applications that exercise complementary aspects of its physical description.
AI.conclusion: By combining quantum and structured-light physics within a single differentiable simulator, esQueranto represents an important step towards a foundational simulator in physics and automated scientific discovery.

title: Conditioning on Subalgebras - Entropy Duality and Generalized Quantum Stein's Lemma in von Neumann Algebras
summary: We establish duality relations for conditional entropies relative to subalgebras of arbitrary von Neumann algebras, including the Umegaki relative entropy as well as the sandwiched- and Petz-Rényi divergences. Even in finite dimensions, these results extend the familiar dualities for conditional entropies from tensor-product subsystems to general subalgebras, while also lifting the framework to the fully infinite-dimensional setting. As an application, we establish an infinite-dimensional extension of quantum Stein's lemma when the alternative hypothesis is the state space of a finite-index subalgebra, which gives an operational interpretation of the relative entropy to a subalgebra as the optimal asymptotic error exponent in composite quantum hypothesis testing-the first beyond finite dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes duality relations for conditional entropies (Umegaki relative entropy, sandwiched- and Petz-Rényi divergences) relative to subalgebras of general von Neumann algebras, extending finite-dimensional tensor-product dualities to arbitrary subalgebras and to infinite dimensions, and applies this to an infinite-dimensional quantum Stein's lemma for composite hypothesis testing.
AI.motivation: Familiar dualities for conditional entropies were limited to tensor-product subsystems in finite dimensions. The authors aim to generalize these to general subalgebras and to the fully infinite-dimensional (von Neumann algebraic) setting, and to give an operational meaning to relative entropy with respect to a subalgebra.
AI.method: Establish duality relations for conditional entropies relative to subalgebras of arbitrary von Neumann algebras, covering the Umegaki relative entropy and the sandwiched- and Petz-Rényi divergences, thereby extending finite-dimensional tensor-product duality results to general subalgebras and to the infinite-dimensional framework.
AI.result: The duality relations are proven for conditional entropies relative to subalgebras of arbitrary von Neumann algebras, generalizing existing finite-dimensional tensor-product dualities to general subalgebras and lifting them to infinite dimensions. An infinite-dimensional extension of quantum Stein's lemma is obtained when the alternative hypothesis is the state space of a finite-index subalgebra.
AI.conclusion: The work provides an operational interpretation of the relative entropy to a subalgebra as the optimal asymptotic error exponent in composite quantum hypothesis testing, the first such result beyond finite dimensions.

title: Real-Time Adaptive Filtering and the Boxcar Limit in Superconducting Qubit Readout
summary:
In dispersive readout of superconducting qubits, the common baseline is a boxcar averager: a uniformly weighted average over a fixed window followed by threshold-based state assignment. We ask when additional digital processing improves fidelity. We evaluated an adaptive finite-impulse-response (FIR) filter trained in real time by the least-mean-squares (LMS) algorithm on an FPGA quantum controller, and analyzed measured readout shots offline to compare the frozen filter with boxcar averaging and to test per-sample weighting and sequential detection.
  For the fixed FIR filters tested, summing the filtered samples gives the boxcar sum multiplied by one complex number, apart from a small edge correction (the kernel collapse). This scales state separation and noise equally, so discrimination cannot improve (the boxcar limit).
  The frozen LMS filter reduces trace noise without a resolved fidelity improvement at the tested readout lengths. Replayed on the same shots offline, each filtered shot carries 99.4% of the boxcar shot's discrimination signal-to-noise ratio at the 8 $μ$s operating point of the 2D transmon qubit (Q1).
  On Q1, optimizing the readout window's start and duration improves contrast readout fidelity by +2.4% to +5.6% across four readout lengths. Per-sample weighting adds up to +3.0% over full-window integration, and only +0.33% beyond the tuned window at 8 $μ$s.
  Remaining results are from a 3D ancilla qubit (Q2), which sits above the early-decision crossover that Q1 sits below. Hardware sweeps locate the crossover window near 1 $μ$s. Offline, the sequential test decided most shots early, with fidelity within 0.5 percentage points of the boxcar. About 30 labeled shots per class build a matched-filter template nearly as good as one from hundreds.
  The results form an operating-point record that separates waveform denoising from decision improvement.

AI.tldr: Adaptive FIR filtering on an FPGA does not improve qubit readout fidelity beyond a boxcar averager because fixed filter kernels only rescale signal and noise identically (the "kernel collapse"), a "boxcar limit." Real gains come from optimizing the readout window and (marginally) per-sample weighting, while sequential detection enables early decisions without fidelity loss.
AI.motivation: Superconducting-qubit dispersive readout conventionally uses a boxcar averager (uniform average over a fixed window) with threshold-based state assignment. The paper asks when extra digital processing actually improves fidelity, aiming to separate mere waveform denoising from genuine decision improvement.
AI.method: An adaptive FIR filter trained in real time by the LMS algorithm on an FPGA quantum controller was evaluated, with measured readout shots analyzed offline. The frozen LMS filter was compared against boxcar averaging, and per-sample weighting and sequential detection were tested. Hardware sweeps located an early-decision crossover, and matched-filter templates were built from few labeled shots. Studies used a 2D transmon (Q1) and a 3D ancilla qubit (Q2).
AI.result: For fixed FIR filters, summing outputs equals the boxcar sum times one complex number (up to a small edge correction), scaling signal and noise equally, so discrimination cannot improve (boxcar limit). The frozen LMS filter reduced trace noise but gave no resolved fidelity gain; it retained 99.4% of the boxcar shot SNR at the 8 µs operating point on Q1. Optimizing window start/duration improved contrast readout fidelity by +2.4% to +5.6% across four readout lengths; per-sample weighting added up to +3.0% over full-window integration but only +0.33% beyond the tuned window at 8 µs. On Q2, the crossover window is near 1 µs; the sequential test decided most shots early with fidelity within 0.5 percentage points of boxcar, and ~30 labeled shots per class produced a matched-filter template nearly as good as one from hundreds.
AI.conclusion: The results form an operating-point record that cleanly separates waveform denoising from decision improvement: filtering alone offers no fidelity gain, whereas readout-window optimization, modest per-sample weighting, and sequential early detection deliver the real benefits.

title: Remote state preparation of a single-spin state via hybrid spin-photon entanglement
summary: Remote state preparation is a fundamental quantum-information protocol that exploits prior knowledge of a target state to reduce the communication resources required for quantum-state distribution. Here, we propose a remote-state-preparation protocol for a stationary electron-spin qubit using hybrid entanglement between the electron spin and a coherent-state light pulse, generated by spin-dependent reflection from a spin-cavity system. Unlike single-photon encodings, the coherent-state encoding is naturally tolerant of photon loss: a loss channel attenuates the coherent-state amplitude, leading to a gradual reduction in preparation fidelity rather than probabilistic protocol failure. The central difficulty---implementing the projection onto superpositions of nonorthogonal coherent states required in the conventional protocol---is circumvented by coupling the transmitted pulse to an auxiliary spin, followed by homodyne detection and a spin projective measurement. The protocol therefore avoids direct coherent-state-superposition measurements and photon-number-resolving detection. In the ideal limit, deterministic preparation of a particular class of target states can be achieved using only one bit of classical communication. We analytically quantify the effects of coherent-state nonorthogonality, fiber loss, and spin dephasing on the preparation fidelity. Increasing the coherent-state amplitude improves state distinguishability and hence the preparation fidelity, but also enhances which-branch information leakage caused by photon loss, resulting in an optimal amplitude at each transmission distance. For experimentally relevant parameters, the optimized average fidelity remains well above the classical benchmark over distances of tens of kilometers. We also discuss a possible implementation using diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers.

AI.tldr: A remote-state-preparation protocol for a stationary electron-spin qubit is proposed using hybrid spin-coherent-state entanglement, circumventing coherent-state-superposition projection via an auxiliary spin, homodyne detection, and spin measurement, achieving deterministic preparation with one bit of classical communication and high fidelity over tens of kilometers.
AI.motivation: Remote state preparation exploits prior knowledge of a target state to reduce communication resources for quantum-state distribution. Single-photon encodings fail probabilistically under photon loss, whereas coherent-state encoding degrades gracefully. The main obstacle is projecting onto superpositions of nonorthogonal coherent states in the conventional protocol.
AI.method: Hybrid entanglement between an electron spin and a coherent-state light pulse is generated via spin-dependent reflection from a spin-cavity system. The required projection is circumvented by coupling the transmitted pulse to an auxiliary spin, followed by homodyne detection and a spin projective measurement, avoiding direct coherent-state-superposition measurements and photon-number-resolving detection.
AI.result: In the ideal limit, deterministic preparation of a particular class of target states is achieved with only one bit of classical communication. Analytical quantification of coherent-state nonorthogonality, fiber loss, and spin dephasing shows increasing amplitude improves fidelity but enhances which-branch information leakage from photon loss, yielding an optimal amplitude per transmission distance. For experimentally relevant parameters, optimized average fidelity stays well above the classical benchmark over tens of kilometers.
AI.conclusion: The protocol enables robust, loss-tolerant remote state preparation of an electron-spin qubit, with a possible implementation using diamond nitrogen-vacancy centers.

title: Neural Fourier Surrogates for Data Reuploading Quantum Neural Networks
summary: For quantum machine learning, the exact boundary between classical and quantum advantage is still poorly understood. Direct comparison between quantum neural networks (QNNs) and existing classical models, which encompass fundamentally different function classes, often fails to provide broader insight into the difference between the two. Inspired by the techniques of Neural Quantum States and Random Fourier Features, this work introduces Neural Fourier Surrogates (NFS), a stochastic classical neural network architecture for efficiently learning coefficients over the same finite Fourier series support as quantum neural networks. Testing on a selection of tabular benchmark datasets, we find that NFS is an effective classifier architecture broadly competitive with established classical baselines, including a comparable Random Fourier Features model, and possessing comparable performance to data-reuploading QNNs; combined with additional analysis comparing the learned Fourier spectra of QNNs and NFS on synthetic data, these results establish NFS as a natural classical baseline for evaluating QNN performance.

AI.tldr: Neural Fourier Surrogates (NFS) is a classical stochastic neural network that learns coefficients over the same finite Fourier series support as quantum neural networks, providing a fair classical baseline for evaluating QNN performance.
AI.motivation: The boundary between classical and quantum advantage in quantum machine learning remains poorly understood. Direct comparisons between QNNs and existing classical models are flawed because they span fundamentally different function classes, limiting broader insight into actual quantum-classical differences.
AI.method: Inspired by Neural Quantum States and Random Fourier Features, the authors introduce NFS, a stochastic classical neural network architecture that efficiently learns coefficients over the identical finite Fourier series support used by QNNs, enabling an apples-to-apples comparison.
AI.result: On tabular benchmark datasets, NFS is an effective classifier broadly competitive with established classical baselines (including a comparable Random Fourier Features model) and achieves performance comparable to data-reuploading QNNs. Additional analysis comparing learned Fourier spectra on synthetic data supports these findings.
AI.conclusion: NFS establishes itself as a natural classical baseline for evaluating QNN performance, as it matches the Fourier support of QNNs and offers competitive classification performance.

title: Beyond IP = PSPACE and QIP = PSPACE: Interactive Proofs in Arbitrary Physical Theories
summary: The equalities IP = PSPACE and QIP = PSPACE, the latter achievable with three messages, raise a basic question: how much of an interactive proof's power comes from the underlying physical theory? We study interactive proofs in general probabilistic theories, which include classical and quantum theory. The answer depends on what the prover and verifier exchange and how the theory specifies efficient operations. When they exchange only classical messages, protocols in every theory satisfying our standard assumptions decide exactly PSPACE. For protocols with a quantum verifier and quantum messages, allowing a prover to use any theory containing quantum theory does not increase the maximum acceptance probability. Thus, the three-message PSPACE result remains valid against such provers. When messages may be arbitrary systems, the interactive-proof class can strictly exceed PSPACE.

AI.tldr: Interactive proof power is largely theory-independent for classical messages and quantum-verifier protocols, but can strictly exceed PSPACE when arbitrary physical systems are exchanged.
AI.motivation: The equalities IP = PSPACE and QIP = PSPACE (with three messages) raise the question of how much of an interactive proof's power derives from the underlying physical theory, a basic issue explored by studying interactive proofs in general probabilistic theories.
AI.method: Interactive proofs are analyzed in general probabilistic theories, including classical and quantum theory, distinguishing cases by what prover and verifier exchange and how the theory defines efficient operations. Cases considered: classical messages only, quantum verifier with quantum messages against provers using any theory containing quantum theory, and arbitrary systems as messages.
AI.result: With classical messages only, protocols in every theory satisfying standard assumptions decide exactly PSPACE; with a quantum verifier and quantum messages, letting the prover use any theory containing quantum theory does not increase maximum acceptance probability, so the three-message PSPACE result remains valid against such provers; when messages may be arbitrary systems, the interactive-proof class can strictly exceed PSPACE.
AI.conclusion: The power of interactive proofs depends critically on the message type and the theory's specification of efficient operations: classical-message and quantum-message settings remain PSPACE-bound under broad theory assumptions, but allowing arbitrary systems as messages enables a class strictly larger than PSPACE.

title: From Steane to A7: Quantum Codes from Invariant States
summary:
We construct a two-parameter family of single-error-correcting seven-ququart codes with transversal $\tilde{A_7}$ symmetry, realizing the finite component of a two-qubit super-golden gate set. These $((7,4,3))_4$ codes encode two logical qubits and support non-Clifford operations by applying the same gate to each physical ququart.
  Our method constructs invariant parent states rather than searching directly for a codespace. For $n$ systems of local dimension $q$, suppose the local symmetry is a unitary $t$-group and the permutation symmetry is $t$-transitive. Maximal mixing of all marginals on at most $t$ sites is then equivalent to linear equations in Schur--Weyl sector weights. Every feasible solution yields parents of pure distance at least $t+1$; puncturing one site produces a $q$-dimensional code of distance at least $t$ with the prescribed local symmetry acting transversally.
  Steane and the nonstabilizer Fake Steane code reveal why the construction leaves continuous freedom. They share the same prescribed transversal Clifford and permutation symmetries, and their eight-qubit purifications lie on a circle: error correction fixes two invariant-sector norms but leaves the relative phase free. Keeping the same permutation group and replacing Clifford symmetry by $\tilde{A_7}$ $\leq SU(4)$ gives three fixed sector norms and two free relative phases, producing the new ququart family.

AI.tldr: A two-parameter family of single-error-correcting seven-ququart ((7,4,3))_4 codes with transversal Ã_7 symmetry is constructed by finding invariant parent states via linear equations on Schur–Weyl sector weights, then puncturing one site.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to realize the finite component of a two-qubit super-golden gate set and support non-Clifford operations via transversal gates, motivating a general construction of codes with prescribed transversal local and permutation symmetries.
AI.method: Rather than directly searching for a codespace, the method constructs invariant parent states. For n systems of local dimension q, with local symmetry a unitary t-group and permutation symmetry t-transitive, maximal mixing of all marginals on at most t sites is shown to be equivalent to linear equations in Schur–Weyl sector weights. Feasible solutions yield parents of pure distance at least t+1; puncturing one site gives a q-dimensional code of distance at least t with the prescribed local symmetry acting transversally.
AI.result: The construction yields a two-parameter family of ((7,4,3))_4 codes with transversal Ã_7 symmetry. Comparison with Steane and nonstabilizer Fake Steane codes shows shared Clifford and permutation symmetries with an eight-qubit purification on a circle (two fixed norms, one free phase). Replacing Clifford symmetry by Ã_7 in SU(4) with the same permutation group gives three fixed sector norms and two free relative phases, producing the new ququart family.
AI.conclusion: Invariant parent states with Schur–Weyl sector-weight linear conditions provide a systematic route to transversal-symmetry codes, and the resulting seven-ququart family realizes the finite component of a two-qubit super-golden gate set with non-Clifford transversal operations.

title: A Quantum Phase Neural Network with Multi-Inputs/Single-Output
summary: A 35 input/single output quantum phase neural network (QPNN) is proposed to recognize the English letters' A 'and' B 'composed 7*5 of pixels. Each node of the proposed QPNN has the input with 0 or 1. Through normalization and quantum phase encoding, each set of 35 with 0 or 1 digital inputs is encoded into a quantum superposition state described by 35 quantum phases. Then, a quantum rotation gate is used to introduce adjustable phase, and a controlled NOT gate is used to entangle the relative phase between the two inputs. The relationship between the input and output of the network is derived. This paper also derived the phase weight learning training algorithm with adaptive learning rate. The solutions with the recognition probability of 1 is designed, and the analytical expressions for all adjustable phase solutions with zero errors are not unique. The experimental performance is verified on the Qiskit platform. This paper uses phase drive to convert the probability calculation into an analytical polynomial function with adjustable rotation angles in the network, avoiding the bottleneck of generating all 2^35 complex exponential amplitudes and providing an effective way to solve the "exponential wall" problem, which provides a new implementation solution for the practical application of multi-input recognition problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 35-input/single-output quantum phase neural network (QPNN) that recognizes 7×5 pixel English letters "A" and "B", encoding binary inputs into quantum phases and using rotation/controlled-NOT gates with a phase-weight learning algorithm to achieve zero-error recognition, verified on Qiskit.
AI.motivation: Multi-input pattern recognition faces the "exponential wall": representing all 2^35 complex exponential amplitudes for 35 binary inputs is computationally prohibitive. The authors seek a phase-driven formulation that sidesteps generating the full amplitude state.
AI.method: A 35-input/single-output QPNN is built from binary (0/1) pixel inputs. Inputs are normalized and quantum-phase encoded into a superposition state described by 35 quantum phases. A quantum rotation gate introduces adjustable phases, and a controlled-NOT gate entangles the relative phase between two inputs. The input-output relationship is derived, and a phase-weight learning algorithm with adaptive learning rate is developed; zero-error adjustable-phase solutions are analytically characterized (and shown to be non-unique). Experiments are run on the Qiskit platform.
AI.result: Solutions achieving recognition probability 1 are designed, and analytical expressions for all adjustable-phase zero-error solutions are obtained, showing the solution set is not unique. Experimental performance is verified on Qiskit.
AI.conclusion: Phase drive converts probability computation into an analytical polynomial function of adjustable rotation angles, avoiding the bottleneck of generating all 2^35 complex exponential amplitudes. This offers an effective route to the "exponential wall" problem and a new implementation scheme for practical multi-input recognition.

title: A Gate-Based Quantum Computing Framework for Codon Optimization
summary: Codon optimization is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem with important applications in synthetic biology, protein expression, and biotechnology. While quantum annealing has previously been explored for this problem, the application of gate-based quantum algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present a gate-based quantum computing framework for codon optimization by formulating the optimization objective as an Ising Hamiltonian and expressing it in terms of Pauli operators suitable for gate-based quantum processors. The proposed framework is investigated using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), Sampling Variational Quantum Eigensolver (SVQE), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with benchmarking against exact diagonalization, classical optimization, and quantum annealing. Using a three-amino-acid benchmark, the proposed implementations successfully reproduce the exact ground-state solutions while identifying optimized ansatz selections, optimization strategies, initialization schemes, and hardware execution settings that provide reproducible performance on current noisy quantum hardware. Hardware demonstrations are performed on IBM Quantum processors to evaluate the practical implementation of the proposed workflow. As a work in progress, this study establishes a reproducible computational framework for gate-based quantum codon optimization and provides the foundation for future investigations of larger protein sequences as quantum hardware and algorithms continue to advance.

AI.tldr: This work introduces a gate-based quantum computing framework for codon optimization by mapping the problem to an Ising Hamiltonian, solving it with VQE, SVQE, and QAOA, and benchmarking against classical and quantum-annealing baselines on IBM Quantum hardware.
AI.motivation: Codon optimization is an important combinatorial optimization problem in synthetic biology and protein expression. While quantum annealing has been explored, gate-based quantum algorithms for this problem remain largely unexplored, leaving a gap in the literature.
AI.method: The optimization objective is formulated as an Ising Hamiltonian expressed in terms of Pauli operators suitable for gate-based processors. The framework is implemented using VQE, SVQE, and QAOA, with systematic exploration of ansatz selection, optimization strategies, initialization schemes, and hardware execution settings.
AI.result: On a three-amino-acid benchmark, the implementations reproduce the exact ground-state solutions. Results are benchmarked against exact diagonalization, classical optimization, and quantum annealing, and hardware demonstrations are performed on IBM Quantum processors.
AI.conclusion: As a work in progress, the study establishes a reproducible computational framework for gate-based quantum codon optimization and lays the foundation for scaling to larger protein sequences as quantum hardware and algorithms advance.

title: Telecom-Band Optical Transitions of Erbium Atoms in Rare-Gas Solids
summary: Rare-earth (RE) atoms, such as erbium (Er), have inner-shell optical transitions in the near-infrared, some of which are in the telecom bands. These transitions are largely insensitive to the host environment due to effective shielding by the filled outer shells. Cryogenic rare-gas (RG) solids, such as solid neon (Ne) and argon (Ar), combine high chemical purity with a nearly nuclear-spin-free environment, making them attractive solid hosts for preserving optical and spin coherence. In this work, we isolate neutral Er atoms in solid Ne and Ar at 6 K and characterize their emission by steady-state and time-resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. In both hosts, we observe several near-infrared transitions between 1000--1500 nm, including inner-shell emission in the telecom O and E bands. The $4f \rightarrow 5d$ transition near 1299 nm forms a multiplet of narrow components, consistent with crystal-field splitting, and decays on a microsecond timescale. The $4f \rightarrow 4f$ transition near 1437 nm shows a matrix shift below 1 cm$^{-1}$ in both hosts. In solid Ne, its inhomogeneous linewidth is bounded by the spectrometer resolution to < 22 GHz, and its PL lifetime reaches up to 78.9 ms, close to the estimated radiative limit. Thermal annealing extends the 1437 nm lifetime in Ne and suppresses the phonon sidebands relative to the zero-phonon lines in Ar. These results identify RG solids as promising hosts for long-lived telecom-band Er emission and provide a foundation for future spin-photon interfaces and hybrid quantum architectures.

AI.tldr: Neutral Er atoms are isolated in solid Ne and Ar at 6 K, showing narrow telecom-band inner-shell emission with lifetimes up to 78.9 ms, identifying rare-gas solids as promising hosts for long-lived Er-based spin-photon interfaces.
AI.motivation: Erbium's inner-shell near-infrared transitions, some in telecom bands, are largely host-insensitive due to shielding by filled outer shells, making them attractive for quantum photonics. Rare-gas solids such as solid Ne and Ar offer high chemical purity and a nearly nuclear-spin-free environment, which could preserve both optical and spin coherence. However, the behavior of isolated neutral Er atoms in these hosts had not been characterized, motivating a systematic spectroscopic study.
AI.method: Neutral Er atoms were isolated in solid Ne and Ar at 6 K. Their emission was characterized by steady-state and time-resolved photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy. The effects of thermal annealing on emission lifetimes and phonon sidebands were also examined.
AI.result: Several near-infrared transitions between 1000 and 1500 nm were observed in both hosts, including inner-shell emission in the telecom O and E bands. The 4f→5d transition near 1299 nm forms a narrow multiplet consistent with crystal-field splitting and decays on a microsecond timescale. The 4f→4f transition near 1437 nm shows a matrix shift below 1 cm⁻¹ in both hosts. In solid Ne its inhomogeneous linewidth is bounded by spectrometer resolution to < 22 GHz, with a PL lifetime up to 78.9 ms, close to the estimated radiative limit. Thermal annealing extends the 1437 nm lifetime in Ne and suppresses phonon sidebands relative to zero-phonon lines in Ar.
AI.conclusion: Rare-gas solids are identified as promising hosts for long-lived telecom-band Er emission, providing a foundation for future spin-photon interfaces and hybrid quantum architectures.

title: TATVA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Quantum Circuit Synthesis
summary: One of the most important initial steps in quantum computing is high-fidelity quantum state preparation, because errors in it can affect the final computational result. Therefore, one of the major challenges is to design a quantum circuit that can achieve the desired target state accurately with a smaller number of gates. Traditionally, circuits are designed using predefined rules and mathematical decompositions, but this makes it difficult to design circuits for different and complex target states. This paper presents TATVA, a reinforcement learning (RL) system for synthesizing quantum circuits. TATVA views circuit synthesis as a sequential decision problem in which the agents select one gate at a time and calculate the fidelity after each applied gate, with the gate producing the highest fidelity selected for the circuit. The system introduces a parallel architecture that uses two RL agents, Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), along with Qiskit's statevector simulator. The system can synthesize up to 5 qubits while achieving a fidelity of 0.999999 and producing compact circuits. After achieving the desired fidelity, it performs a post-hoc optimization step that reduces the circuit depth while preserving the achieved fidelity. The circuit is finalized using fidelity, success rate, gate count, and circuit depth. Target states that are not used during training are used to test whether the system has learned effectively and can generalize beyond the training states. This approach aims to enable automatic quantum circuit synthesis with high fidelity using reinforcement learning.

AI.tldr: TATVA is a reinforcement learning system that synthesizes high-fidelity quantum circuits for quantum state preparation, using dual RL agents and a statevector simulator to achieve fidelity up to 0.999999 for up to 5 qubits, with post-hoc optimization to reduce circuit depth.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity quantum state preparation is a critical initial step in quantum computing, as errors can affect final computational results. A key challenge is designing quantum circuits that reach the target state accurately with fewer gates. Traditional rule-based and mathematical-decomposition circuit design struggles to handle diverse and complex target states, motivating an automated approach.
AI.method: TATVA treats circuit synthesis as a sequential decision problem where agents select one gate at a time and compute fidelity after each applied gate, choosing the gate yielding highest fidelity. It employs a parallel architecture with two RL agents, Deep Q-Network (DQN) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), integrated with Qiskit's statevector simulator. After reaching desired fidelity, a post-hoc optimization step reduces circuit depth while preserving fidelity.
AI.result: TATVA can synthesize circuits up to 5 qubits, achieving fidelity of 0.999999 while producing compact circuits. Circuits are evaluated using fidelity, success rate, gate count, and circuit depth. Target states not used during training are used to test generalization beyond training states.
AI.conclusion: The approach enables automatic quantum circuit synthesis with high fidelity using reinforcement learning, demonstrating effective generalization and compact, optimized circuits.

title: Sublinear-depth Quantum Simulation of Electrons with Atomic Orbitals
summary: Discretizing electronic degrees of freedom into atomic orbitals is the default choice to accurately model electrons in molecules in a compact and flexible way. We consider the task of simulating such electronic structure models on a quantum computer for $N$ orbitals, keeping the number of orbitals per atom constant. Atomic orbitals give rise to Hamiltonians with potentially up to $\mathcal{O}(N^4)$ terms and little structure, which made it challenging to match the complexity of methods based on plane waves and real-space grids. In this work, we show that a Trotter step for atomic orbitals can be implemented in depth $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{polylog}(N))$ without ancillas by combining a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits. By bounding the Trotter error, we obtain sublinear simulation depth, and our total gate count $N^{5/3 + o(1)}$ matches the best scaling known for any basis.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a Trotter step for atomic-orbital electronic-structure Hamiltonians can be implemented in polylogarithmic depth without ancillas, and that the total gate count scales as N^{5/3+o(1)}, matching the best known scaling for any basis.
AI.motivation: Atomic orbitals are the default compact and flexible basis for modeling electrons in molecules, but they yield Hamiltonians with up to O(N^4) terms and little structure, making it difficult to match the complexity of plane-wave and real-space-grid methods on a quantum computer.
AI.method: The authors combine a rigorous treatment of orbital localization, a hierarchical Hamiltonian decomposition based on the Fast Multipole Method, and shallow quantum Fourier arithmetic circuits, together with a bound on the Trotter error.
AI.result: A Trotter step for atomic orbitals is implemented in depth O(polylog(N)) without ancillas, yielding sublinear simulation depth and a total gate count of N^{5/3+o(1)}, matching the best scaling known for any basis.
AI.conclusion: Atomic-orbital-based quantum simulation can achieve depth and gate-count scaling competitive with plane-wave and real-space-grid approaches, despite the unfavorable term count and structure of the underlying Hamiltonians.

title: Exact $T$-counts of Toffoli layers from an isotropy bound
summary: The $T$-count is the dominant cost of fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ computation. We prove that a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates, the diagonal core of a parallel Toffoli layer, needs exactly $6m+1$ $T$ gates in every Hadamard-free Clifford+$T$ circuit with clean ancillas. Campbell and Howard gave the matching construction. To our knowledge this is the first proof that it is optimal for general $m$ (for $m=1$ the value $7$ is classical, and Campbell and Howard state the value $13$ at $m=2$). On every controlled unitary the same floor comes within one of their exact count, and it recovers their $4m+3$ for a fan-out of $m$ Toffolis from one control. The proof rests on an isotropy constraint: for a pure-cubic phase, the vectors recording which $T$ gates touch each qubit span a totally isotropic subspace. In general the constraint gives the isotropy floor $δ\ge2(n-d^{\ast})-r$ for every diagonal level-three gate, computed from the phase polynomial in polynomial time. The floor is never below stabilizer nullity $ν$, which equals $n-d^{\ast}$ on this class, and a separate parity argument raises it to $2ν+1$ on non-Clifford pure-cubic gates. On the output of the TODD optimizer for the $24$ benchmark circuits it completes, the floor certifies $193$ of its $311$ merged phase-polynomial blocks optimal for their Hadamard layering ($186$ to $193$ across five optimizer seeds), against $113$ for nullity. The floor also holds, under stated conditions, for circuits whose only internal Hadamards form unitarily uncomputed temporary AND blocks, while under adaptive feedforward only $t\geν$ is proved.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates requires exactly $6m+1$ $T$ gates in any Hadamard-free Clifford+$T$ circuit with clean ancillas, establishing the first general- $m$ optimality proof, via a totally isotropic subspace constraint that yields a broadly applicable isotropy lower bound on $T$ -count.
AI.motivation: The $T$ -count dominates the cost of fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ quantum computation, so tight lower bounds on $T$ -gate usage are central to resource estimation and to judging the optimality of synthesis and optimizer outputs. Prior to this work, exact optimality for a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates was known only for $m=1$ (value 7) and stated for $m=2$ (value 13); no proof existed for general $m$ , and stabilizer nullity alone gave weaker bounds.
AI.method: The authors analyze Hadamard-free Clifford+$T$ circuits with clean ancillas and prove a lower bound via an isotropy constraint: for a pure-cubic phase, the vectors recording which $T$ gates touch each qubit span a totally isotropic subspace. This yields the isotropy floor $δ≥2(n−d* )−r$ for every diagonal level-three gate, computable in polynomial time from the phase polynomial, and a separate parity argument raises it to $2ν+1$ on non-Clifford pure-cubic gates.
AI.result: A layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates needs exactly $6m+1$ $T$ gates in every Hadamard-free Clifford+$T$ circuit with clean ancillas, matching the Campbell–Howard construction. The same floor lies within one of their exact count for every controlled unitary, and recovers their $4m+3$ for a fan-out of $m$ Toffolis from one control. On the output of the TODD optimizer for 24 benchmark circuits, the floor certifies 193 of 311 merged phase-polynomial blocks optimal for their Hadamard layering (186–193 across five optimizer seeds), versus 113 for nullity.
AI.conclusion: The isotropy floor provides a polynomial-time, general- $m$ lower bound on $T$ -count that strictly generalizes and strengthens the stabilizer-nullity bound (which it never falls below), and it empirically certifies a large fraction of optimizer-produced blocks as optimal. The bound also extends, under stated conditions, to circuits whose only internal Hadamards form unitarily uncomputed temporary AND blocks, though under adaptive feedforward only the weaker bound $t≥ν$ is proved.

title: Device-Independent Conference Keys from Parity-Extended Games
summary: Device-independent conference key agreement (DI-CKA) lets a group of parties establish a shared secret key from untrusted quantum devices, with security certified by non-locality. Existing DI-CKA protocols are each built around a single Bell inequality, typically a multiparty variant of the CHSH game. DI-QKD protocols, in contrast, have been built from a much richer landscape of non-local games, and it has remained unclear how to carry this landscape over to the conference setting. We introduce $\textit{Parity-$G$ games}$, which extend any two-player game $G$ to $N$ players, for every $N$, provided $G$ has an optimal strategy in which one player measures Pauli observables. The extension preserves the quantum and classical values of $G$, and the security of the resulting $N$-party protocol follows from an analysis of the two-player game alone. Our framework recovers the Parity-CHSH game of Ribeiro, Murta and Wehner (Phys. Rev. A, 2018) as a special case. Applied to the Mermin--Peres Magic Square Game, it yields a new $N$-player pseudo-telepathy game, the $\textit{Parity Magic Square Game}$, which ideal devices win in every round. We use it to construct the $\textit{first}$ DI-CKA protocol based on a pseudo-telepathy game. We prove the protocol secure against coherent attacks. It produces up to two key bits per round, and at low noise its key rate exceeds that of the DI-CKA protocol based on the Parity-CHSH game.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Parity-G games, a family of N-player non-local games extending any two-player game G that admits an optimal strategy using Pauli measurements. This extension preserves quantum and classical values and enables security analysis via the two-player game, generalizing the Parity-CHSH game. Applying it to the Mermin-Peres Magic Square yields the Parity Magic Square Game, a pseudo-telepathy game used to construct the first DI-CKA protocol based on pseudo-telepathy, proven secure against coherent attacks, generating up to two key bits per round with a higher low-noise key rate than Parity-CHSH DI-CKA.
AI.motivation: Existing DI-CKA protocols are each limited to a single Bell inequality, typically a multiparty CHSH variant, whereas DI-QKD has exploited a much richer landscape of non-local games. It was unclear how to transfer this diversity of non-local games to the conference (multiparty key agreement) setting.
AI.method: The authors define Parity-G games, which extend any two-player game G to N players for all N, provided G has an optimal strategy in which one player measures Pauli observables. The construction preserves both quantum and classical values of G and permits the security of the resulting N-party protocol to be established from the two-player game alone. They apply this framework to the Mermin-Peres Magic Square Game, producing the Parity Magic Square Game, and use it to build a DI-CKA protocol, proving security against coherent attacks.
AI.result: The framework recovers the Parity-CHSH game of Ribeiro, Murta, and Wehner (2018) as a special case. Applied to the Mermin-Peres Magic Square Game, it gives a new N-player pseudo-telepathy game, the Parity Magic Square Game, which ideal devices win in every round. This yields the first DI-CKA protocol based on a pseudo-telepathy game, proven secure against coherent attacks, producing up to two key bits per round, and achieving a key rate that exceeds the Parity-CHSH-based DI-CKA at low noise.
AI.conclusion: Parity-G games provide a general and composable route to extend two-player non-local games to the multiparty conference setting while retaining favorable quantum/classical values and enabling security proofs from two-player analysis. This uncovers new pseudo-telepathy-based DI-CKA protocols, notably the Parity Magic Square Game protocol, which is secure against coherent attacks and outperforms prior Parity-CHSH DI-CKA in the low-noise regime.

title: Function-like pseudorandom unitaries generate pseudorandom quantum processes
summary: Haar-random unitaries provide a canonical model of generic random quantum evolution, but they typically have exponential description and circuit complexity. Although pseudorandom unitaries efficiently emulate a single Haar-random unitary, many tasks require an entire reusable family of independently random-looking operations. We introduce pseudorandom function-like unitaries (PRFU), which generate such a family indexed by public labels using only a single short key. We distinguish classical- and coherent-label access and establish security under adaptive quantum queries. For classical labels, we provide a generic construction from a post-quantum pseudorandom function and a pseudorandom unitary. For coherent labels, we use an indexed path-recording framework to analyze interference across labels and prove security of a construction based on quantum-secure function and permutation primitives. We further show that PRFUs generate pseudorandom channels and quantum combs with private memory, which are secure against adaptive interventions and concurrent sessions. Combining PRFUs with unitary gluing yields a one-key family of pseudorandom unitaries whose supported register widths can be chosen after key generation. Further applications include nonce-resolved quantum authentication, coherently masked QRAM queries, and efficient emulation of random multi-time dynamics. Our results extend quantum pseudorandomness from individual operations to efficiently generated families of random-looking quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces pseudorandom function-like unitaries (PRFUs), which generate a reusable family of random-looking quantum operations from a single short key, extending quantum pseudorandomness from individual unitaries to efficiently generated families.
AI.motivation: Haar-random unitaries model generic random quantum evolution but have exponential description and circuit complexity, and while pseudorandom unitaries efficiently emulate a single Haar-random unitary, many tasks require an entire reusable family of independently random-looking operations indexed by labels.
AI.method: The authors define PRFUs with public labels and a single short key, distinguishing classical- and coherent-label access and establishing security under adaptive quantum queries. For classical labels they give a generic construction from a post-quantum pseudorandom function and a pseudorandom unitary; for coherent labels they use an indexed path-recording framework to analyze interference across labels and prove security of a construction based on quantum-secure function and permutation primitives.
AI.result: PRFUs are shown to generate pseudorandom channels and quantum combs with private memory that are secure against adaptive interventions and concurrent sessions. Combining PRFUs with unitary gluing yields a one-key family of pseudorandom unitaries whose supported register widths can be chosen after key generation. Further applications include nonce-resolved quantum authentication, coherently masked QRAM queries, and efficient emulation of random multi-time dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The results extend quantum pseudorandomness from individual operations to efficiently generated families of random-looking quantum dynamics.

title: Learned Parallel Bit-Flipping Sequential Belief Propagation Decoding of Quantum LDPC Codes
summary: Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their practical use requires fast, low-complexity, and reliable decoders. Belief propagation (BP) is attractive because of its local message-passing structure, yet standard flooding BP often suffers from convergence failures on QLDPC codes due to short cycles, degeneracy, and symmetric decoding trajectories. Learned sequential BP improves convergence by using a reinforcement-learning policy to choose variable-node update orders, but a single learned trajectory can still be sensitive to unfavorable local Pauli decisions. We propose a learned parallel bit-flipping sequential BP decoder with a new quaternary score combining syndrome gain, a quantized Pauli log-likelihood penalty, and Q-table lookahead at hypothetical post-flip states. Our decoder first runs learned sequential BP for a fixed number of iterations. If the syndrome is not satisfied, it constructs quaternary bit-flipping candidates, each corresponding to changing the current Pauli decision of one qubit. The selected candidates initialize independent learned sequential BP continuations from the same decoder state. Since these continuations are independent, they can be executed in parallel, so testing several candidates mainly increases parallel hardware resources rather than sequential decoding latency. Simulations on representative QLDPC codes over the depolarizing channel show that the proposed decoder improves the reliability of learned sequential BP while having a parallel low-latency structure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a learned parallel bit-flipping sequential BP decoder for QLDPC codes that uses a quaternary score (syndrome gain, quantized Pauli log-likelihood penalty, Q-table lookahead) to branch into independent parallel BP continuations when standard learned sequential BP fails to converge.
AI.motivation: QLDPC codes promise low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation, but need fast, low-complexity, reliable decoders. Standard flooding BP fails to converge on QLDPC codes due to short cycles, degeneracy, and symmetric decoding trajectories. Learned sequential BP improves convergence via an RL policy selecting variable-node update orders, yet a single learned trajectory remains sensitive to unfavorable local Pauli decisions.
AI.method: The decoder first runs learned sequential BP for a fixed number of iterations. If the syndrome is unsatisfied, it constructs quaternary bit-flipping candidates, each flipping the current Pauli decision of one qubit, ranked by a new quaternary score combining syndrome gain, a quantized Pauli log-likelihood penalty, and Q-table lookahead at hypothetical post-flip states. Selected candidates initialize independent learned sequential BP continuations from the same decoder state; being independent, these run in parallel, trading parallel hardware for latency.
AI.result: Simulations on representative QLDPC codes over the depolarizing channel show improved reliability over learned sequential BP while retaining a parallel, low-latency structure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed learned parallel bit-flipping sequential BP decoder enhances the reliability of learned sequential BP and offers a parallel low-latency implementation, making it a promising direction for practical QLDPC decoding.

title: The stationarity test: a framework for learning quantum many-body systems from their thermal states
summary:
The task of learning the Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum system, given samples of its thermal (or 'Gibbs') states, is a foundational question at the intersection of quantum learning theory and many-body physics. In this paper, we draw connections to the quantum Gibbs sampling literature to introduce a natural learning algorithm we call the stationarity test: which simply "guesses" the Hamiltonian, and measures the rate-of-change of local observables, under the associated detailed-balanced quantum Markov chain [CKG23]. We leverage the stationarity test to address the following applications:
  1. To give the first learning algorithm for the underlying interaction graph, i.e. structure learning, of lattice Hamiltonians at all temperatures, given copies of their Gibbs states.
  2. To give the first learning algorithm for the coefficients of a lattice Hamiltonian, given only copies of its thermal metastable states, modeled as the "local minima" of the free energy.
  3. In addition, we present a refinement to the recent area law for thermal metastable states [BCV25], which holds in the thermodynamic limit.
  Our learning algorithms are rigorous, time-efficient, and nearly sample-optimal in system size and accuracy. At a technical level, our arguments are based on new approximate locality and convexity properties for the quantum Fisher information of these Gibbs sampling algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "stationarity test" that connects quantum Gibbs sampling to Hamiltonian learning, yielding the first algorithms for learning the interaction graph and coefficients of lattice Hamiltonians from Gibbs and thermal metastable states, plus a refinement of a thermal area law.
AI.motivation: Learning the Hamiltonian interactions governing a quantum system from samples of its thermal (Gibbs) states is a foundational problem at the intersection of quantum learning theory and many-body physics. Prior work lacked algorithms for structure learning of lattice Hamiltonians at all temperatures and for learning coefficients from metastable states.
AI.method: The authors draw connections to quantum Gibbs sampling literature and introduce a stationarity test: it guesses the Hamiltonian and measures the rate-of-change of local observables under the associated detailed-balanced quantum Markov chain [CKG23]. Technically, the arguments rely on new approximate locality and convexity properties of the quantum Fisher information of these Gibbs sampling algorithms.
AI.result: The stationarity test yields: (1) the first learning algorithm for the underlying interaction graph (structure learning) of lattice Hamiltonians at all temperatures from Gibbs state copies; (2) the first algorithm for learning lattice Hamiltonian coefficients from thermal metastable states modeled as free-energy local minima; (3) a refinement of the recent thermal metastable area law [BCV25] valid in the thermodynamic limit. The algorithms are rigorous, time-efficient, and nearly sample-optimal in system size and accuracy.
AI.conclusion: By linking Hamiltonian learning to quantum Gibbs sampling via the stationarity test, the paper achieves new, provably efficient and nearly sample-optimal learning guarantees for lattice Hamiltonians, and refines a thermal area law.

title: Quantum synchronization in atom-cavity coupled systems
summary: We consider a cavity quantum electrodynamics (CQED) setup where an ensemble of spin-1 atoms driven by a classical field interacts with two driven cavity field modes. We show that the two sub-systems - the atoms and the two-mode cavity field, exhibit limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on the cavity drive strengths and other system parameters. In order to visualize the limit cycle and synchronization in the field, we introduce generalized two-mode field Husimi-Q function using SU(2) coherent states. For atomic spin states, we make use of spin-1 Husimi-Q function to visualize the same. We further corroborate the occurrence of field synchronization and limit cycle by analyzing $U(1)$ symmetry breaking, Wigner quasi-probability distribution, coherence properties of reduced field density matrix. Our results reveal intriguing interplay between the limit-cycle and quantum synchronization behavior, highlighting emergent quantum phenomena in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems. Additionally, we calculate Wehrl mutual information between the two modes and find that the field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are mutually exclusive. Our study would be important to extract quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.

AI.tldr: A driven spin-1 atomic ensemble interacting with two driven cavity modes exhibits limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on drive strengths, visualized via generalized two-mode and spin-1 Husimi-Q functions, corroborated by symmetry breaking, Wigner distributions, and coherence analysis; field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are found to be mutually exclusive.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to explore emergent quantum phenomena—specifically limit-cycle and quantum synchronization—in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems, and to understand their interplay, with potential implications for extracting quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.
AI.method: The authors study a CQED setup with a spin-1 atomic ensemble driven by a classical field interacting with two driven cavity modes. They introduce a generalized two-mode field Husimi-Q function using SU(2) coherent states and a spin-1 Husimi-Q function for atomic states to visualize limit cycles and synchronization. They further analyze U(1) symmetry breaking, Wigner quasi-probability distribution, and coherence properties of the reduced field density matrix, and compute Wehrl mutual information between the two modes.
AI.result: The atoms and the two-mode cavity field exhibit limit-cycle or quantum synchronization depending on cavity drive strengths and other parameters. Field synchronization is corroborated by U(1) symmetry breaking, Wigner distributions, and coherence properties. Field synchronization and Wehrl mutual information are found to be mutually exclusive.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal an intriguing interplay between limit-cycle and quantum synchronization behavior, highlighting emergent quantum phenomena in driven dissipative interacting quantum systems. The study is expected to be important for extracting quantum advantages in quantum metrology using coupled atom-cavity systems.

title: Constant-Per-Layer-Depth MPS-Pretrained Ansatz for Noisy Distributed Quantum Processors
comment: 24 pages, 8 figures; Supplementary Information (22 pages) appended
summary: Distributed quantum processors could scale variational algorithms beyond single devices, but circuit depth, communication overhead, and noise limit their performance. We compare ladder, mixed-canonical, and brick-wall realizations of matrix-product-state (MPS) pretraining with matched per-layer two-qubit-block resources. Despite comparable ideal variational quantum eigensolver performance and gradient scales, the shallower brick-wall architecture reduces circuit duration, idle-time decoherence, and zero-noise-extrapolation (ZNE) overhead, yielding superior noisy and ZNE-assisted performance. We then extend MPS-pretrained circuits to modular processors with one communication qubit per quantum processing unit (QPU); a nearest-neighbor QPU-path schedule keeps the per-layer depth constant as QPUs are added. Distributed circuits whose inter-QPU links realize long-range interactions of the target Hamiltonian match or outperform the single-processor brick-wall under noise when communication idle time is short compared with the coherence time. These results establish hardware-aware co-design of tensor-network pretraining, circuit scheduling, and communication topology as a principle for variational quantum computation on noisy modular hardware.

AI.tldr: This work benchmarks MPS-pretraining circuit architectures and extends them to modular quantum processors, showing that hardware-aware co-design of circuit depth, scheduling, and communication topology improves noisy variational performance.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum processors can scale variational algorithms beyond single devices, but circuit depth, communication overhead, and noise constrain performance. There is a need for hardware-aware design that jointly optimizes tensor-network pretraining, circuit scheduling, and communication topology under realistic noise.
AI.method: The authors compare ladder, mixed-canonical, and brick-wall realizations of matrix-product-state (MPS) pretraining under matched per-layer two-qubit-block resources. They then extend MPS-pretrained circuits to modular processors with one communication qubit per QPU, using a nearest-neighbor QPU-path schedule that holds per-layer depth constant as QPUs are added.
AI.result: Ideal variational quantum eigensolver performance and gradient scales are comparable across architectures, but the shallower brick-wall design reduces circuit duration, idle-time decoherence, and ZNE overhead, giving better noisy and ZNE-assisted results. In the distributed setting, circuits whose inter-QPU links realize long-range Hamiltonian interactions match or outperform the single-processor brick-wall under noise when communication idle time is short relative to coherence time.
AI.conclusion: Hardware-aware co-design of tensor-network pretraining, circuit scheduling, and communication topology is established as a guiding principle for variational quantum computation on noisy modular hardware.

title: Dissipation-Sensitivity Trade-Off in Dissipative Bosonic Systems
summary: We discover a universal trade-off between the dissipation required to maintain a quantum state more sensitive than a thermal one and the sensitivity gain for a driven single-mode bosonic system under a thermal environment. Specifically, for Gaussian states, we rigorously derive a lower bound on the entropy production rate in the steady state in terms of the quantum Fisher information gain relative to a thermal reference state. Numerical investigations of Kerr nonlinearities further support that these bounds can hold beyond the Gaussian regime. Our results establish a new connection between steady-state thermodynamics and quantum metrological performance.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a universal trade-off showing that maintaining a bosonic steady state more sensitive than a thermal state requires a minimum entropy production rate that scales with the metrological (quantum Fisher information) gain, and evidences this bound beyond Gaussian regimes.
AI.motivation: Quantum states offering sensitivity beyond the thermal noise limit are valuable for metrology, but under a thermal environment they generally require dissipation (entropy production) to be sustained in steady state. The relationship between this thermodynamic cost and the achievable metrological advantage was not previously quantified, motivating a formal link between steady-state thermodynamics and quantum metrological performance.
AI.method: Focus on a driven single-mode bosonic system in a thermal environment. For Gaussian states, rigorously derive a lower bound on the steady-state entropy production rate expressed in terms of the quantum Fisher information gain relative to a thermal reference state. Complement the analytical treatment with numerical investigations of Kerr nonlinearities to test validity beyond the Gaussian regime.
AI.result: A rigorous lower bound is obtained: the steady-state entropy production rate is bounded below by a function of the quantum Fisher information gain over the thermal reference. Numerical Kerr-nonlinearity studies indicate the same trade-off holds beyond Gaussian states.
AI.conclusion: A universal trade-off connects the dissipation needed to sustain a thermally non-classical sensitivity advantage with the metrological gain itself, establishing a new bridge between steady-state thermodynamics and quantum metrology.

title: Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing
summary: We develop Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing for designing matrix-valued transformations of multiple noncommuting nonnormal block-encoded matrices. Our framework equips quantum transducers with the analytic structure of multiport Infinite-Impulse-Response (IIR) filters and establishes a transfer-function methodology for designing quantum query algorithms.
