Efficiently computable analytic bounds that hold uniformly across the oracle promise yield efficient quantum circuits with logarithmic error dependence and near-unity success probability, paralleling the approximation-theoretic guarantees of univariate QSP/QSVT. We provide a complete characterization of achievable transfer functions and a principled library of analytic IIR components. Our modular designs greatly improve or resolve the per-oracle query complexity of open multi-oracle problems: (1) Hamiltonian simulation under $H=\sum_j H_j$ with weighted quasinorm cost $\approx t\langle\vecλ,\vec C\rangle_{1/2}+\mathcal{O}(\|\vec C\|_1\log(1/ε))$ for block-encoding normalizations $\vecλ$ and costs $\vec C$; (2) sparse simulation with optimal time--norm $Θ(\sqrt{d}\|H\|_{\rm 1\to2}t)$ and additive error dependence; (3) solving linear systems and (4) differential equations under minimal matrix assumptions with optimal weighted state-preparation and multi-term cost; (5) ground-state preparation and energy estimation; (6) generalized eigenvalue problems. We apply these to exactly simulate downfolded Hamiltonians with leading cost $t\langle\vecλ_{\rm eff},\vec C_{\rm eff}\rangle_{1/2}$ further reduced by fractional dynamic correlation energy contributions from coarse-grained Hamiltonians, and show similar classical-data-input-reduction results for multiscale graph classification via Kron reduction. We also show the online generalization with anisotropic Kalman filtering of streaming quantum data.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Multivariate Quantum Signal Processing (Multivariate QSP), a framework that designs matrix-valued transformations of multiple noncommuting, nonnormal block-encoded matrices by equipping quantum transducers with the analytic structure of multiport Infinite-Impulse-Response (IIR) filters. It yields efficient quantum circuits with logarithmic error dependence and near-unity success probability, provides a complete characterization of achievable transfer functions, and resolves or improves per-oracle query complexity for numerous multi-oracle problems.
AI.motivation: Existing univariate QSP/QSVT handles single (or commuting) block-encoded operators and cannot naturally design transformations of multiple noncommuting, nonnormal matrices. Many open multi-oracle problems—Hamiltonian simulation of sums, sparse simulation, linear systems, differential equations, ground-state preparation, and generalized eigenvalue problems—require a principled multivariate framework with approximation-theoretic guarantees comparable to those of univariate QSP.
AI.method: The authors develop Multivariate QSP by establishing an analogy between quantum transducers and multiport IIR filters, deriving a transfer-function methodology for designing quantum query algorithms. They prove efficiently computable analytic bounds holding uniformly across the oracle promise, characterize the full set of achievable transfer functions, and build a modular library of analytic IIR components. This supports online generalization via anisotropic Kalman filtering of streaming quantum data.
AI.result: The framework delivers efficient quantum circuits with logarithmic error dependence and near-unity success probability. It resolves or greatly improves per-oracle query complexity for: (1) Hamiltonian simulation under H=ΣH_j with weighted quasinorm cost ≈ t⟨λ⃗,C⃗⟩_{1/2}+O(‖C⃗‖₁log(1/ε)); (2) sparse simulation with optimal time–norm Θ(√d‖H‖_{1→2}t) and additive error dependence; (3) linear systems and (4) differential equations under minimal matrix assumptions with optimal weighted state-preparation and multi-term cost; (5) ground-state preparation and energy estimation; (6) generalized eigenvalue problems. Applications include exactly simulating downfolded Hamiltonians with leading cost t⟨λ⃗_eff,C⃗_eff⟩_{1/2}, further reduced by fractional dynamic correlation energy from coarse-grained Hamiltonians, plus classical-data-input-reduction results for multiscale graph classification via Kron reduction.
AI.conclusion: Multivariate QSP generalizes QSP/QSVT to multiple noncommuting, nonnormal block-encoded matrices, providing a transfer-function design methodology with strong approximation-theoretic guarantees. It unifies and advances the per-oracle query complexity of a broad class of multi-oracle problems and extends to online/streaming settings, demonstrating wide applicability across simulation, linear algebra, and graph-classification tasks.

title: Classical Hardness of Learning Functions of Hamiltonians
summary: Morohoshi, Nakayama, Manabe, and Mitarai proposed a physically motivated quantum machine learning problem in which the goal is to predict quantities of the form $\operatorname{Tr}[f(H)ρ]$ from classical descriptions of a Hamiltonian $H$ and a quantum state $ρ$, where $f$ is an unknown function. We call this problem Hamiltonian function learning in this paper. They constructed an efficient quantum learning algorithm under suitable conditions, while leaving a rigorous proof of average-case classical hardness open. In this paper, we rigorously prove the average-case classical hardness for two distribution-specific Hamiltonian function learning problems for $f_{\cos,π}(λ)=\cos(πλ)$ and $f_{\exp,β}(λ)=e^{-βλ}$ discussed in the paper of Morohoshi et al. under the assumption of the average-case hardness of factoring random RSA moduli. More specifically, we show that an efficient classical randomized learner under squared loss whose output hypotheses are evaluable in classical polynomial time for either problem would yield a classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm for factoring random RSA moduli.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously proves average-case classical hardness of two distribution-specific Hamiltonian function learning problems, showing that an efficient classical learner for either would imply a polynomial-time algorithm for factoring random RSA moduli.
AI.motivation: Morohoshi et al. proposed Hamiltonian function learning—predicting Tr[f(H)ρ] from classical descriptions of H and ρ—and gave an efficient quantum algorithm, but left open a rigorous proof of average-case classical hardness. This paper fills that gap.
AI.method: A reduction-based hardness argument: under the assumption of average-case hardness of factoring random RSA moduli, the authors show that any efficient classical randomized learner under squared loss with classically polynomial-time evaluable hypotheses for either problem yields a classical randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm for random RSA moduli.
AI.result: Average-case classical hardness is established for two distribution-specific Hamiltonian function learning problems, corresponding to f_cos,π(λ)=cos(πλ) and f_exp,β(λ)=e^{-βλ}, assuming the average-case hardness of factoring random RSA moduli.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the missing rigorous average-case classical hardness proof for the problems discussed by Morohoshi et al., supporting a quantum advantage for Hamiltonian function learning under a standard cryptographic assumption.

title: Robustness hierarchy of bipartite quantum correlations under noisy dynamics
summary: Quantum correlations are fragile under noise, motivating quantitative measures that track not only their presence but also their degradation during physical evolution. We develop a robustness framework for the hierarchy of Bell nonlocality, EPR steering, and entanglement, establishing an ordering of the corresponding robustness measures and relating robustness to noise-induced transition times. We further formulate the instantaneous robustness decay along Lindblad dynamics as a directional derivative determined by both the evolution and the robustness functional. Applications to isotropic depolarizing noise and amplitude damping illustrate, respectively, the resulting resource transition times and the directional dependence of steering robustness. The framework provides an approach to characterizing the degradation and lifetime of bipartite quantum correlations under noisy dynamics.

AI.tldr: A robustness framework is developed for the hierarchy of Bell nonlocality, EPR steering, and entanglement, ordering the robustness measures, linking robustness to noise-induced transition times, and formulating instantaneous robustness decay as a directional derivative under Lindblad dynamics.
AI.motivation: Quantum correlations are fragile under noise, so quantitative measures are needed that track not only their presence but also their degradation during physical evolution.
AI.method: The authors build a robustness framework for the hierarchy of Bell nonlocality, EPR steering, and entanglement; establish an ordering of the corresponding robustness measures; relate robustness to noise-induced transition times; and formulate instantaneous robustness decay along Lindblad dynamics as a directional derivative determined by both the evolution and the robustness functional.
AI.result: An ordering of robustness measures across the correlation hierarchy is established, robustness is connected to noise-induced transition times, and instantaneous robustness decay is expressed as a directional derivative. Applications to isotropic depolarizing noise and amplitude damping illustrate resource transition times and the directional dependence of steering robustness, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an approach to characterizing the degradation and lifetime of bipartite quantum correlations under noisy dynamics.

title: Vector chiral order and dynamical quantum phase transitions in an Ising chain with dimerized anisotropic Gamma interaction
summary: We investigate a transverse-field Ising chain with dimerized anisotropic Gamma interactions and demonstrate that, both in the absence and presence of Ising interactions, the competition between Gamma anisotropy and the transverse field gives rise to vector chiral order and dynamical quantum phase transitions. The phase diagram comprises positive and negative vector chiral phases and a paramagnetic phase, characterized by the vector spin chirality and the vector chiral order parameter. In the absence of Ising interactions, we identify a gapless critical line that exhibits no finite-size drift, along which the spin-spin correlations and subsystem entanglement entropy display behavior distinct from that of Ising criticality. Furthermore, we find that the critical times of dynamical quantum phase transitions form periodic or aperiodic sequences, depending on the quench path. Our findings highlight how dimerized off-diagonal exchange enriches both equilibrium ordering and dynamical critical behavior in a quantum Ising chain.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a dimerized anisotropic transverse-field Ising chain with Gamma (off-diagonal) interactions, showing that Gamma anisotropy competes with the transverse field to produce vector chiral order and dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs), with a rich phase diagram and distinct critical behavior.
AI.motivation: Off-diagonal (Gamma) exchange interactions in quantum spin chains are less understood than conventional Ising couplings, and the interplay between dimerized Gamma anisotropy and a transverse field remains largely unexplored. The authors aim to clarify how this competition affects both equilibrium ordering and non-equilibrium critical dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze a transverse-field Ising chain with dimerized anisotropic Gamma interactions, with and without Ising interactions, using phase-diagram construction and order parameters (vector spin chirality and vector chiral order parameter), spin-spin correlation functions, subsystem entanglement entropy, and quench protocols to probe DQPT critical times.
AI.result: The phase diagram contains positive and negative vector chiral phases plus a paramagnetic phase. Without Ising interactions, a gapless critical line appears with no finite-size drift, and its spin-spin correlations and subsystem entanglement entropy differ from Ising criticality. DQPT critical times form periodic or aperiodic sequences depending on the quench path.
AI.conclusion: Dimerized off-diagonal (Gamma) exchange enriches both equilibrium ordering and dynamical critical behavior in the quantum Ising chain, revealing chiral order and tunable DQPT sequences as key consequences.

title: Rapid mixing of quantum spin chains at any finite temperature
summary: We prove that a quasi-local quantum Gibbs sampler rapidly mixes to the Gibbs state of any 1D finite-range Hamiltonian at all finite temperatures in $\mathcal{O}\left(\log (n/\varepsilon)\right)$ time. Each update traces out a contiguous block of constant length and reconstructs it using the Petz recovery map, following early proposals for quantum heat-bath Gibbs samplers by Kastoryano and Brandão~\cite{kastoryano2016quantum}. Our proof directly bounds the distance between the updated state and the target Gibbs state using quantum Wasserstein distance of order $1$. We further provide $\mathcal{O}(\text{polylog}(n/\varepsilon))$ depth of quantum circuits to prepare these Gibbs states. We hope these techniques will facilitate the analysis and design of other Gibbs samplers.

AI.tldr: Quasi-local Gibbs sampler using Petz recovery maps mixes in O(log(n/ε)) time to Gibbs states of 1D finite-range Hamiltonians at all finite temperatures, with O(polylog(n/ε)) circuit depth for preparation.
AI.motivation: Preparing Gibbs states of quantum many-body Hamiltonians efficiently is a central task in quantum computing and condensed matter. Early proposals for quantum heat-bath Gibbs samplers (Kastoryano, Brandão) lacked a rigorous proof of rapid mixing; this work aims to establish fast convergence guarantees.
AI.method: A quasi-local quantum Gibbs sampler that traces out a contiguous block of constant length and reconstructs it via the Petz recovery map. The proof directly bounds the distance between the updated state and the target Gibbs state using the quantum Wasserstein distance of order 1.
AI.result: The sampler rapidly mixes to the Gibbs state in O(log(n/ε)) time for any 1D finite-range Hamiltonian at all finite temperatures. Additionally, O(polylog(n/ε)) circuit depth suffices to prepare these Gibbs states.
AI.conclusion: The sampler achieves rapid mixing with rigorous guarantees, and the quantum Wasserstein distance technique is expected to facilitate analysis and design of other Gibbs samplers.

title: Fermionic Gaussian Scrooge Ensembles in Deep Thermalization
summary: Measuring part of a many-body wave function generates a projected ensemble of pure quantum states on the unmeasured subsystem. Recent advances in deep thermalization have shown that, in chaotic systems, this ensemble universally converges to the maximally random ensemble compatible with its average density matrix, known as the Scrooge ensemble. By contrast, free-fermion systems are nonchaotic, and their quantum states are constrained to remain Gaussian. Motivated by this distinction, we introduce the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble to describe deep thermalization in generic free-fermion systems. This ensemble is defined as a distortion of the Gaussian Haar ensemble by the average density matrix, and its moments reveal an enlarged symmetry of Gaussian states in the replicated Hilbert space. We demonstrate the emergence of the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble in two complementary settings: (1) we analytically prove that the projected ensemble of the SYK$_2$ model follows the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble at arbitrary evolution times; (2) we provide numerical evidence that it emerges at sufficiently long times in random Gaussian circuits with charge conservation. Our results establish the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble as a universal description of deep thermalization in free-fermion systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble to describe deep thermalization in generic free-fermion systems, showing it emerges in both the SYK$_2$ model (analytically, at all times) and random charge-conserving Gaussian circuits (numerically, at long times).
AI.motivation: Deep thermalization studies how the projected ensemble from measuring part of a many-body wave function converges to a universal random ensemble. In chaotic systems, this limit is the Scrooge ensemble. However, free-fermion systems are nonchaotic and their states are constrained to be Gaussian, so the standard Scrooge ensemble does not apply. The authors are motivated to find the correct universal ensemble describing deep thermalization when Gaussianity is enforced.
AI.method: The authors define the fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble as a distortion of the Gaussian Haar ensemble by the average density matrix, and analyze its moments, which reveal an enlarged symmetry of Gaussian states in the replicated Hilbert space. They verify its emergence in two settings: (1) an analytic proof that the projected ensemble of the SYK$_2$ model follows this ensemble at arbitrary evolution times; (2) numerical evidence that it emerges at sufficiently long times in random Gaussian circuits with charge conservation.
AI.result: The fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble is analytically shown to describe the projected ensemble of the SYK$_2$ model at all evolution times, and numerically shown to emerge at long times in random Gaussian circuits with charge conservation.
AI.conclusion: The fermionic Gaussian Scrooge ensemble provides a universal description of deep thermalization in free-fermion systems, extending the Scrooge-ensemble paradigm beyond chaotic systems to Gaussian-constrained nonchaotic dynamics.

title: Experimental quantification of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states
summary: We present a direct experimental verification of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states in a basis-independent manner. We find that the theory of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states matches our experimental results perfectly and can be applied to protocols like BB84 and quantum secure direct communication. Using a Sagnac interferometer, we experimentally quantify the quantum coherence for two sets of experimental states. Moreover, we introduce a novel application of set coherence, illustrating that the states employed in the BB84 protocol exhibit maximal set coherence. Our results pave the way for wider applications of quantum coherence for a set of quantum states, including quantum key distribution protocols and probabilistic quantum cloning.

AI.tldr: This work provides a direct experimental verification of basis-independent quantum coherence for a set of quantum states using a Sagnac interferometer, showing that theoretical predictions match experimental results and that BB84 states exhibit maximal set coherence.
AI.motivation: Quantum coherence is typically studied for individual states, but protocols such as BB84 and quantum secure direct communication rely on coherence across a set of states. A basis-independent, experimentally verified framework for set coherence was missing.
AI.method: The authors employ a Sagnac interferometer to experimentally quantify quantum coherence for two sets of experimental states in a basis-independent manner, comparing measurements against the theoretical framework of set coherence.
AI.result: Experimental results match the theory of quantum coherence for a set of states perfectly. Two sets of experimental states are quantified successfully, and the states used in the BB84 protocol are shown to exhibit maximal set coherence.
AI.conclusion: The verified framework enables wider applications of set coherence, including quantum key distribution protocols and probabilistic quantum cloning.

title: Linear-Time Encodable Quantum Codes near the CSS GV Bound
summary: We construct quantum CSS codes with rate-distance tradeoff approaching the CSS GV bound, which can be encoded by a quantum circuit of logarithmic depth and a linear number of gates. Our construction is heavily inspired by a work of Brehm and Resch and can be viewed as a quantum analogue of classical repeat multiple accumulate codes. The encoder has a particularly simple structure, consisting of a single constant depth outer quantum circuit followed by several classical accumulation and inverse-accumulation layers.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs quantum CSS codes whose rate-distance tradeoff approaches the CSS Gilbert–Varshamov bound, encodable by log-depth circuits with a linear number of gates, inspired by Brehm–Resch and analogous to classical repeat-multiple-accumulate codes.
AI.motivation: Achieving quantum codes that simultaneously approach the CSS GV bound and admit efficient (low-depth) encoding is challenging; the goal is to build such codes with a practically simple encoder structure.
AI.method: A quantum analogue of classical repeat-multiple-accumulate codes: a single constant-depth outer quantum circuit followed by several classical accumulation and inverse-accumulation layers, drawing on the Brehm–Resch construction.
AI.result: Quantum CSS codes with a rate-distance tradeoff approaching the CSS GV bound, encodable by a logarithmic-depth quantum circuit using a linear number of gates.
AI.conclusion: Efficiently encodable quantum CSS codes near the CSS GV bound are achievable via a simple encoder combining a constant-depth quantum outer circuit with classical accumulate/inverse-accumulate layers.

title: Preservability of Measurement Incompatibility: Purification, Activation, and a No-Go Theorem
summary: Measurement incompatibility is a fundamental quantum resource that enables advantages in many quantum information tasks, including cryptography and communication. However, unavoidable interactions between a system and its environment can degrade or even completely destroy measurement incompatibility; such a process is referred to as a measurement-incompatibility-annihilating channel. Recently, the capability of noisy quantum dynamics to preserve measurement incompatibility has been characterized within the resource theory of measurement incompatibility preservability. This motivates studying how to purify the preservation of measurement incompatibility and how to activate it from a measurement-incompatibility-annihilating channel. To this end, we first introduce our figures of merit as robustness-based resource monotones within this resource theory. We demonstrate that while pre-filtering operations can strengthen measurement incompatibility preservability, they cannot activate it from an incompatibility-annihilating channel, establishing a no-go theorem. Furthermore, we explicitly demonstrate that an incompatibility-annihilating channel can be stochastically activated via post-filtering operations. Our results provide a practical framework for exploiting measurement incompatibility in quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This work studies how to purify and activate the preservation of measurement incompatibility, proving a no-go theorem for pre-filtering and showing stochastic activation via post-filtering.
AI.motivation: Measurement incompatibility is a fundamental quantum resource enabling advantages in quantum information tasks such as cryptography and communication, but environmental interactions can degrade or destroy it through measurement-incompatibility-annihilating channels. While the ability of noisy dynamics to preserve measurement incompatibility has recently been characterized within the resource theory of measurement incompatibility preservability, it remained unclear how to purify this preservability and how to activate it from such annihilating channels.
AI.method: The authors introduce robustness-based resource monotones as figures of merit within the resource theory of measurement incompatibility preservability. They then analyze the effects of pre-filtering and post-filtering operations on measurement incompatibility preservability in the context of incompatibility-annihilating channels.
AI.result: The analysis shows that pre-filtering operations can strengthen measurement incompatibility preservability but cannot activate it from an incompatibility-annihilating channel, yielding a no-go theorem. Conversely, it is explicitly demonstrated that an incompatibility-annihilating channel can be stochastically activated through post-filtering operations.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a practical framework for exploiting measurement incompatibility in quantum information processing, clarifying the distinct roles of pre- and post-filtering in purifying and activating measurement incompatibility preservability.

title: Achieving Identical Stored Energy in Cascaded Collisional Quantum Battery Charging: Analytical Result
summary: Charging uniformity across distinct trials is an essential requirement for reliable quantum batteries. Nevertheless, intrinsic quantum stochasticity poses a fundamental challenge to this goal. This work investigates a two-qubit quantum battery within the framework of cascaded collision models. We propose an adaptive measurement on the charger after each collision, yielding two conditional battery states of equal expected stored energy. For chargers prepared in the excited state, we analytically prove that complete suppression of trajectory-dependent stored-energy fluctuations is attainable; for chargers prepared in general superposition states, our theory reveals that full suppression is fundamentally prohibited owing to battery-phase-dependent recursive dynamics. Numerical simulations are in excellent quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. These findings provide a feasible pathway toward high-uniformity quantum-battery charging.

AI.tldr: This work studies a two-qubit quantum battery in a cascaded collision model and proposes an adaptive measurement protocol on the charger after each collision to suppress trajectory-dependent fluctuations in stored energy, enabling uniform charging.
AI.motivation: Charging uniformity across trials is essential for reliable quantum batteries, but intrinsic quantum stochasticity fundamentally challenges this goal.
AI.method: A two-qubit quantum battery is investigated within cascaded collision models. An adaptive measurement is applied to the charger after each collision, producing two conditional battery states with equal expected stored energy. Analytical treatment covers chargers in the excited state and in general superposition states, supported by numerical simulations.
AI.result: For chargers prepared in the excited state, complete suppression of trajectory-dependent stored-energy fluctuations is analytically proven attainable. For general superposition states, full suppression is shown to be fundamentally prohibited due to battery-phase-dependent recursive dynamics. Numerical simulations agree quantitatively with theoretical predictions.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive measurement offers a feasible pathway toward high-uniformity quantum-battery charging, with achievable complete fluctuation suppression for excited-state chargers and an intrinsic limitation for general superposition states.

title: Vacuum entanglement in a time-dependent electric field
summary: We analyze the correlations of the vacuum state of a charged scalar field by constructing localized observables in two disjoint regions. We consider a time-dependent homogeneous electric field and examine the time evolution of correlations by relating it with the particle-antiparticle creation through the Schwinger effect. Our results show that the electric field increases the mixedness of the states and enhances total correlations, while the distillable entanglement among the regions decreases, vanishing at a finite time for sufficiently intense pulses within the non-perturbative pair-production regime. We also discuss the effect of anisotropy induced by the external background, showing that the distribution of correlations acquires a nontrivial directional dependence.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how a time-dependent electric field affects quantum correlations between two disjoint regions of a charged scalar field vacuum, linking the evolution to Schwinger pair production. It finds the field increases mixedness and total correlations but reduces distillable entanglement, which can vanish at finite time for intense pulses, and induces anisotropic directional dependence of correlations.
AI.motivation: The vacuum state of a quantum field encodes rich correlations between spatial regions, and an external electric field can create particle-antiparticle pairs (Schwinger effect). The authors aim to understand how such pair production dynamically modifies the entanglement and correlation structure between disjoint regions.
AI.method: They construct localized observables in two disjoint spatial regions for a charged scalar field and compute their correlations. They consider a time-dependent homogeneous electric field and relate the time evolution of these correlations to particle-antiparticle creation via the Schwinger effect, analyzing mixedness, total correlations, and distillable entanglement.
AI.result: The electric field increases the mixedness of the states and enhances total correlations, while the distillable entanglement between the regions decreases and vanishes at a finite time for sufficiently intense pulses in the non-perturbative pair-production regime. The external background also induces anisotropy, giving the distribution of correlations a nontrivial directional dependence.
AI.conclusion: External electric fields qualitatively reshape inter-region quantum correlations: they boost overall correlations and mixedness but degrade usable entanglement, which can disappear entirely within finite time, with a directional (anisotropic) structure imprinted by the background.

title: Optimal initial states for quantum Fisher information in linearized cavity optomechanics
summary: We find the optimal initial states of a linearized cavity-optomechanical system for estimating the single-photon coupling by quantum Fisher information. In the red-detuned (beam-splitter) regime the interaction exchanges excitations between the two modes, and for pure inputs the Fisher information is four times the variance of the excitation-exchange operator, reducing the optimization to variance maximization with a closed-form solution. With the mechanical mode in a Fock state the probe is degenerate: any state saturating the photon-number constraint is optimal, and a Fock reference with many phonons enhances the per-photon sensitivity linearly. For an arbitrary fixed mechanical reference it becomes a phase-matched squeezed vacuum, from an exact bound on that coherence obtained by a Lagrange-dual argument. Jointly optimizing both modes at fixed total excitation number, the quantum Fisher information obeys a Heisenberg bound quadratic in the energy, saturated by equal superpositions of the two extremal eigenstates of the generator, equivalently a two-mode NOON state after a balanced beam splitter; balanced product Fock states reach only a linear enhancement. Exact diagonalization in truncated Fock spaces confirms all the results, the familiar single-photon input being the simplest saturating case. Three extensions are worked out: the blue sideband has an unbounded two-mode-squeezing spectrum, so the entangled optimum becomes impossible and the balanced product Fock state is exactly optimal at definite energy; under cavity loss the information accumulation turns linear on the cavity-lifetime timescale, at a renewal-optimal duration of about two and a half lifetimes; and for a state-of-the-art quantum-coherent coupling experiment the per-hour relative precision lies between one part in a million and ten parts in a million, number and thermal references being the most robust.

AI.tldr: The paper determines optimal initial states of a linearized cavity-optomechanical system for estimating the single-photon coupling, using quantum Fisher information, identifying Fock, squeezed-vacuum, and NOON-type optimal probes and extending the analysis to the blue sideband, cavity loss, and a realistic experimental regime.
AI.motivation: Estimating the single-photon coupling is a central metrological task in cavity optomechanics, yet the optimal choice of initial quantum states for this estimation had not been fully characterized. The authors aim to find the best achievable precision and the probe states that attain it, while accounting for practical regimes such as the blue sideband and cavity loss.
AI.method: Quantum Fisher information is used as the figure of merit for a linearized cavity-optomechanical system. In the red-detuned (beam-splitter) regime, the Fisher information is expressed as four times the variance of the excitation-exchange operator for pure inputs, reducing the problem to variance maximization solved in closed form. Optimization is performed over mechanical Fock reference states, arbitrary fixed mechanical references (via a Lagrange-dual bound on coherence), and jointly over both modes at fixed total excitation number. Results are verified by exact diagonalization in truncated Fock spaces, and three extensions are analyzed: the blue sideband, cavity loss, and a state-of-the-art quantum-coherent coupling experiment.
AI.result: For a mechanical Fock state the probe is degenerate: any state saturating the photon-number constraint is optimal, and a many-phonon Fock reference enhances per-photon sensitivity linearly. For an arbitrary fixed mechanical reference the optimum is a phase-matched squeezed vacuum. Joint optimization at fixed total excitation number yields a quantum Fisher information obeying a Heisenberg bound quadratic in energy, saturated by equal superpositions of the two extremal eigenstates of the generator (a two-mode NOON state after a balanced beam splitter), whereas balanced product Fock states give only linear enhancement. The blue sideband has an unbounded two-mode-squeezing spectrum, making the entangled optimum impossible and the balanced product Fock state exactly optimal at definite energy. Under cavity loss information accumulation becomes linear on the cavity-lifetime timescale, with a renewal-optimal duration of about two and a half lifetimes. For a state-of-the-art quantum-coherent coupling experiment the per-hour relative precision lies between one part in a million and ten parts in a million, with number and thermal references being the most robust.
AI.conclusion: The optimal initial states for single-photon-coupling estimation in a linearized cavity-optomechanical system are identified, ranging from Fock references and phase-matched squeezed vacuum to a two-mode NOON state that saturates a quadratic Heisenberg bound at fixed energy. Practical extensions show that the blue sideband, cavity loss, and realistic experimental conditions modify these optima, with number and thermal references being most robust. The work provides a closed-form metrological characterization of cavity optomechanics with verified numerical confirmation.

title: Robust and leakage-resilient device-independent oblivious transfer in MiniQCryp
summary:
Assuming post-quantum one-way functions, we construct device-independent (DI) oblivious transfer (OT) and bit commitment: honest parties use only trusted classical computation to operate untrusted quantum devices, which may share arbitrary entanglement and behave non-IID. Security is simulation-based against quantum polynomial-time adversaries and composes sequentially with efficient simulators. One protocol skeleton serves both, in two regimes. With isolated laboratories and coordinate-local measurements in the honest receiver's device, it tolerates a constant rate of honest-device faults. With polylogarithmically many qubits of adaptive leakage between the laboratories and arbitrary joint measurements, it tolerates an inverse-polylogarithmic rate. Each elementary DI call uses a fresh, isolated batch of polylogarithmically many device coordinates, and total device use in the compiled OT protocol is polynomial. The commitment has efficient simulators against both parties and yields DI coin tossing with abort.
  Because OT is complete for secure computation, the construction yields a DI protocol, with abort, for every efficiently computable classical functionality on a fixed number of parties, secure against static corruption of any proper subset of them.
  The commitment's extractor changes a public parity relation through classical equivocation and leaves the device execution, hence its leakage, unchanged. A commit-and-prove functionality, disjoint audits, and an affine consistency check link the certified correlations to ideal OT. Sender security rests on a selector-aware parallel-repetition bound for the Magic Square game, which we derive from the two-round threshold theorem of Kundu and Tan.

AI.tldr: Assuming post-quantum one-way functions, the authors construct device-independent oblivious transfer and bit commitment where honest parties use only trusted classical computation to drive untrusted quantum devices (arbitrary entanglement, non-IID behavior), with simulation-based security against quantum polynomial-time adversaries that composes sequentially.
AI.motivation: Secure computation typically requires trusting quantum devices. This work aims for device-independent (DI) security, removing trust in the quantum hardware, while keeping honest parties' computation classical and tolerating realistic device imperfections and leakage.
AI.method: A single protocol skeleton serves both OT and commitment in two regimes: (1) isolated laboratories with coordinate-local measurements on the honest receiver's device, tolerating a constant fault rate; (2) polylogarithmically many qubits of adaptive leakage plus arbitrary joint measurements, tolerating an inverse-polylogarithmic fault rate. Each elementary DI call uses a fresh isolated batch of polylogarithmically many device coordinates; total device use is polynomial. Tools include a commit-and-prove functionality, disjoint audits, an affine consistency check, and a selector-aware parallel-repetition bound for the Magic Square game derived from the two-round threshold theorem of Kundu and Tan.
AI.result: The protocols achieve simulation-based security with efficient simulators and sequential composition. The commitment has efficient simulators against both parties and yields DI coin tossing with abort. Because OT is complete for secure computation, this gives a DI protocol (with abort) for every efficiently computable classical functionality on a fixed number of parties, secure against static corruption of any proper subset.
AI.conclusion: Under post-quantum one-way functions, device-independent secure computation is achievable with classical honest-party computation, tolerating device faults and leakage. The commitment's extractor modifies a public parity relation via classical equivocation without altering the device execution or its leakage.

title: Unflattening by Flattening -- How Input Distributions Shape Output Variance in Angle-Encoded Circuits
summary: Barren plateaus hinder training of parameterized quantum circuits by making loss gradients exponentially small in the number of qubits. For angle-encoded product states, we show how the input distribution affects output variation through algebraic input purity, i.e. the input's overlap with the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra. With the specified readouts and Haar or exact group 2-design sampling, matchgate circuits on $n$ qubits retain output variance of order $1/n$ for every pure product input. The off-diagonal family instead has zero output on computational-basis inputs at any depth and for every parameter choice. Independent uniform angles yield mean variance of the same order as matchgates. A count of diagonal Pauli strings identifies these zero-output endpoints. For any fixed dataset of nonzero inputs with at least $2n$ coordinates, we construct a classical preprocessing certificate. A shared random rotation is accepted only when the dataset's mean purity passes a computable threshold. This certifies mean output variance of order $1/n$ for the off-diagonal family before circuit execution, with a constant expected number of trials. Binary and ternary weighted encodings also recover the independent-angle mean purity from one uniform scalar input. Numerical experiments examine training behavior and extensions to larger algebras. The guarantee concerns output variance averaged over inputs, while successful learning also depends on the task and information preserved by the encoding.

AI.tldr: For angle-encoded product states, output variance is governed by algebraic input purity (overlap with the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra). With Haar/2-design sampling, matchgate circuits retain output variance ~1/n for every pure product input; the off-diagonal family yields exactly zero output on computational-basis inputs at any depth, but a classical preprocessing certificate can pre-verify ~1/n mean variance for fixed datasets.
AI.motivation: Barren plateaus make loss gradients in parameterized quantum circuits exponentially small with qubit number, impeding trainability. The paper aims to characterize how the input distribution, specifically the input's algebraic relation to the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra, controls output variation, thereby explaining and predicting trainability without full circuit execution.
AI.method: The authors analyze angle-encoded product states via 'algebraic input purity', the input's overlap with the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra. They study matchgate circuits and an off-diagonal family under specified readouts with Haar or exact group 2-design sampling. They count diagonal Pauli strings to identify zero-output endpoints, and construct a classical preprocessing certificate based on a shared random rotation that is accepted when a dataset's mean purity exceeds a computable threshold. They also test binary and ternary weighted encodings that recover independent-angle mean purity from a single uniform scalar input, and run numerical experiments.
AI.result: Matchgate circuits preserve output variance of order 1/n for every pure product input. The off-diagonal family has zero output on computational-basis inputs at any depth and for all parameters. Independent uniform angles yield mean variance of the same order as matchgates. The preprocessing certificate certifies mean output variance of order 1/n for datasets with at least 2n coordinates and nonzero inputs, before circuit execution, with a constant expected number of trials. Weighted encodings recover the independent-angle mean purity from one uniform scalar input.
AI.conclusion: Input purity, defined through the dynamical Lie algebra, quantitatively determines output variance and trainability. Trainability can be certified classically prior to execution for certain input families. The guarantee applies to input-averaged output variance; successful learning additionally depends on the task and on information preserved by the encoding.

title: Unbounded separation between definite and indefinite causal order in finite-dimensional quantum metrology
summary: Indefinite causal order is known to offer enhancements in quantum metrology, notably including an unbounded advantage in the measurement of a geometric phase of a harmonic oscillator. This advantage, however, is specific to the infinite dimensional setting, and its finite dimensional analogue remains elusive, with recent findings suggesting that advantages in finite dimensions may be fundamentally limited to bounded constant factors. Here we show that, in fact, arbitrarily large advantages arise for finite dimensional systems in the finite sample regime. Specifically, we establish an unbounded separation between definite and indefinite causal order in the estimation of a geometric phase associated to two sets of $N$ displacements generated by discrete position and momentum operators on a $d$-dimensional quantum system: for any given constant $R$, there exist values of $N$ and $d=Ω(N^2)$ such that a strategy with indefinite order uses an initial probe with $R$ times less energy than the probe required by every strategy with definite order achieving the same mean squared error, whenever the number of measurement shots $ν$ is bounded as $ν=\mathcal{O}(\exp(πd/16)/\mathrm{poly}(d))$. In other words, indefinite order offers an energy saving that grows arbitrarily large with the parameters of the problem. To prove this result, we establish an approximate Weyl relation for discrete Gaussian wavepackets, which is of independent technical interest.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that indefinite causal order yields arbitrarily large energy-savings advantages over definite causal order in finite-dimensional quantum systems, specifically in the finite-sample regime, for estimating a geometric phase associated with discrete displacement operators.
AI.motivation: Indefinite causal order is known to provide an unbounded metrological advantage for measuring a geometric phase of a harmonic oscillator, but this advantage was thought to be specific to infinite dimensions. Recent findings suggested that in finite dimensions, any advantage over definite order might be limited to bounded constant factors, leaving the finite-dimensional analogue of the unbounded advantage elusive.
AI.method: The authors establish an approximate Weyl relation for discrete Gaussian wavepackets and analyze the estimation of a geometric phase associated to two sets of N displacements generated by discrete position and momentum operators on a d-dimensional quantum system, comparing strategies with definite versus indefinite causal order under a finite number of measurement shots ν.
AI.result: They establish an unbounded separation between definite and indefinite causal order: for any constant R, there exist N and d=Ω(N²) such that an indefinite-order strategy achieves the same mean squared error as any definite-order strategy while using an initial probe with R times less energy, provided ν=O(exp(πd/16)/poly(d)). Thus the energy saving grows arbitrarily large with the problem parameters.
AI.conclusion: Indefinite causal order can offer arbitrarily large advantages even in finite-dimensional systems, contrary to the view that such advantages are confined to infinite dimensions or bounded by constant factors. This demonstrates a genuine unbounded finite-dimensional metrological advantage in the finite-sample regime.

title: Zero- Versus Infinite-Temperature Damping in Variational Quantum Circuits: Feature Scale, Sampling Cost, and Frame Gauge
summary: The Pauli twirl of amplitude damping (AD) is generalized amplitude damping at infinite temperature: it keeps the contraction of AD and removes its non-unital term, so comparing the two in variational circuits isolates the zero-temperature bias, which acts mainly through the scale of the features. For random parameters, features under AD settle on a floor, which at strong damping is set by the last layer, has a closed form, and at fixed $T_1$ falls with temperature as $\tanh(\hbarω/2k_BT)$; under the twirls they shrink by a constant factor per layer, up to eight qubits. A trainable output scale removes most of the resulting accuracy differences, leaving AD ahead of its twirls by at most about three percentage points in our simulations; what it removes reappears as a cost in measurement shots: trained and tested with $10^3$ shots per image, a four-qubit classifier under AD at $p=0.3$ stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy, while the twirled classifiers lose up to 33. At weaker damping the separation depth grows roughly as $(np)^{-1}\ln(1/p)$. The damping direction is a gauge when the damping follows complete entangling layers and the circuit boundaries are trainable; in an eigensolver it becomes physical inside a decomposed two-qubit gate.

AI.tldr: Pauli-twirling amplitude damping equals generalized amplitude damping at infinite temperature; comparing both in variational circuits isolates the zero-temperature (non-unital) bias, which mainly rescales features and can be compensated by a trainable output scale at the cost of far more measurement shots.
AI.motivation: To disentangle which part of amplitude damping (AD) noise actually harms variational quantum circuits: the unital contraction that Pauli twirling preserves, or the non-unital zero-temperature term that twirling removes.
AI.method: Analytically compare AD with its Pauli twirl (generalized AD at infinite temperature) in variational circuits; derive closed forms for feature floors and shrinkage under random parameters; simulate classifiers with and without a trainable output scale; test shot-noise budgets (10^3 shots/image); analyze the gauge freedom of the damping direction and a decomposed two-qubit gate eigensolver.
AI.result: Under AD, features settle on a floor set by the last layer at strong damping, falling with temperature as tanh(hbar*omega/2k_BT) at fixed T1; under twirls features shrink by a constant factor per layer up to eight qubits. A trainable output scale removes most accuracy gaps, leaving AD ahead of its twirls by at most ~3 percentage points, but the removed gap reappears in shot cost: at p=0.3 with 10^3 shots/image a four-qubit AD classifier stays within 1.5 points of noiseless accuracy while twirled ones lose up to 33. At weaker damping the separation depth grows roughly as (np)^{-1} ln(1/p).
AI.conclusion: The non-unital zero-temperature term, not the unital contraction, drives the accuracy advantage of AD over its twirls; this advantage is equivalent to a feature rescaling recoverable by a trainable scale, but only at a substantial sampling cost. The damping direction is a gauge when damping follows complete entangling layers with trainable boundaries, and becomes physical inside a decomposed two-qubit gate (eigensolver).

title: Continuous-Process Randomized Compilation for Quantum Process Tensors
summary: Traditional discrete randomized compiling (RC) tailors errors with random control frames at logical-gate boundaries, but fails to capture intra-instrument control evolution or persistent system-environment coupling. In memory-bearing environments, errors correlate across times, not just single gates. We build continuous-process randomized compilation (CPRC) in the continuous process tensor (cPT) framework, unifying random unitary control trajectories, pointwise-covariant finite-duration instruments, and environmental dynamics on one time axis. We study four protocols: fixed Pauli refresh, bounded Cayley paths, unitary Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driving. We obtain three key results: (1) Pointwise covariance ensures each trajectory exactly reproduces the target logic without system-environment coupling; a closed-frame counterexample proves endpoint-only compensation causes first-order instrument errors. (2) Independent Pauli conjugations over full intervals diagonalize error histories at boundaries, but classical labels retain environment-induced correlations, confirmed by an exact static-bath solution. (3) We derive a total-variation error bound for full adaptive output records under bounded centered coupling and mixing conditions. We prove convergence of trajectory-averaged cPT coefficients in fixed particle sectors for finite non-Gaussian environments and Gaussian baths with time-integrable covariance, including the uncut Drude spectrum. We numerically validate the theory in a qubit model via output probabilities, operator conditional mutual information, and all two-particle coefficients for both qubit and thermal Drude baths. This work extends RC from discrete circuits to continuous-time memory-bearing quantum processes, offering a unified framework, quantitative tools, implementable schemes, and benchmarks for non-Markovian error tailoring.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces continuous-process randomized compilation (CPRC) within the continuous process tensor (cPT) framework, extending traditional discrete randomized compiling to continuous-time, memory-bearing quantum processes. It provides three key theoretical results, convergence proofs, and numerical validations in a qubit model.
AI.motivation: Traditional discrete randomized compiling (RC) tailors errors with random control frames only at logical-gate boundaries, so it cannot capture intra-instrument control evolution or persistent system-environment coupling. In memory-bearing environments, errors correlate across time rather than being confined to single gates, motivating a continuous-time framework.
AI.method: The authors build CPRC in the cPT framework, unifying random unitary control trajectories, pointwise-covariant finite-duration instruments, and environmental dynamics on a single time axis. They study four protocols: fixed Pauli refresh, bounded Cayley paths, unitary Brownian motion, and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driving. Analysis includes pointwise covariance, a closed-frame counterexample, independent Pauli conjugations, an exact static-bath solution, a total-variation error bound under bounded centered coupling and mixing conditions, and convergence proofs of trajectory-averaged cPT coefficients for finite non-Gaussian environments and Gaussian baths with time-integrable covariance (including uncut Drude spectrum).
AI.result: (1) Pointwise covariance ensures each trajectory exactly reproduces the target logic without system-environment coupling, and a closed-frame counterexample proves endpoint-only compensation causes first-order instrument errors. (2) Independent Pauli conjugations over full intervals diagonalize error histories at boundaries, but classical labels retain environment-induced correlations, confirmed by an exact static-bath solution. (3) A total-variation error bound is derived for full adaptive output records. Convergence of trajectory-averaged cPT coefficients is proven in fixed particle sectors. Numerical validation in a qubit model uses output probabilities, operator conditional mutual information, and all two-particle coefficients for qubit and thermal Drude baths.
AI.conclusion: CPRC extends randomized compiling from discrete circuits to continuous-time memory-bearing quantum processes, offering a unified framework, quantitative tools, implementable schemes, and benchmarks for non-Markovian error tailoring.

title: Efficient learning of quantum interactions from thermal metastable states
summary: Learning quantum interactions from finite-temperature many-body systems is a central task in emerging quantum platforms. Recently, the problem of learning from lattice quantum Gibbs states has found rigorous, efficient protocols. Nevertheless, exact Gibbs states, as the input premise, are in fact computationally intractable to prepare and may not faithfully represent generic finite-temperature quantum systems. In contrast, a system coupled to a heat bath can be stuck at an approximate stationary state (metastable state) long before it truly equilibrates. Here, we formulate a physically and algorithmically consistent alternative: learning from such metastable states of detailed-balanced master equations (Lindbladians) arising from system-bath interactions. We distill the algorithmic mechanism and structural condition underlying Gibbs-state learning and extend it in full to metastable states, attaining nearly optimal sample and computational complexity (in the system size and the precision). More broadly, we sharpen notions of metastability and develop a unified framework for finite-temperature learning.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes finite-temperature quantum Hamiltonian learning by replacing intractable exact Gibbs states with physically realistic metastable states of detailed-balanced Lindbladians, extending Gibbs-state learning algorithms to this setting with nearly optimal sample and computational complexity.
AI.motivation: Learning quantum interactions from finite-temperature many-body systems is central to emerging quantum platforms. While learning from lattice quantum Gibbs states has rigorous, efficient protocols, exact Gibbs states are computationally intractable to prepare and may not faithfully represent generic finite-temperature quantum systems. In practice, a system coupled to a heat bath can remain stuck in an approximate stationary (metastable) state long before true equilibration, motivating a more physically and algorithmically consistent learning formulation.
AI.method: The authors formulate learning from metastable states of detailed-balanced master equations (Lindbladians) arising from system-bath interactions. They distill the algorithmic mechanism and structural condition underlying Gibbs-state learning and extend it in full to metastable states. They also sharpen notions of metastability and develop a unified framework for finite-temperature learning.
AI.result: The proposed approach attains nearly optimal sample and computational complexity in terms of system size and precision.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a physically and algorithmically consistent alternative to Gibbs-state learning, extending rigorous efficient protocols to metastable states and offering a unified framework for finite-temperature quantum learning.

title: Molecular Dynamics with Nuclear Effects on Quantum Computers
summary: Nuclear quantum effects are critical for describing proton transfer and hydrogen bonding, but their incorporation into quantum chemistry calculations is often computationally prohibitive on classical hardware. A promising alternative are quantum computers due to their linear scaling in the space requirements with system size. We introduce a novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for ab-initio molecular dynamics that incorporates nuclear quantum effects via the nuclear-electronic orbital method. The proposed algorithm evaluates ground state energies and forces on the quantum computer using a variational quantum eigensolver, while the molecular geometries are updated classically. We validate our approach through simulations of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and the Zundel ion $\text{H}_5\text{O}_2^+$, comparing the simulated vibrational spectra with experimental data. Upon inclusion of nuclear quantum effects, the proton shuttling movement in the Zundel ion becomes effectively barrierless, and errors in the simulated frequencies improve significantly. Employing compact hardware-efficient ansatz circuits we achieve results comparable to the more accurate UCCSD ansatzes, which hints towards the feasibility of executing our algorithm on near-term quantum devices.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical ab-initio molecular dynamics algorithm incorporates nuclear quantum effects via the nuclear-electronic orbital method, computing energies and forces with a variational quantum eigensolver, and reproduces experimental vibrational spectra of H2, H2O and H5O2+.
AI.motivation: Nuclear quantum effects are essential for describing proton transfer and hydrogen bonding, but including them in quantum chemistry calculations is often computationally prohibitive on classical hardware. Quantum computers offer a promising alternative due to linear scaling of space requirements with system size.
AI.method: A novel hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for ab-initio molecular dynamics that incorporates nuclear quantum effects through the nuclear-electronic orbital (NEO) method. Ground state energies and forces are evaluated on the quantum computer using a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), while molecular geometries are updated classically. Compact hardware-efficient ansatz circuits are used and compared against UCCSD ansatzes.
AI.result: The approach is validated by simulating H2, H2O and the Zundel ion H5O2+, comparing simulated vibrational spectra with experimental data. With nuclear quantum effects included, proton shuttling in the Zundel ion becomes effectively barrierless, and errors in the simulated frequencies improve significantly. Hardware-efficient ansatzes yield results comparable to the more accurate UCCSD ansatzes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating nuclear quantum effects via the NEO-based hybrid quantum-classical scheme markedly improves vibrational frequency accuracy and renders proton shuttling in the Zundel ion effectively barrierless; the comparability of hardware-efficient and UCCSD ansatzes hints toward the feasibility of executing the algorithm on near-term quantum devices.

title: Efficient certification of time-reversal symmetry requires entanglement
summary: Time-reversal symmetry is a fundamental principle of physics describing the invariance of physical laws under reversal of the direction of time. We formulate a Bell-inequality-like test of this antiunitary symmetry using only forward access and trusted quantum operations: entanglement converts temporal input--output relations into measurable spatial exchange symmetry. For $n$-qubit unitary dynamics, we prove that reliably distinguishing the time-reversal-symmetric circular ensembles from Haar-random dynamics requires $Ω(\min\{2^{n/2},2^{n-e}\})$ queries for any classically adaptive protocol. Here, $e=\min\{e_{\mathrm s},e_{\mathrm m}\}$ with $e_{\mathrm s}$ and $e_{\mathrm m}$ representing the probe and measurement logarithmic entanglement negativities, respectively. Maximally entangled probes and SWAP measurements reduce this cost to a constant number of queries. Furthermore, we develop a time-reversal symmetry test for arbitrary fixed, compatible probes and measurements, relate its query complexity to their logarithmic negativities, and match the lower-bound scaling in the high-entanglement regime by optimizing the probe and measurement. Our results establish a quantitative connection between entanglement and time-reversal symmetry, bridging two central concepts in quantum information science and fundamental physics.

AI.tldr: A Bell-inequality-like test of time-reversal symmetry is formulated using only forward access and trusted quantum operations, showing that entanglement converts temporal input-output relations into measurable spatial exchange symmetry, with query complexity governed by probe and measurement entanglement.
AI.motivation: Time-reversal symmetry is a fundamental principle of physics, but testing such an antiunitary symmetry had not been framed via a Bell-inequality-like construction that uses only forward (non-time-reversed) access and trusted operations. The paper seeks a quantitative connection between entanglement and time-reversal symmetry to bridge quantum information science and fundamental physics.
AI.method: The authors exploit entanglement to map temporal input-output relations into measurable spatial exchange symmetry. For n-qubit unitary dynamics, they prove a query-complexity lower bound Ω(min{2^{n/2}, 2^{n−e}}) for any classically adaptive protocol that reliably distinguishes time-reversal-symmetric circular ensembles from Haar-random dynamics, where e = min{e_s, e_m} and e_s, e_m are probe and measurement logarithmic entanglement negativities. They also develop a test for arbitrary fixed, compatible probes and measurements that relates its query complexity to their logarithmic negativities, and optimize probe and measurement to match the lower-bound scaling.
AI.result: Reliably distinguishing time-reversal-symmetric circular ensembles from Haar-random dynamics requires Ω(min{2^{n/2}, 2^{n−e}}) queries. Maximally entangled probes together with SWAP measurements reduce the cost to a constant number of queries. In the high-entanglement regime, optimizing probe and measurement matches the lower-bound scaling.
AI.conclusion: Entanglement and time-reversal symmetry are quantitatively linked, establishing a bridge between two central concepts in quantum information science and fundamental physics. The scheme enables testing antiunitary time-reversal symmetry using only forward access and trusted quantum operations.

title: Adversarial Robustness in Fake Quantum Simulators
summary: This paper investigates the performance scalability and adversarial robustness of Quantum Machine Learning (QML) models deployed on noise-model-based fake simulators. We conduct a dual-phased study, first benchmarking the computational throughput of Qiskit's Aer simulation engine across varying hardware architectures, and second, evaluating the effectiveness of Projected Gradient Descent (PGD) attacks and adversarial retraining strategies under realistic noise conditions. Our results quantify the runtime tradeoffs and scaling behavior for medium-scale simulations (projected up to 8 qubits) and demonstrate that high adversarial-to-benign retraining ratios (50/50) are essential for achieving practical model robustness for 4-qubit classifiers under realistic noise conditions.

AI.tldr: A dual-phased study benchmarks Qiskit Aer simulator throughput across hardware and evaluates PGD adversarial attacks plus retraining on noise-model-based QML classifiers, finding 50/50 adversarial-to-benign retraining is essential for robustness in 4-qubit models.
AI.motivation: QML models face both performance scalability limits on noisy simulators and adversarial vulnerabilities, yet the interaction between realistic noise and adversarial robustness remains underexplored and practical guidance is lacking.
AI.method: Phase one benchmarks computational throughput of Qiskit's Aer simulation engine across varying hardware architectures for medium-scale simulations (up to 8 qubits). Phase two evaluates PGD attacks and adversarial retraining strategies under realistic noise-model-based conditions on quantum classifiers.
AI.result: Runtime tradeoffs and scaling behavior for medium-scale simulations up to 8 qubits are quantified. High adversarial-to-benign retraining ratios (50/50) are shown to be essential for achieving practical model robustness for 4-qubit classifiers under realistic noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: Scaling behavior on noisy simulators is characterized, and balanced adversarial retraining is necessary, not optional, for practical QML classifier robustness, offering empirical guidance for noise-aware QML development.

title: Electromagnetic Side-Channel Vulnerability in QKD Equipment
summary: Actual quantum key distribution network nodes may be vulnerable to side-channel attacks such as electromagnetic leakage. In this study, we measured electromagnetic emissions from a prototype quantum key distribution device implementing a time-bin decoy-state BB84 protocol with Y and Z bases. We measured the electromagnetic spectra and waveforms at distances of 0 m and 3 m from the transmitter and receiver inside an anechoic chamber. The results showed that the transmitter was the primary source of electromagnetic leakage, and distinct differences were observed between the quantum states generated at the third harmonic of the 1241.6 MHz clock.

AI.tldr: Electromagnetic emissions from a time-bin decoy-state BB84 QKD prototype were measured at 0 m and 3 m in an anechoic chamber. The transmitter dominates leakage, and quantum states are distinguishable at the third harmonic of the 1241.6 MHz clock.
AI.motivation: Real QKD network nodes may be exposed to side-channel attacks, including electromagnetic leakage. Characterizing such emissions is needed to assess the practical security of deployed QKD hardware.
AI.method: Electromagnetic spectra and waveforms were measured from a prototype QKD device implementing a time-bin decoy-state BB84 protocol with Y and Z bases. Measurements were taken inside an anechoic chamber at distances of 0 m and 3 m from both the transmitter and the receiver.
AI.result: The transmitter was identified as the primary source of electromagnetic leakage. Distinct differences were observed between the quantum states generated, appearing at the third harmonic of the 1241.6 MHz clock.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate a potential state-dependent side channel in the tested QKD device, highlighting the need to account for electromagnetic emanation in the security evaluation of QKD network nodes.

title: Dissipation-Enabled Operator-Norm Locality Bounds for Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonians
summary: Closed bosonic lattice systems do not generally admit operator norm Lieb--Robinson bounds uniformly in the initial state. The reason is that the information propagation velocity can grow with the local boson occupancy, which can be macroscopically large. Here, we show that local dissipation restores an operator-norm Lieb--Robinson bound. We consider the dissipative Bose--Hubbard model described by a Lindbladian operator with on-site $\ell$-photon loss, $\ell>2$ and, for our main result, we establish an almost-ballistic Lieb-Robinson bound. Dissipation rapidly depletes highly occupied sites, thus regularizing the state on the Sobolev-type scale of local particle moments. The resulting moment bounds diverge as time approaches zero but remain integrable near zero at sufficiently low orders. We extend these ideas to treat cat-code dissipation and, for initial states in the code space, we prove a local adiabatic approximation uniform in the total volume. Further consequences include local channel approximation, a thermodynamic limit, and efficient digital quantum simulation. The point is that these applications are now available \textit{uniformly in the input state}, as for quantum spin systems, but in contrast to closed Bose--Hubbard systems.

AI.tldr: Local dissipation in open bosonic lattice systems restores an operator-norm Lieb-Robinson bound, yielding almost-ballistic information propagation, a volume-uniform local adiabatic approximation for cat-code states, and efficient digital quantum simulation—all uniformly in the input state, unlike closed Bose-Hubbard systems.
AI.motivation: Closed bosonic lattice systems generally lack operator-norm Lieb-Robinson bounds uniform in the initial state, because the information propagation velocity can grow with local boson occupancy, which may be macroscopically large. The authors aim to show that local dissipation can regularize this behavior and recover spin-system-like uniform bounds.
AI.method: They study the dissipative Bose-Hubbard model governed by a Lindbladian with on-site ℓ-photon loss (ℓ>2). Dissipation rapidly depletes highly occupied sites, regularizing the state on a Sobolev-type scale of local particle moments. The resulting moment bounds diverge as time approaches zero but remain integrable near zero at sufficiently low orders. They extend the approach to cat-code dissipation and, for initial states in the code space, prove a local adiabatic approximation uniform in total volume.
AI.result: They establish an almost-ballistic Lieb-Robinson bound in operator norm. The moment bounds diverge as time approaches zero yet stay integrable near zero at sufficiently low orders. For cat-code dissipation with code-space initial states, they prove a local adiabatic approximation uniform in the total volume. Further consequences include local channel approximation, a thermodynamic limit, and efficient digital quantum simulation, all uniform in the input state.
AI.conclusion: Local dissipation restores operator-norm Lieb-Robinson bounds and related applications uniformly in the input state for dissipative bosonic lattice systems, paralleling quantum spin systems and contrasting with closed Bose-Hubbard systems.

title: A Code-Agnostic Graph Neural Network Decoder from the Detection Error Model
summary: We present POLYMECHANON, a graph neural network (GNN) decoder for quantum error correction whose only input is the detection error model (DEM) of a quantum code under a given noise model. We represent the DEM as a tripartite graph of detectors, error mechanisms and logical observables, where every input feature is computed by using the quantum code as data rather than design choice. In this way, the same architecture decodes in principle any stabiliser code, under any noise model that can be expressed as a detection error model, once trained on the DEM. We test this approach along four directions. Firstly, on the rotated surface code the decoder outperforms correlated MWPM under both phenomenological and circuit-level noise, with up to $25\%$ fewer logical failures. Secondly, on a family of high-rate qLDPC codes it matches BP+OSD on the smaller codes and surpasses it on the larger ones, with up to $16\%$ fewer logical failures on $[\![130,4,6]\!]$. Thirdly, its decoding time does not depend on the physical error rate, whereas that of BP+OSD grows with it: on $[\![130,4,6]\!]$ its effective cost per shot is of the order of a few ms on a single GPU against a few tens of milliseconds for BP+OSD on a single CPU core, and its fixed computational graph makes it a candidate for real-time decoding on neutral-atom processors. Finally, a single model trained across codes of different families outperforms uncorrelated MWPM on the graph-like codes seen during training and stays within $10\%$ of BP+OSD on the others, while it tends to fail to generalize to unseen codes, particularly larger ones. Its probabilistic output enables confidence-based post-selection, lowering the logical error rate by more than an order of magnitude on the surface code while keeping more than $90\%$ of the shots. Since only the DEM changes, new codes and noise models can be decoded without redesigning the decoder.

AI.tldr: PolyMechAnon is a GNN decoder for quantum error correction that takes only the detection error model as input, representing it as a tripartite graph of detectors, error mechanisms, and logical observables, enabling code-agnostic decoding of any stabiliser code.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum error correction decoders are typically tied to specific codes or noise models, requiring redesign when either changes. The authors aim to build a single decoder architecture that generalizes across codes and noise models by deriving all input features from the quantum code itself rather than from design choices.
AI.method: The DEM is encoded as a tripartite graph of detectors, error mechanisms, and logical observables, with features computed from the quantum code as data. A GNN decoder is trained on the DEM and evaluated along four directions: rotated surface code under phenomenological and circuit-level noise, high-rate qLDPC codes, decoding time across physical error rates, and cross-code generalization.
AI.result: On the rotated surface code it outperforms correlated MWPM with up to 25% fewer logical failures. On qLDPC codes it matches BP+OSD on smaller codes and surpasses it on larger ones, with up to 16% fewer logical failures on [[130,4,6]]. Decoding time is independent of physical error rate (a few ms per shot on one GPU vs. tens of ms for BP+OSD on a CPU core). A single cross-family model beats uncorrelated MWPM on trained graph-like codes and stays within 10% of BP+OSD on others, though generalization to unseen (especially larger) codes is limited. Probabilistic outputs enable confidence-based post-selection, reducing logical error rate by over an order of magnitude while retaining more than 90% of shots.
AI.conclusion: A DEM-based GNN decoder can decode any stabiliser code under any noise model expressible as a DEM without architectural redesign, offering competitive accuracy, error-rate-independent latency suitable for real-time decoding, and confidence-based post-selection, with cross-code generalization remaining an open challenge for unseen larger codes.

title: Mentor-Initiated Asymmetric Bidirectional Quantum Teleportation Protocol for Arbitrary Qubit States
summary: In this paper, a mentor-initiated bidirectional asymmetric quantum teleportation protocol is proposed. Unlike existing schemes that restrict the two-qubit state transmitted from Bob to Alice to a Bell-like form $α|00\rangle+β|11\rangle$, our protocol allows an arbitrary two-qubit state to be teleported from Bob to Alice within the mentor-initiated framework. The required entangled resources are constructed using standard quantum gates, and the protocol is illustrated through its quantum-circuit implementation in Qiskit.

AI.tldr: A mentor-initiated bidirectional asymmetric quantum teleportation protocol is proposed that removes the Bell-like restriction on the Bob-to-Alice two-qubit state, enabling teleportation of an arbitrary two-qubit state, with entangled resources built from standard quantum gates and verified via a Qiskit circuit implementation.
AI.motivation: Existing bidirectional asymmetric teleportation schemes constrain the two-qubit state sent from Bob to Alice to a Bell-like form α|00⟩+β|11⟩, which limits the class of states that can be teleported and thus the protocol's generality. The paper aims to lift this restriction within a mentor-initiated framework so that an arbitrary two-qubit state can be transmitted from Bob to Alice.
AI.method: The protocol adopts a mentor-initiated bidirectional asymmetric teleportation architecture. The required entangled resources are constructed explicitly from standard quantum gates (rather than assumed pre-shared), and the full procedure is specified as a quantum circuit and implemented in Qiskit to illustrate the sequence of gate operations and measurements.
AI.result: The protocol succeeds in teleporting an arbitrary two-qubit state from Bob to Alice, generalizing prior Bell-like-restricted schemes. The entangled resource construction using standard quantum gates is shown to be sufficient, and the Qiskit quantum-circuit implementation demonstrates the protocol's operational validity.
AI.conclusion: By removing the Bell-like constraint on the Bob-to-Alice state and constructing the entanglement from standard gates, the proposed mentor-initiated bidirectional asymmetric protocol broadens the applicability of bidirectional quantum teleportation, with a Qiskit circuit confirming its feasibility.

title: Predicting electric-field noise in ion traps using fluctuation electrodynamics
summary: Electric-field noise in microfabricated surface ion traps contributes to gate errors in trapped-ion quantum computers, but this noise has been challenging to predict. Here, we present a method to predict the electric-field noise arising from fluctuations in the bulk of dielectric and metallic materials. The method is valid for arbitrary trap geometries, and the only relevant material property is energy loss. We apply it to an ion trap with an electrically floating electrode and find the contribution from dielectrics to be dominant. Our model predicts the observed noise for this trap within a factor of four. In addition, we apply our model to typical surface trap designs and analyze how the electrode structures shield the noise.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to predict bulk-originating electric-field noise in microfabricated surface ion traps, valid for arbitrary geometries and dependent only on material energy loss, and validates it against experiments.
AI.motivation: Electric-field noise in microfabricated surface ion traps causes gate errors in trapped-ion quantum computers, yet predicting this noise has remained difficult.
AI.method: A predictive model is developed for electric-field noise arising from fluctuations in the bulk of dielectric and metallic materials. The method applies to arbitrary trap geometries and requires only the material's energy loss as the relevant property. It is applied to an ion trap with an electrically floating electrode and to typical surface trap designs, including analysis of electrode shielding.
AI.result: For the trap with a floating electrode, the dielectric contribution dominates, and the model predicts the observed noise within a factor of four. Application to typical surface trap designs reveals how electrode structures shield the noise.
