AI.conclusion: The proposed method enables prediction of bulk electric-field noise in arbitrary trap geometries using a single material property, offering a practical tool for designing low-noise surface ion traps.

title: Efficiently Optimizing the Quantum Value of Bell Inequalities using Batched Gradient Descent
summary: Exploring the world of Bell inequalities requires numerical methods that scale effectively with the number of parties, inputs, and outputs. Such methods can be used to study large-scale Bell inequalities beyond the reach of analytic methods, to design experiments for violating more complicated Bell inequalities, and to enable applications of Bell inequality violation. Such applications include randomness generation and multi-agent coordination with restricted communication. However, current general purpose optimizers such as the see-saw method struggle to handle Bell inequalities with only a dozen inputs and outputs. We introduce an optimizer for the quantum value of a Bell inequality based on batched gradient descent (BGD). More precisely, our BGD optimizer is a differentiable search over feasible quantum strategies in which states and projective measurements are generated from unconstrained variables. The Bell expression is evaluated by a direct tensor contraction without forming the prohibitively large Bell operator. This formulation makes parallel random restarts inexpensive and is thus naturally implemented by a GPU. We evaluate our optimizer against the see-saw method and find a significant speedup for a wide variety of Bell inequality families. Implemented on a GPU, our BGD optimizer can optimize Bell inequalities in our numerical experiments with more than a thousand inputs or outputs within minutes. For these large-scale Bell inequalities, we also efficiently compute the classical value by enumerating possible strategies using a GPU or expressing the optimization as a mixed-integer linear program. Our optimizers can serve as numerical evaluation tools for Bell experiments and multi-agent coordination problems modeled by Bell inequalities with many inputs and outputs, a common feature of real-world scenarios such as high frequency trading and distributed systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a GPU-accelerated batched gradient descent (BGD) optimizer for computing the quantum value of Bell inequalities, using differentiable search over feasible quantum strategies and direct tensor contraction to handle large-scale problems with thousands of inputs/outputs.
AI.motivation: Studying Bell inequalities requires numerical methods that scale with the number of parties, inputs, and outputs, enabling applications like randomness generation and multi-agent coordination. Existing general-purpose optimizers such as the see-saw method struggle with even a dozen inputs and outputs, limiting exploration of large-scale Bell inequalities.
AI.method: The authors propose a BGD optimizer performing differentiable search over feasible quantum strategies, where states and projective measurements are generated from unconstrained variables. The Bell expression is evaluated via direct tensor contraction, avoiding construction of the prohibitively large Bell operator. This formulation enables inexpensive parallel random restarts, naturally suited to GPU parallelization. Classical values for large-scale inequalities are computed by GPU-based strategy enumeration or by formulating the optimization as a mixed-integer linear program (MILP).
AI.result: Benchmarked against the see-saw method, the BGD optimizer achieves significant speedups across a wide variety of Bell inequality families. On GPU, it optimizes inequalities with more than a thousand inputs or outputs within minutes.
AI.conclusion: The BGD optimizer and associated classical-value methods serve as practical numerical evaluation tools for Bell experiments and multi-agent coordination problems involving Bell inequalities with many inputs and outputs, relevant to real-world scenarios such as high frequency trading and distributed systems.

title: Exact first-detection probability in a locally monitored solvable quantum circuit
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 19 pages, 4 figures
summary: We study the interplay between local stroboscopic measurements and the unitary quantum circuit dynamics of the deterministic Floquet-quantum East model. We derive exact analytical results for the probability of first detecting a subset of qubits back in their initial state. This is achieved via a renewal equation linking the first-detection probability to the subsystem Loschmidt echo, which encodes the effective open dynamics of the monitored qubits. The resulting statistics exhibit two regimes set by the competition between the measurement probing time and the relaxation timescale of the unitary circuit dynamics: while infrequent monitoring leads to geometric first-detection statistics, frequent monitoring induces correlations that manifest as deviations from this geometric behavior. These results provide a rare exact characterization of how local measurement backaction reshapes detection statistics in an interacting quantum many-body system. In our local protocol, return probabilities are controlled by the size of the monitored subregion and can therefore be accessed on digital quantum simulators via local mid-circuit measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper derives exact analytical results for the first-detection probability of qubit subsets in the monitored deterministic Floquet-quantum East model, revealing geometric versus non-geometric statistics governed by the measurement-to-relaxation timescale competition.
AI.motivation: Understanding how local stroboscopic measurements and measurement backaction reshape detection statistics in interacting quantum many-body systems is poorly characterized, and exact analytical results are rare.
AI.method: The authors analytically study the deterministic Floquet-quantum East model under local stroboscopic measurements, using a renewal equation that links the first-detection probability to the subsystem Loschmidt echo, which encodes the effective open dynamics of the monitored qubits.
AI.result: Two regimes emerge from the competition between the measurement probing time and the circuit relaxation timescale: infrequent monitoring yields geometric first-detection statistics, whereas frequent monitoring induces correlations producing deviations from geometric behavior. Return probabilities are controlled by the monitored subregion size.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rare exact characterization of local measurement backaction on detection statistics in an interacting quantum many-body system, and the protocol is accessible on digital quantum simulators via local mid-circuit measurements.

title: Less precise but less noisy: local circuits for momentum-space state preparation and measurement
summary: Quantum algorithms are usually optimized for gate count or circuit depth. We find on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer that for a tight-binding chain ground state preparation, there is a system size $N$ beyond which the adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT), with the same number of gates, and with the same circuit depth. We attribute this high noise sensitivity of the FFT to its high precision, being able to distinguish momenta by $1/N$. This high resolution in momentum space requires long-range couplings in real space, which propagates errors faster. In contrast, although local and physical circuits such as the adiabatic evolution have a coarser momentum resolution, they also propagate errors more slowly. For physical applications, high momentum resolution is rarely required and is often worth trading for low noise sensitivity. We also introduce a momentum measurement scheme that although less precise than FFT, is less costly and less noisy. We show that it achieves better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer. Our work emphasizes the importance of reducing the noise sensitivity of quantum algorithms, beyond the number of gates or circuit depth.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that beyond gate count and circuit depth, noise sensitivity is a crucial metric for quantum algorithms: for tight-binding chain ground state preparation on Quantinuum H2, adiabatic evolution outperforms the Fermionic Fourier Transform (FFT) at the same gate count and depth for large system sizes N, because FFT's high momentum resolution (1/N) demands long-range couplings that propagate errors faster. A cheaper, less noisy momentum measurement scheme is introduced that beats FFT for spectral function measurement.
AI.motivation: Quantum algorithms are conventionally optimized for gate count or circuit depth, implicitly treating these as the primary cost metrics. The authors argue this is insufficient because noise sensitivity—determined by circuit structure such as coupling range—can dominate performance on real hardware. High-precision algorithms like FFT, while gate- and depth-efficient, may be intrinsically more noise-prone, so a noise-sensitivity-aware design principle is needed.
AI.method: The authors compare, on the Quantinuum System Model H2 quantum computer, adiabatic evolution versus the Fermionic Fourier Transform for tight-binding chain ground state preparation at matched gate count and circuit depth, across varying system size N. They analyze the relationship between momentum resolution (1/N), real-space coupling range, and error propagation speed. They also design a new momentum measurement scheme with coarser resolution but lower cost and noise, and benchmark it against FFT for spectral function measurement.
AI.result: A system size N threshold exists beyond which adiabatic evolution reaches significantly lower energies than FFT at identical gate count and circuit depth. FFT's high momentum resolution (distinguishing momenta by 1/N) requires long-range couplings, causing faster error propagation and thus high noise sensitivity, whereas local physical circuits like adiabatic evolution have coarser resolution but slower error propagation. The new momentum measurement scheme, though less precise than FFT, is cheaper and less noisy, achieving better performance than FFT for spectral function measurement on the H2 device.
AI.conclusion: Noise sensitivity should be treated as a first-class optimization objective for quantum algorithms, alongside gate count and circuit depth. Since high momentum resolution is rarely required for physical applications, it is often worth trading for lower noise sensitivity, and algorithm design should explicitly account for how circuit locality and precision affect error propagation.

title: Near-optimal quantum query lower bounds on bipartiteness and expansion testing in the bounded-degree graph model
summary: In this work, we study bipartiteness and expansion testing, two canonical problems in graph property testing in the bounded-degree model through the lens of quantum query complexity. In the classical setting, it is known that $\widetildeΘ(\sqrt{N})$ queries are necessary and sufficient for both these testing problems (Goldreich and Ron, 1999, 2000 & 2002), where $N$ denotes the number of vertices of the input graph. Due to their significance, (Ambainis, Childs, and Liu, 2011) initiated the study of these problems in the quantum setting and designed quantum algorithms for bipartiteness and expansion testing that perform $\widetilde{O}(N^{1/3})$ queries, showing a polynomial speedup. They also proved that $\widetildeΩ(N^{1/4})$ queries are necessary for expansion testing, but the possibility of an exponential quantum advantage for bipartiteness testing remained open. Despite significant effort, there has been no improvement in these results in the last decade and a half. In this work, we prove essentially tight $\widetildeΩ(N^{1/3})$ quantum query lower bounds for both bipartiteness and expansion testing, thereby completely characterizing the quantum query complexity of these problems up to polylogarithmic factors. While our proofs use the polynomial method similarly to Ambainis, Childs, and Liu, we use intermediate problems that we relate to the main problems via reductions, and perform a more precise analysis of the resulting polynomials, leading to the near-optimal lower bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper proves essentially tight Ω̃(N^{1/3}) quantum query lower bounds for bipartiteness and expansion testing in the bounded-degree model, matching the known upper bounds and fully characterizing their quantum query complexity up to polylogarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: Bipartiteness and expansion testing are canonical graph property testing problems. Classically, both require Θ̃(√N) queries. Ambainis, Childs, and Liu (2011) gave quantum algorithms using Õ(N^{1/3}) queries and proved an Ω̃(N^{1/4}) lower bound for expansion testing, leaving open whether bipartiteness admits an exponential quantum advantage. Despite significant effort, no progress had been made for over a decade.
AI.method: The authors use the polynomial method, as in Ambainis, Childs, and Liu, but introduce intermediate problems related to the main problems via reductions and perform a more precise analysis of the resulting polynomials.
AI.result: The paper establishes essentially tight Ω̃(N^{1/3}) quantum query lower bounds for both bipartiteness and expansion testing.
AI.conclusion: Combined with the known Õ(N^{1/3}) upper bounds, these results completely characterize the quantum query complexity of bipartiteness and expansion testing up to polylogarithmic factors, closing the open question on the possibility of an exponential quantum advantage for bipartiteness testing.

title: Efficient quantum phase estimation with adaptive entanglement-assisted Hadamard test
summary: The entanglement-assisted Hadamard test (EHT) is a practical method for estimating a quantum phase by amplifying the phase signal. However, the feasible amplification is fundamentally limited by the accuracy of the reference phase, such that the method is inefficient in the high-precision regime. In this work, we propose an algorithm, called adaptive entanglement-assisted Hadamard test (AEHT), that iteratively refines the reference phase, enabling progressively stronger amplification as the iteration goes by. We further consider the imperfect eigenstate preparation scenario, where a systematic bias is unavoidable when estimating the quantum phase with the conventional EHT. Such a bias can be suppressed by the proposed AEHT. Moreover, taking physical implementation into consideration, we adopt device-restart count to measure the cost of quantum phase estimation, rather than shot count. The numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed AEHT compared with conventional methods under this measure. By unlocking the full amplification power of large entangled states, this work offers an efficient method to estimate high-precision quantum phase on near-term quantum processors.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the adaptive entanglement-assisted Hadamard test (AEHT), which iteratively refines the reference phase to enable progressively stronger phase amplification, suppressing systematic bias and achieving efficient high-precision quantum phase estimation.
AI.motivation: The entanglement-assisted Hadamard test (EHT) estimates quantum phases by amplifying the phase signal, but its feasible amplification is fundamentally limited by reference-phase accuracy, making it inefficient in the high-precision regime. Additionally, imperfect eigenstate preparation introduces an unavoidable systematic bias with conventional EHT.
AI.method: AEHT iteratively refines the reference phase so that amplification strength increases progressively across iterations. It is designed to suppress the systematic bias arising from imperfect eigenstate preparation. For practical relevance, the cost of phase estimation is measured using device-restart count instead of shot count.
AI.result: Numerical experiments confirm AEHT's effectiveness relative to conventional methods under the device-restart-count cost measure, and demonstrate bias suppression in the imperfect eigenstate preparation scenario.
AI.conclusion: By unlocking the full amplification power of large entangled states, AEHT provides an efficient route to high-precision quantum phase estimation on near-term quantum processors.

title: QUFIG: GNN-Based Prediction of Quantum Fault Injection Vulnerabilities with Gate-Level Precision
comment: Accepted by IEEE International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD) 2026
summary: The growing scale and accessibility of quantum hardware exposed new reliability and security challenges in the quantum computing workflow, such as the run-time fault injection attacks in cloud-based quantum computing platforms. However, existing works fail to identify vulnerabilities with gate-level precision or adapt to run-time environments. In this work, we formulate gate-level fault analysis as a learning-guided prioritization problem under restricted fidelity budgets. The framework uses a circuit-DAG-based GNN backbone to predict the vulnerability score of each gate to each type of injected fault, defined as the impact of the gate-fault pair on circuit fidelity. The gate-fault pairs are then ranked by their vulnerability score. Experiments on QASMbench and HamLib MaxCut show that QUFIG recovers high-impact vulnerable gate-fault pairs with fewer inspections than random and depth-based heuristics. Our results show that QUFIG can reduce the number of gates requiring inspection by 2.9--19.8% while maintaining effective fault identification, allowing quantum circuit designers to identify vulnerabilities and apply targeted defenses more efficiently.

AI.tldr: QUFIG formulates gate-level fault analysis as a learning-guided prioritization problem under fidelity budgets, using a circuit-DAG GNN to score and rank gate-fault pairs by vulnerability, cutting inspection needs by 2.9-19.8%.
AI.motivation: Growing quantum hardware scale and accessibility expose reliability and security issues like run-time fault injection attacks in cloud-based quantum platforms. Existing approaches cannot pinpoint vulnerabilities at gate-level precision or adapt to run-time environments.
AI.method: Gate-level fault analysis is cast as a learning-guided prioritization problem under restricted fidelity budgets. A circuit-DAG-based GNN backbone predicts a vulnerability score for each gate to each injected fault type, defined as the impact of the gate-fault pair on circuit fidelity. Gate-fault pairs are then ranked by vulnerability score.
AI.result: On QASMbench and HamLib MaxCut, QUFIG recovers high-impact vulnerable gate-fault pairs with fewer inspections than random and depth-based heuristics, reducing the number of gates requiring inspection by 2.9-19.8% while maintaining effective fault identification.
AI.conclusion: QUFIG enables quantum circuit designers to identify vulnerabilities and apply targeted defenses more efficiently through learning-guided, gate-level fault prioritization.

title: Non-Markovian effects on informational steady states
summary: Informational steady states (ISSs) arise when the rate at which information is gained from continuous measurements is exactly balanced by the rate at which information from earlier measurements is lost to the environment. While ISSs have been studied in Markovian settings, relatively little is known about how memory effects influence their formation and steady-state properties. In this work, we investigate non-Markovian effects on ISSs within the framework of continuously monitored collision models. We model the environment as a sequence of two-qubit ancillas and find that, for this specific model, the steady-state information gain per measurement is negatively correlated with the degree of non-Markovianity. Numerical results further characterize how the system-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction parameters influence both the degree of non-Markovianity and the steady-state information gain.

AI.tldr: This work studies informational steady states (ISSs) under non-Markovian dynamics using continuously monitored collision models with two-qubit ancillas, finding that steady-state information gain per measurement is negatively correlated with the degree of non-Markovianity.
AI.motivation: ISSs, where information gain from continuous measurements balances information loss to the environment, are well studied in Markovian settings, but how memory effects influence their formation and steady-state properties remains largely unexplored.
AI.method: The environment is modeled as a sequence of two-qubit ancillas within a continuously monitored collision-model framework, enabling examination of non-Markovian effects on ISSs. Numerical analysis then characterizes how system-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction parameters affect both the degree of non-Markovianity and the steady-state information gain.
AI.result: For this specific model, the steady-state information gain per measurement is negatively correlated with the degree of non-Markovianity. System-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction parameters are shown to influence both non-Markovianity and steady-state information gain.
AI.conclusion: Non-Markovian memory effects, tunable via collision-model interaction parameters, suppress steady-state information gain per measurement, establishing a negative correlation between non-Markovianity and ISS information gain in this setting.

title: Learnt Attacks on Quantum Key Distribution under Channel Noise and Device Drift
comment: Presented as submission 202 at QCrypt 2026 qcrypt.net/2026/technical/accepted-papers/. A parallel work exploring the machine-learning aspects of this approach, titled "Sparsity for Free: A Budget-Induced Equilibrium in Joint Topology-Parameter Search'', has been accepted for NeurIPS 2026
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) links are provisioned from security analyses of stationary channels, whereas the devices that determine the channel drift between recalibrations. Whether an eavesdropper who cannot alter the channel's own noise gains by following that drift has not been quantified. Adaptive eavesdropping is posed here as a constrained Markov decision process in which the attacker selects one circuit per round while the noise level follows an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process and the abort condition is a budget over each block of rounds. The value of adaptation is bounded by the best fixed circuit and a dynamic-programming upper bound. The actions are learnt attacks. Whereas Decker et al. trained a parametrised circuit on a fixed gate template against a fixed channel, here the gate structure and rotation angles are searched jointly. This yields circuits compact enough to form a discrete action set, extending the construction to noise models lacking a known template, including the amplitude damping channel. On device-independent E91 under bilateral depolarising noise, a reinforcement-learning attacker raises her Holevo information from $0.135$ for the best fixed circuit to $0.348$ at zero detection, $98\%$ of the upper bound. On BB84 under a drifting bit-flip channel, she exceeds a conservative noise-indexed rule by $0.024$ in fidelity, reaching $99\%$ of the upper bound. Under stationary noise, the attacker's gain from basis asymmetry changes sign between an averaged and a per-basis error-rate constraint. The search, started from random gate sequences, recovers the analytical cloners and the collective-attack key rate, and meets the lower bound of the Winick--Lütkenhaus--Coles objective from above.

AI.tldr: This work models adaptive eavesdropping on drifting QKD channels as a constrained Markov decision process and shows that a reinforcement-learning attacker can substantially outperform the best fixed attack circuit, approaching theoretical upper bounds.
AI.motivation: QKD security analyses typically assume stationary channels and fixed attacker circuits, but real channels drift between recalibrations. The gain available to an eavesdropper who passively follows this drift (without altering the channel noise) had not been quantified.
AI.method: Adaptive eavesdropping is cast as a constrained Markov decision process: the attacker picks one circuit per round, the noise follows an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, and abort is governed by a per-block budget. Gate structure and rotation angles are searched jointly (unlike prior fixed-template training), yielding compact circuits that form a discrete action set and extend to noise models without a known template, e.g. amplitude damping. Bounds are given by the best fixed circuit and a dynamic-programming upper bound.
AI.result: On device-independent E91 under bilateral depolarising noise, the RL attacker raises Holevo information from 0.135 (best fixed circuit) to 0.348 at zero detection, 98% of the upper bound. On BB84 under a drifting bit-flip channel, it exceeds a conservative noise-indexed rule by 0.024 in fidelity, reaching 99% of the upper bound. Under stationary noise, the gain from basis asymmetry changes sign between averaged and per-basis error-rate constraints. Random-initialised search recovers analytical cloners and the collective-attack key rate, meeting the Winick–Lütkenhaus–Coles lower bound from above.
AI.conclusion: Adaptation to channel drift provides a significant, quantifiable advantage to an eavesdropper, and jointly searching gate structure and angles yields compact, generalisable attack circuits whose performance closely tracks dynamic-programming bounds and recovers known analytical optima.

title: Collision models: Markovian and Non-Markovian impurity models
summary: Collision models provide a flexible framework for studying open quantum systems and introducing non-Markovianity. We present a novel class of collision models, which we term Markovian impurity models, motivated by physical scenarios in which information backflow is periodically blocked. Using the Breuer-Laine-Piilo (BLP) measure of non-Markovianity, we show that if a $p$-impurity model is non-Markovian, then the corresponding $(p+1)$-impurity model is also non-Markovian, implying the existence of a critical $p$ at which the process transitions from Markovian to non-Markovian. Numerical simulations are used to investigate how this critical parameter depends on the system-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction strengths. We find that, altough exceptions exist, increasing either interaction strength generally lowers the critical $p$, while sufficiently weak ancilla-ancilla interactions lead to a regime in which the dynamics remain Markovian even in the absence of impurities. Finally, we briefly introduce the complementary non-Markovian impurity model.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Markovian impurity models," a novel class of collision models where information backflow is periodically blocked, and shows that non-Markovianity is monotonic in the number of impurities $p$, establishing a critical threshold $p$ for the Markovian-to-non-Markovian transition that depends on interaction strengths.
AI.motivation: Collision models offer a flexible framework for studying open quantum systems and non-Markovianity. The authors are motivated by physical scenarios in which information backflow is periodically blocked, prompting them to construct a model class capturing this behavior.
AI.method: They define Markovian impurity models and quantify non-Markovianity using the Breuer-Laine-Piilo (BLP) measure. They prove a monotonicity result: if a $p$-impurity model is non-Markovian, the corresponding $(p+1)$-impurity model is also non-Markovian. Numerical simulations examine how the critical $p$ depends on system-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction strengths. They also briefly introduce a complementary non-Markovian impurity model.
AI.result: Non-Markovianity is monotone in $p$, implying a critical $p$ marking the Markovian-to-non-Markovian transition. Generally, increasing either the system-ancilla or ancilla-ancilla interaction strength lowers the critical $p$, though exceptions exist. Sufficiently weak ancilla-ancilla interactions produce a regime where dynamics remain Markovian even without impurities.
AI.conclusion: Markovian impurity models provide a tractable framework linking impurity structure and interaction strengths to the onset of non-Markovianity, with a well-defined critical $p$. The complementary non-Markovian impurity model is introduced as a counterpart for future study.

title: QPI-DeepONet-MAC: A Scalable and Stable Hybrid Classical-Quantum Architecture for Physics-Informed Deep Operator Networks
summary: General operator learning for parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) is a fundamental challenge at the intersection of artificial intelligence and physics-based modeling. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) incorporate governing equations into learning, but face optimization difficulties in high dimensions. Quantum extensions offer additional representational capacity, yet their trainability can be hindered by barren plateaus. Here, we introduce QPI-DeepONet-MAC, a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that integrates parameterized quantum circuits into PI-DeepONets through a multiplicative-and-additive coupling (MAC) of classical representations and quantum expectation values. We prove analytically that the proposed architecture retains universal operator approximation capabilities. Furthermore, we derive bounds on quantum parameter gradients, establishing explicit conditions to avoid barren plateaus alongside a scaling criterion for trainability. Additionally, we derive a lower bound on the number of sensors required for a target accuracy, directly linking sampling requirements to input function regularity, domain dimension, and PDE dynamical growth. Finally, we propose an informational regularization scheme based on quantum coherence and state fidelity dynamics to prevent coherence loss and preserve quantum structure during training. Together, these results establish a theoretical foundation for quantum-enhanced physics-informed operator learning and position QPI-DeepONet-MAC as a scalable, stable framework for solving parametric PDEs.

AI.tldr: QPI-DeepONet-MAC is a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that embeds parameterized quantum circuits into physics-informed DeepONets via a multiplicative-and-additive coupling of classical and quantum representations, with proven universal approximation, trainability guarantees, sensor lower bounds, and a coherence-based regularization scheme.
AI.motivation: Solving parametric PDEs with operator learning is a core AI-for-physics problem. PI-DeepONets embed governing equations but suffer optimization difficulties in high dimensions, while quantum extensions add representational capacity but risk barren plateaus and poor trainability.
AI.method: The authors introduce QPI-DeepONet-MAC, integrating parameterized quantum circuits into PI-DeepONets through multiplicative-and-additive coupling (MAC) of classical representations and quantum expectation values. They analytically prove universal operator approximation, derive quantum parameter gradient bounds with explicit barren-plateau-avoidance conditions and a trainability scaling criterion, derive a lower bound on sensors needed for target accuracy, and propose an informational regularization scheme based on quantum coherence and state fidelity dynamics.
AI.result: The architecture retains universal operator approximation capability; gradient bounds yield explicit conditions to avoid barren plateaus and a scaling criterion for trainability; a sensor lower bound links sampling requirements to input function regularity, domain dimension, and PDE dynamical growth; the coherence/fidelity regularization prevents coherence loss and preserves quantum structure during training.
AI.conclusion: These results provide a theoretical foundation for quantum-enhanced physics-informed operator learning and position QPI-DeepONet-MAC as a scalable, stable framework for solving parametric PDEs.

title: Experimental realization of Wheeler's delayed-choice experiment with dual selections
summary: Wheeler's delayed-choice experiment demonstrates wave-particle duality of particles using different experimental configurations of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. In a quantum version of this experiment, the wave-particle behavior of photons can be observed by controlling presence or absence of the second beam splitter. Here, we implement a delayed-choice experiment with dual selections based on entangled photons, experimentally controlling both of two beam splitters in the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, where the presence and absence of the second beam splitter are simultaneously controlled through path encoding. Our experiment reveals the wave-particle behavior of single photons under different configurations of two beam splitters. We further discuss the scenario when two beam splitters are in a quantum superposition of being present and absent, photons will be in a wave-particle quantum superposition state.

AI.tldr: A delayed-choice experiment is demonstrated with entangled photons where both beam splitters in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer are controlled, revealing wave-particle behavior of single photons and their quantum superposition under simultaneous presence/absence configurations.
AI.motivation: Wheeler's delayed-choice experiment probes wave-particle duality, and its quantum version allows observing photon wave-particle behavior by controlling the second beam splitter. Extending this to control both beam splitters provides a richer testbed for understanding wave-particle duality.
AI.method: The authors implement a delayed-choice experiment with dual selections based on entangled photons, experimentally controlling both of the two beam splitters in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The presence and absence of the second beam splitter are simultaneously controlled through path encoding.
AI.result: The experiment reveals the wave-particle behavior of single photons under different configurations of the two beam splitters. Additionally, the scenario where both beam splitters are in a quantum superposition of present and absent is discussed, in which photons occupy a wave-particle quantum superposition state.
AI.conclusion: Dual-controlled delayed-choice experiments with entangled photons demonstrate controllable wave-particle behavior and suggest wave-particle quantum superposition states when both beam splitters are in quantum superposition.

title: Toward Optimal Circuit Depth for Geometrically Local Hamiltonian Simulation
summary:
Understanding the dynamics of interacting quantum systems is a central goal of quantum simulation. For geometrically local Hamiltonians, locality suggests that digital simulation should retain much of the parallelism of the underlying dynamics. For a target accuracy $ε$, we construct a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit that simulates the dynamics of an $n$-qubit, time-independent, finite-range Hamiltonian with normalized local interaction strength on a fixed-dimensional lattice for time $T\ge1$, with circuit depth $O(T\log(nT/ε))$ and gate count $O(nT\log(nT/ε))$. This reduces the polylogarithmic overhead of Haah, Hastings, Kothari, and Low to a single logarithm. On logarithmic-scale blocks from the Lieb--Robinson decomposition, a shallow but highly accurate implementation is essential for reducing the circuit depth. Our key observation is that spatial localization also controls the cost of high precision. In each block, the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated for by a correction, yielding exponential accuracy. The correction can be implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, introducing no additional asymptotic depth scale beyond that required by spatial localization.
  Furthermore, we prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians: at fixed evolution time $T$ in the stated regime and sufficiently small fixed error $ε$, any nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating these dynamics requires depth $Ω(\log n/\log\log n)$. This matches our $O(\log n)$ upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor, establishing near-optimal circuit depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation in this regime. Together, these results clarify the role of locality and precision in determining the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics and suggest broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs a nearest-neighbor quantum circuit simulating finite-range lattice Hamiltonian dynamics of n qubits for time T with depth O(T log(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nT log(nT/ε)), improving prior polylogarithmic overhead to a single logarithm, and proves a matching unconditional depth lower bound of Ω(log n/log log n) for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians, showing near-optimality.
AI.motivation: Digital quantum simulation of geometrically local Hamiltonians should exploit the parallelism inherent in local dynamics, but existing algorithms carry polylogarithmic overhead that limits circuit depth. The paper aims to reduce this overhead and to characterize the fundamental depth limits imposed by locality and precision.
AI.method: The authors use a Lieb-Robinson decomposition into logarithmic-scale blocks. Within each block, they exploit spatial localization to control high-precision cost: the error of a constant-order product formula is compensated by a correction term implemented with depth proportional to the block diameter, yielding exponential accuracy without adding asymptotic depth beyond that required by locality. They also prove an unconditional circuit-depth lower bound for uniform XXZ Hamiltonians via a suitable argument in the stated regime.
AI.result: The construction achieves circuit depth O(T log(nT/ε)) and gate count O(nT log(nT/ε)) for time-independent finite-range Hamiltonians on a fixed-dimensional lattice with normalized local interaction strength, reducing the previous polylogarithmic overhead to a single logarithm. The lower bound shows any nearest-neighbor circuit simulating uniform XXZ dynamics at fixed T and sufficiently small ε requires depth Ω(log n/log log n), matching the O(log n) upper bound up to a doubly logarithmic factor.
AI.conclusion: Locality and precision jointly determine the circuit complexity of quantum dynamics: spatial localization controls both parallelism and the cost of high precision. The near-optimal depth for lattice Hamiltonian simulation suggests broader principles for spatially constrained quantum computation.

title: Trapdoored Clifford Operators and Applications
summary:
Random Clifford operators have numerous applications in quantum computing, including randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, and quantum authentication. However, sampling and implementing uniformly random $n$-qubit Clifford incur near-quadratic complexity due to the size of Clifford group.
  We introduce a cryptographic way to overcome these barriers: trapdoored Clifford operator distributions whose samples are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random Cliffords, yet implementing them can be much faster given the trapdoor. We construct a distribution of trapdoored Clifford operators whose elements can be sampled and implemented in near-linear time under a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption. Our constructions allow fast tableau action on Pauli labels for classical simulation, and also can be optimized to admit polylogarithmic-depth implementation. Along the way, we construct trapdoored matrices over finite fields that support efficient multiplication by both a matrix and its inverse, resolving an open question left by Vaikuntanathan and Zamir [SODA'26].
  We use these constructions to obtain faster protocols based on random Cliffords. We also explore their applications to the worst-case to average-case reductions for matrix and Clifford problems including the iterated matrix multiplication and Clifford circuit synthesis. In particular, we show the hardness of batching Clifford circuits: synthesizing circuits that apply the same Clifford to multiple registers is at least as hard as worst-case matrix multiplication, even when synthesis succeeds on a small constant fraction of random Cliffords. This extends to approximate implementations by general quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces trapdoored Clifford operator distributions that are computationally indistinguishable from uniform random Cliffords but can be sampled and implemented in near-linear time given a trapdoor, under a variant of the learning parity with noise (LPN) assumption. These constructions yield faster random-Clifford-based protocols and new worst-case-to-average-case hardness results, including the hardness of batching Clifford circuits.
AI.motivation: Uniformly random n-qubit Clifford operators are widely used in randomized benchmarking, classical shadows, and quantum authentication, but sampling and implementing them incur near-quadratic complexity due to the size of the Clifford group. The work seeks a cryptographic means to bypass this efficiency barrier while preserving the pseudorandom behavior that makes uniform Cliffords useful.
AI.method: The authors construct a distribution of trapdoored Clifford operators whose samples are computationally indistinguishable from uniformly random Cliffords, yet become efficiently samplable and implementable given a trapdoor. Security relies on a variant of the learning parity with noise assumption. The construction supports fast tableau action on Pauli labels for classical simulation and can be optimized for polylogarithmic-depth implementation. As a building block, they construct trapdoored matrices over finite fields supporting efficient multiplication by both a matrix and its inverse, resolving an open question of Vaikuntanathan and Zamir.
AI.result: The constructions enable near-linear-time sampling and implementation of pseudorandom Cliffords, polylogarithmic-depth implementations, and faster protocols based on random Cliffords. They also yield worst-case-to-average-case reductions for matrix and Clifford problems, including iterated matrix multiplication and Clifford circuit synthesis. In particular, batching Clifford circuits—synthesizing circuits that apply the same Clifford to multiple registers—is shown to be at least as hard as worst-case matrix multiplication, even when synthesis succeeds on only a small constant fraction of random Cliffords; this extends to approximate implementations by general quantum circuits.
AI.conclusion: Trapdoored Clifford distributions offer a cryptographic route to efficient, pseudorandom Clifford sampling and implementation, with implications for speeding up random-Clifford protocols and for establishing average-case hardness of matrix and Clifford synthesis tasks. The work also resolves an open problem on trapdoored finite-field matrices with efficient forward and inverse multiplication.

title: Quantum Optimal Transport Barycenters: Existence, Duality, and Gaussian Rigidity
summary:
We develop a Quantum Optimal Transport (QOT) barycenter framework for quantum states, as an analog of Wasserstein barycenters~\cite{AguCar}, and establish existence and duality results for a broad class of possibly unbounded transport costs on separable Hilbert spaces. Our framework provides, in particular, a unified treatment of $2$-quantum Wasserstein (QW) barycenters in both the quantum-state and quantum-channel formulations by specializing to the canonical quadratic cost operators associated with the $2$-quantum Wasserstein distances of Caglioti--Golse--Mouhot--Paul~\cite{caglioti2021towards,Golse-Mouhot-Paul:2016} and De Palma--Trevisan~\cite{DPaTre19}.
  The central results concern Gaussian input states and, in particular, Gaussian rigidity: whether Gaussian input states force the 2-QW barycenter itself to be Gaussian and uniquely determined when the minimization is taken over all quantum states. We first show that the barycenter problem admits a Gaussian minimizer and reduces to a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem over covariance matrices.
  The main difficulty is that uniqueness of the optimal covariance does not, in general, imply uniqueness of the underlying quantum state. We bridge this gap through a state-reconstruction principle under covariance complementary slackness that upgrades uniqueness of the optimal covariance to uniqueness of the full quantum state, and thereby prove a global rigidity theorem: if at least one Gaussian input is faithful, then the barycenter is unique among all quantum states and is necessarily Gaussian. Faithfulness is sufficient but not necessary: families of pure inputs still determine a unique barycenter, whereas partially pure nonfaithful Gaussian inputs may admit multiple barycenters.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a Quantum Optimal Transport (QOT) barycenter framework for quantum states, proving existence and duality for general unbounded transport costs on separable Hilbert spaces, and establishes Gaussian rigidity: if one Gaussian input is faithful, the 2-QW barycenter is unique and Gaussian.
AI.motivation: Wasserstein barycenters are well understood classically, but a unified quantum analog is lacking. The authors aim to provide a general QOT barycenter theory and to settle whether Gaussian inputs force the barycenter to be Gaussian and unique.
AI.method: The authors formulate QOT barycenters as an analog of Wasserstein barycenters, establish existence and duality for broad classes of possibly unbounded transport costs on separable Hilbert spaces, and specialize to canonical quadratic cost operators to unify the 2-quantum Wasserstein barycenter in state and channel formulations. They reduce the problem to finite-dimensional convex optimization over covariance matrices and introduce a state-reconstruction principle under covariance complementary slackness.
AI.result: A Gaussian minimizer is shown to exist, reducing the barycenter problem to convex optimization over covariance matrices. The state-reconstruction principle upgrades uniqueness of the optimal covariance to uniqueness of the full quantum state, yielding a global rigidity theorem: if at least one Gaussian input is faithful, the barycenter is unique among all quantum states and is Gaussian. Faithfulness is sufficient but not necessary; families of pure inputs still determine a unique barycenter, while partially pure nonfaithful Gaussian inputs may admit multiple barycenters.
AI.conclusion: The QOT barycenter framework provides a unified treatment of 2-QW barycenters and establishes Gaussian rigidity under a faithful Gaussian input, with faithfulness being sufficient but not necessary for uniqueness.

title: Approximation theorems for fermionic Gaussian states
summary: A recurring principle in many-body physics is that sufficiently distributed interactions or correlations lead to an effectively mean-field description. For fermionic Gaussian states, we establish a quantitative version of this principle directly at the level of Majorana covariance matrices. The main observation is that the admissibility condition for fermionic covariance matrices imposes a quantitative monogamy constraint on two-point correlations: a fixed region has only a bounded covariance budget to distribute among many disjoint regions. We use this principle in three directions. First, for quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians on finite simple graphs of high degree, we obtain product-state approximations to both the ground-state energy and the finite-temperature free energy, with error of order \(D^{-1/2}\) for \(D\)-regular graphs. Second, we prove a finite fermionic Gaussian de Finetti theorem: a \(k\)-copy Gaussian state that is \(n\)-exchangeable under graded fermionic copy permutations is \(O(k/n)\)-close in trace norm to the product of its one-copy marginal. In particular, infinite exchangeability within the Gaussian class implies exact product structure. Third, for spatial fermionic Gaussian states with exponentially clustering mutual information, we prove that the conditional mutual information across a separating buffer decays as \(O(r^{-1})\), and hence, by recoverability, the state admits an \(O(r^{-1/2})\) trace-norm approximation by a recovered state. These results show that product and de Finetti approximations and recoverability estimates for fermionic Gaussian systems can all be derived directly from covariance-level structure.

AI.tldr: Fermionic Gaussian states obey a covariance-level "monogamy" constraint on two-point correlations, from which the authors derive product-state, de Finetti, and recoverability approximations.
AI.motivation: Many-body physics heuristically holds that sufficiently distributed interactions/correlations yield an effectively mean-field description. The paper aims to make this principle quantitative for fermionic Gaussian states, working directly at the level of Majorana covariance matrices rather than the full state.
AI.method: The key observation is that the admissibility condition for fermionic covariance matrices enforces a quantitative monogamy constraint on two-point correlations: a fixed region has a bounded covariance budget to distribute among many disjoint regions. This covariance-level structure is then applied in three directions: (1) quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians on high-degree finite simple graphs, (2) a finite fermionic Gaussian de Finetti theorem for k-copy states n-exchangeable under graded fermionic copy permutations, and (3) spatial fermionic Gaussian states with exponentially clustering mutual information via conditional mutual information and recoverability.
AI.result: (1) For quadratic fermionic Hamiltonians on D-regular finite simple graphs, product-state approximations to ground-state energy and finite-temperature free energy with error of order D^{-1/2}. (2) A k-copy Gaussian state n-exchangeable under graded fermionic copy permutations is O(k/n)-close in trace norm to the product of its one-copy marginal; infinite exchangeability within the Gaussian class implies exact product structure. (3) For spatial fermionic Gaussian states with exponentially clustering mutual information, conditional mutual information across a separating buffer decays as O(r^{-1}), yielding an O(r^{-1/2}) trace-norm approximation by a recovered state.
AI.conclusion: Product and de Finetti approximations and recoverability estimates for fermionic Gaussian systems can all be derived directly from covariance-level structure, providing a unified quantitative manifestation of the mean-field principle.

title: Fourier Symmetrization for Geometric Quantum Machine Learning
summary: Geometric quantum machine learning incorporates symmetry into quantum models, but how symmetry shapes their expressivity and guides effective model design remains insufficiently understood. We address this question through the Fourier representation of quantum Fourier models (QFMs). Symmetry organizes the frequency spectrum into orbits and sums the Fourier coefficients within each orbit into a symmetrized coefficient. When QFM trainable layers form independent exact 2-designs, the variance of each symmetrized coefficient equals the sum of the coefficient variances in its orbit. For single-layer QFMs with $\varepsilon$-approximate 2-design trainable layers, we bound the deviation from this identity. The resulting bound for individual Fourier coefficients can be exponentially tighter than an existing bound. The hyperoctahedral group provides an example of orbit growth that can mitigate vanishing expressivity of the symmetrized coefficients. Symmetrization of QFMs over an elementary abelian 2-group also yields pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions. We introduce randomized encoding, which implements invariant models without ancilla qubits or the additional circuit depth for quantum twirling. We evaluate the models as quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) on two-dimensional screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations. Under hard boundary constraints, QPINNs using exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieve the lowest mean errors in the two benchmarks, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how symmetry shapes the expressivity of geometric quantum machine learning via Fourier analysis of quantum Fourier models (QFMs), showing spectral orbits and symmetrized coefficients, and introduces randomized encoding to build invariant QPINNs that outperform alternatives on two PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Symmetry is commonly incorporated into quantum models, yet its effect on expressivity and its role in guiding effective model design are not well understood. This work aims to clarify how symmetry structures the Fourier representation of QFMs and to translate that understanding into practical invariant model construction.
AI.method: The authors analyze QFMs through their Fourier representation: symmetry partitions the frequency spectrum into orbits and sums Fourier coefficients within each orbit into a symmetrized coefficient. They examine variance identities for these coefficients when trainable layers form independent exact 2-designs, and bound the deviation for single-layer QFMs with epsilon-approximate 2-design layers. They study orbit growth via the hyperoctahedral group and show that symmetrization over an elementary abelian 2-group yields pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions. They also introduce randomized encoding, an invariant-model implementation avoiding ancilla qubits and extra twirling depth.
AI.result: When trainable layers are independent exact 2-designs, each symmetrized coefficient's variance equals the sum of coefficient variances in its orbit; for single-layer QFMs with epsilon-approximate 2-design layers the deviation is bounded, and the bound for individual Fourier coefficients can be exponentially tighter than a prior bound. Symmetrization over an elementary abelian 2-group produces pure multivariate Chebyshev polynomial basis functions, and hyperoctahedral orbit growth can mitigate vanishing expressivity. As QPINNs on 2D screened Poisson and stationary viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations under hard boundary constraints, models using exact symmetrization and randomized encoding achieve the lowest mean errors, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Symmetry imposes an orbit-based structure on QFM Fourier spectra that governs expressivity, and careful symmetrization choices (e.g., elementary abelian 2-groups, hyperoctahedral groups) can control or mitigate vanishing expressivity. Randomized encoding enables practical invariant models without ancilla qubits or extra circuit depth, and the resulting QPINNs are competitive or best-performing on the tested PDE benchmarks.

title: Floquet-Universal Hamiltonian Simulation
summary:
Analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation represent two distinct approaches to making one quantum system replicate the physical properties of another, with consequences ranging from practical applications to complexity theory and quantum gravity. They are rooted in two distinct regimes of quantum dynamics: time-independent Hamiltonians for the former; fully controllable time-dependent quantum circuits in the latter. Time-periodic Hamiltonians represent an intermediate regime. In this work, we establish a theory of Floquet simulation where we use periodically driven Hamiltonians to synthesise time-independent ones.
  We show that a set of interactions $S$ can Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in the Lie algebra $\mathrm{Lie}(S)$, and consequently we give a complete and constructive characterisation of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians that are able to produce any target Hamiltonian. Notably, our construction uses only $O(1)$ local interaction strengths and ratios thereof, avoiding the impractical multi-scale local interaction strengths often required in analogue simulation via time-independent Hamiltonians. Instead, the construction requires a range of driving frequencies which scales polynomially with system size for important classes such as $k$-local lattice Hamiltonians. This has immediate complexity-theoretic implications, including numerous BQP-completeness and QMA-hardness results for natural physical properties and quantities studied in Floquet physics.

AI.tldr: This work develops a theory of Floquet simulation, using time-periodic (driven) Hamiltonians to synthesize time-independent ones. It gives a complete, constructive characterization of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians via the Lie algebra generated by a set of interactions, achieving this with O(1) local interaction strengths and polynomially scaling driving frequencies, with complexity-theoretic consequences including BQP-completeness and QMA-hardness results.
AI.motivation: Analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation occupy two distinct regimes—time-independent Hamiltonians and fully controllable time-dependent circuits. Time-periodic (Floquet) Hamiltonians represent an intermediate regime that was previously less theoretically characterized. A key practical obstacle in analogue simulation is the need for multi-scale local interaction strengths, which is impractical. The paper is motivated by the need for a unified theory of Floquet simulation that bridges these regimes and overcomes the multi-scale strength requirement.
AI.method: The authors establish a theory of Floquet simulation in which periodically driven Hamiltonians synthesize time-independent ones. They prove that a set of interactions S can Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in the Lie algebra Lie(S), yielding a complete and constructive characterization of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians capable of producing any target Hamiltonian. The construction uses only O(1) local interaction strengths and their ratios, instead of multi-scale strengths, while requiring a range of driving frequencies that scales polynomially with system size for important classes such as k-local lattice Hamiltonians.
AI.result: A set of interactions S is shown to Floquet-simulate every Hamiltonian in Lie(S). A complete, constructive characterization of Floquet-universal Hamiltonians is obtained. The construction uses only O(1) local interaction strengths and ratios, and the required driving frequencies scale polynomially with system size for classes such as k-local lattice Hamiltonians. These results yield numerous BQP-completeness and QMA-hardness results for natural physical properties and quantities in Floquet physics.
AI.conclusion: Floquet simulation forms a coherent intermediate regime between analogue and digital Hamiltonian simulation. By leveraging periodically driven Hamiltonians, one can synthesize time-independent Hamiltonians with practical O(1) interaction strengths and polynomially scaling driving frequencies, providing a complete constructive theory of Floquet universality. This bridges practical applications with complexity theory and quantum gravity, with immediate complexity-theoretic implications.

title: Exponential quantum advantages for decoded quantum interferometry in the streaming setting
summary:
Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm introduced by Jordan et al. (Nature 2025). For a natural optimization problem, known as optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it achieves approximation guarantees in regimes where all known classical algorithms require exponential time.
  Besides time, space is another central resource: storing and manipulating a massive input can be very challenging, especially when logical qubits carry substantial fault-tolerant implementation overhead. This motivates the following question: does DQI yield quantum advantages in memory, and can we prove it unconditionally?
  We give an affirmative answer to this question in the streaming setting. In particular, we consider a natural generalization of OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, which asks for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many constraints on its values and derivatives as possible. As a concrete example, we show
  [Quantum efficiency.] An adaptation of the DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying $93\%$ of the constraints; moreover, it only reads the input stream in one pass, uses polylogarithmic space, and has polylogarithmic computation time per stream entry.
  [Classical hardness.] Any classical algorithm that produces an answer satisfying just $76\%$ of the constraints requires polynomial space, even if it can read the input stream with polynomially many passes and can use unlimited time.
  Our result provides a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters, and implies that DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that a streaming adaptation of the Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) algorithm achieves provable quantum advantages in memory, obtained unconditionally under a streaming model.
AI.motivation: Space is a central quantum resource: storing and manipulating massive inputs is challenging, especially given the fault-tolerant overhead of logical qubits. While DQI (Jordan et al., Nature 2025) achieves time advantages for optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), it is unknown whether DQI also yields quantum advantages in memory, and whether such advantages can be proven unconditionally.
AI.method: The authors study a streaming model and generalize OPI using Hermite interpolation and Hasse derivatives, asking for a low-degree polynomial satisfying as many value and derivative constraints as possible. They adapt the DQI algorithm to this streaming setting and analyze a complete tradeoff curve over tunable parameters, contrasting the quantum algorithm against classical algorithms.
AI.result: Quantum efficiency: the adapted DQI algorithm produces a polynomial satisfying 93% of the constraints, reading the input in one pass, using polylogarithmic space and polylogarithmic time per stream entry. Classical hardness: any classical algorithm satisfying just 76% of the constraints requires polynomial space, even with polynomially many passes and unlimited time.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a complete tradeoff curve for the tunable parameters and provides an affirmative answer to whether DQI yields provable, unconditional memory advantages. It implies DQI has provable quantum advantages for the original OPI problem.

title: Loss-tolerant distributed lattice surgery using fusion networks
summary: Networking matter-based quantum processing units (QPUs) offers a promising route to scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers. This requires distributed logical operations to be performed across photonic links, where noise is characteristically different from and stronger than in local QPUs owing to photon loss and probabilistic linear-optical operations. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are designed to be robust against loss and probabilistic photonic operations, suggesting they could complement circuit-based error correction at the interface between networked QPUs. We use ZX calculus transformations to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols and apply them to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery, demonstrating that several protocols attain a $50\%$ interface-erasure threshold when local noise is absent, including circuit-based lattice surgery using fused Bell pairs and hybrid protocols using linear cluster states. Relative to a straight Bell-pair interface geometry, the hybrid protocols increase the merge-observable interface distance from $d+1$ to $2d+1$ and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from $\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor$ to $d$. We calculate how the threshold decreases when using truncated resource states and map correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. We then convert these erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds and probe subthreshold performance using fusion boosting. At circuit and resource-state error rates of $10^{-3}$, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage. As local noise is reduced to $10^{-4}$ and below, the linear-chain protocols improve more rapidly with decreasing erasure, suggesting that interface distance enhancements are effective in low local noise regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper uses ZX calculus to design hybrid syndrome extraction protocols for interfacing networked matter-based QPUs, showing that fusion- and measurement-based approaches can achieve 50% interface-erasure thresholds and improve interface distances in the low local-noise regime.
AI.motivation: Scaling fault-tolerant quantum computers via networked QPUs requires distributed logical operations over photonic links, where noise (photon loss, probabilistic linear-optical operations) is stronger and characteristically different from local QPU noise. Measurement- and fusion-based quantum computing are robust to loss and probabilistic photonic operations, potentially complementing circuit-based error correction at network interfaces.
AI.method: ZX calculus transformations are used to construct hybrid syndrome extraction protocols, applied to distributed rotated surface code lattice surgery. The authors analyze straight Bell-pair interfaces versus hybrid protocols using linear cluster states and fused Bell pairs, compute 50% interface-erasure thresholds, derive correctable regions under resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure, convert erasure thresholds into photon-loss thresholds, and probe subthreshold performance via fusion boosting.
AI.result: Several protocols reach a 50% interface-erasure threshold with no local noise, including circuit-based lattice surgery with fused Bell pairs and hybrid linear-cluster-state protocols. Hybrid protocols raise the merge-observable interface distance from d+1 to 2d+1 and restore the perpendicular-observable interface distance from ⌊(d+1)/2⌋ to d. Threshold degradation is quantified for truncated resource states, and correctable regions are mapped for resource-state errors, local circuit noise, and fusion erasure. At 10^-3 circuit and resource-state error rates, local errors largely mask the interface-distance advantage; at 10^-4 and below, linear-chain protocols improve faster as erasure decreases.
AI.conclusion: Interface-distance enhancements from hybrid protocols are effective primarily in low local-noise regimes, where linear-chain protocols benefit more rapidly from reduced erasure. These results position measurement- and fusion-based techniques as a viable complement to circuit-based error correction at networked QPU interfaces.

title: Avoiding Exponentially Large Groups with Open Quantum System Technology
summary: We propose a novel approach to state preparation by embracing the full power of open quantum systems. Instead of working with the whole unitary group in $n$ qubits, we identify a small Lie group $G$ in $(n+3)$ qubits. The dimension of its Lie algebra is $\text{poly}(n)$. Every state can be approximated starting from any fixed input state by repeatedly using partial trace and state preparation in the environment alongside group operations. Moreover, we also identify a single (open system magic) interaction Hamiltonian whose unitary group can be combined with open system quantum technology mentioned above to achieve transitivity on the space of all densities. Similarly, we show that all channels on $n$ qubits can be approximated by using a larger environment, achieving channel universality. The interesting small groups we identify are derived from Lie algebras of local Pauli strings and lead to a new landscape of cheap and expensive states, densities, and channels.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a state-preparation framework using open quantum systems, replacing the full unitary group on n qubits with a small poly(n)-dimensional Lie group G acting on (n+3) qubits, and extends it to full channel universality via a single interaction Hamiltonian.
AI.motivation: Conventional state preparation relies on the full unitary group on n qubits, which is exponentially large and thus expensive. There is a need for more resource-efficient schemes that exploit open-system dynamics (partial trace, environment state preparation) rather than purely unitary control.
AI.method: Identify a small Lie group G on (n+3) qubits whose Lie algebra has dimension poly(n), derived from Lie algebras of local Pauli strings. State preparation proceeds by repeatedly interleaving group operations with partial trace and environment state preparation. A single open-system "magic" interaction Hamiltonian is identified whose unitary group, combined with these open-system operations, yields transitivity on the space of all density matrices. A larger environment is used to approximate all channels on n qubits, achieving channel universality.
AI.result: Any state can be approximated from any fixed input state using the small group plus open-system operations. Combining the magic interaction Hamiltonian with open-system technology achieves transitivity over all densities. Channel universality is attained with a larger environment. The identified groups yield a new landscape classifying states, densities, and channels as cheap or expensive.
AI.conclusion: Embracing open quantum systems enables resource-efficient preparation and universality. Small poly(n)-dimensional Lie groups from local Pauli strings, plus one open-system interaction Hamiltonian, suffice for state transitivity and channel universality, providing a new complexity landscape of cheap versus expensive objects.

title: Optimal query complexity for fractional quantum evolution
summary: Given oracle access to an unknown unitary $U=e^{iH}$ , the fractional query problem asks how many queries are required to implement a noninteger power $U^t=e^{itH}$, $0<t<1$, when the spectrum is separated from the branch cut by a gap $δ$. Quantum singular value transformation gives an upper bound of $O\!\left(\frac{1}δ\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$ queries for approximation error $\varepsilon$. We prove a matching lower bound for arbitrary query algorithms. Our argument reduces any $N$-query circuit to the approximation of $e^{itθ}$ by a trigonometric polynomial with degree bounded by $O(N)$, together with Remez inequality. This allows us to establish the lower bound of $Ω_τ\!\left(\frac{1}δ\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$. Consequently, the optimal query complexity for fractional query problem is $Θ_τ\!\left(\frac{1}δ\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$, showing that the known QSVT construction is asymptotically optimal. We also give an alternative lower bound proof based on constructing a linear functional that annihilates the approximant space, yielding a $Ω_τ\!\left(\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right)$ bound uniform to $δ$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a tight lower bound for the fractional quantum query problem, showing that the known QSVT upper bound O((1/δ)log(1/ε)) is asymptotically optimal, with optimal query complexity Θ_τ((1/δ)log(1/ε)).
AI.motivation: The fractional query problem asks how many oracle queries are needed to implement U^t = e^{itH} for non-integer 0<t<1 when the spectrum is gapped from the branch cut by δ. While QSVT provides an upper bound of O((1/δ)log(1/ε)), it was unknown whether this construction is optimal; the paper resolves this by establishing a matching lower bound.
AI.method: The authors reduce any N-query quantum circuit to the approximation of e^{itθ} by a trigonometric polynomial of degree bounded by O(N), then apply the Remez inequality to derive the lower bound. They also provide an alternative proof by constructing a linear functional that annihilates the approximant space, yielding a δ-uniform Ω_τ(log(1/ε)) bound.
AI.result: The paper establishes a lower bound of Ω_τ((1/δ)log(1/ε)) for arbitrary query algorithms, matching the QSVT upper bound and thus proving the optimal query complexity is Θ_τ((1/δ)log(1/ε)). The alternative linear-functional argument gives a δ-uniform Ω_τ(log(1/ε)) lower bound.
AI.conclusion: The optimal query complexity for the fractional query problem is Θ_τ((1/δ)log(1/ε)), demonstrating that the known QSVT construction is asymptotically optimal. This settles the query complexity of fractional queries up to constants.

title: Universality Sacrifices Reliability in Classical-Quantum Channel Coding
summary: Universal channel coding enables communication without a complete description of the channel. For classical channels, universal codes can attain both capacity and the optimal high-rate reliability. We show that this compatibility fails for classical-quantum channels in general; that is, the optimal reliability in the channel-aware scenario is not always achievable with universal coding due to the ignorance of the unitary rotation of the output system. We exhibit a family of classical-quantum channels for which one cannot achieve the channel-aware optimal reliability by a fixed coding scheme. We further derive a converse bound on the reliability for unitary-invariant decoders, a natural assumption for the universal coding scheme, that can be strictly smaller than the optimal channel-aware error exponent. Conversely, we construct a channel-independent encoder-decoder pair and establish a universally achievable bound on the reliability that matches this converse bound in the high-rate regime, thereby characterizing the optimal universal reliability. Specifically, the channel-aware and universal exponents are governed by the Petz and sandwiched Rényi divergences, respectively. These divergences coincide for commuting outputs but differ for noncommuting ones, explaining why universality preserves optimal reliability classically but can reduce it quantumly. Our results showcase the fundamental reliability cost of performing the classical-quantum channel coding task universally.

AI.tldr: Universal channel coding, which enables communication without full channel knowledge, attains both capacity and optimal high-rate reliability for classical channels. This paper shows this compatibility fails for classical-quantum (CQ) channels: the optimal channel-aware reliability is not always achievable universally due to ignorance of the output system's unitary rotation. The channel-aware and universal exponents are governed by Petz and sandwiched Rényi divergences, respectively, which coincide for commuting outputs but differ for noncommuting ones, explaining the classical-quantum gap.
AI.motivation: Universal coding is highly desirable: it allows reliable communication without a complete description of the channel. Classically, universal codes achieve both capacity and optimal high-rate reliability, so universality comes at no reliability cost. The authors ask whether this appealing compatibility extends to classical-quantum channels, where the encoder is classical but the channel output is quantum and may involve unknown unitary rotations. Establishing whether universal coding preserves optimal reliability in the quantum setting is fundamental to understanding the intrinsic cost of channel ignorance.
AI.method: The authors analyze classical-quantum channel coding in both the channel-aware and channel-universal (channel-independent encoder-decoder) scenarios, focusing on the high-rate reliability (error exponent) regime. They construct a family of CQ channels for which no fixed universal coding scheme can achieve the channel-aware optimal reliability. They derive a converse bound on the reliability for unitary-invariant decoders, a natural assumption for universal schemes, and conversely construct a channel-independent encoder-decoder pair attaining a universally achievable reliability bound. This bound matches the converse in the high-rate regime, characterizing the optimal universal reliability. The analysis identifies the governing divergences: Petz Rényi divergence for the channel-aware exponent and sandwiched Rényi divergence for the universal exponent.
AI.result: The paper proves that the classical compatibility between universality and optimal reliability fails for CQ channels in general. A family of CQ channels is exhibited for which the channel-aware optimal reliability cannot be achieved by any fixed coding scheme. A converse bound on reliability for unitary-invariant decoders is derived that can be strictly smaller than the channel-aware optimal error exponent. A matching universally achievable bound is established via an explicit channel-independent encoder-decoder pair, which coincides with the converse in the high-rate regime, thereby characterizing the optimal universal reliability. The channel-aware exponent is governed by the Petz Rényi divergence, while the universal exponent is governed by the sandwiched Rényi divergence; these coincide for commuting outputs but differ for noncommuting outputs.
AI.conclusion: Universality and optimal high-rate reliability, which are compatible for classical channels, are not generally compatible for classical-quantum channels. The failure stems from ignorance of the unitary rotation of the output system. The distinction is precisely captured by the Petz versus sandwiched Rényi divergences, which agree only for commuting (classical) outputs and diverge for noncommuting (genuinely quantum) outputs. These findings reveal a fundamental reliability cost of performing classical-quantum channel coding universally, quantifying the price of channel ignorance in the quantum regime.

title: Hardware-Efficient Ground-State Preparation using Variational Imaginary-Time Majorana Evolution
summary: Compact ground-state preparation circuits are essential for early fault-tolerant quantum chemistry. We introduce Variational Imaginary-time Majorana Evolution (VIME), a classical pre-training algorithm that extends operator-projected variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (OVQITE) to molecular electronic structure using a single compiled Majorana-propagation (MP) surrogate graph. We pair VIME with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz that we develop to reduce both classical simulation and quantum state-preparation costs. In the strongly correlated ruthenium complex TLD-1411, active-space calculations requiring up to 52 qubits achieve chemical precision against DMRG reference energies, with energy errors approximately $400\times$ smaller than those from ADAPT-VQE-based variational Majorana-propagation (ADAPT-VMPE). Across the strongly multireference acene series up to heptacene (60 qubits), VIME matches or improves on the MP-reported energy accuracy of the ADAPT-VMPE comparison points with up to $26\times$ fewer CNOTs and $167\times$ lower two-qubit depth. These results establish imaginary-time classical pre-training of compressed variational ansätze as a promising route to resource-efficient molecular ground-state preparation.

AI.tldr: VIME is a classical pre-training algorithm extending operator-projected variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to molecular electronic structure using a single Majorana-propagation surrogate graph, paired with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz for resource-efficient ground-state preparation.
AI.motivation: Compact ground-state preparation circuits are essential for early fault-tolerant quantum chemistry, motivating the need for resource-efficient methods that reduce both classical simulation and quantum state-preparation costs.
