AI.method: VIME extends operator-projected variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (OVQITE) to molecular electronic structure using a single compiled Majorana-propagation (MP) surrogate graph. It is combined with a compressed tiled Unitary Product State (c-tUPS) ansatz designed to lower classical simulation and quantum state-preparation costs.
AI.result: For the strongly correlated ruthenium complex TLD-1411, active-space calculations up to 52 qubits reach chemical precision against DMRG references, with energy errors about 400× smaller than ADAPT-VQE-based variational Majorana-propagation (ADAPT-VMPE). Across the acene series up to heptacene (60 qubits), VIME matches or improves MP-reported energy accuracy of ADAPT-VMPE with up to 26× fewer CNOTs and 167× lower two-qubit depth.
AI.conclusion: Imaginary-time classical pre-training of compressed variational ansätze offers a promising route to resource-efficient molecular ground-state preparation.

title: Fully tolerant product state testing and closest product state learning
summary:
We address the problem of testing whether an unknown $n$-qudit state $ρ$ is $a$-close to a product state or $b$-far away from any product state, as measured in terms of state overlap. We provide a time-efficient algorithm to solve this problem that requires an $n$-independent number of copies of the unknown state. Our random coloring argument shows that for any unknown state there always exists a partition of $[n]$ into $q$ parts such that the square of the overlap with the closest product state with respect to this partition is only an additive factor $O(1/q)$ larger. This reduces the problem to tolerant testing of $q$ parties, with potentially growing local dimensions. Combining this insight with blockwise spectral projection arguments we can show that the natural $k$-copy generalization of Harrow & Montanaro's product state test provides an efficient tolerant tester.
  We use the same random coloring and blockwise spectral projection techniques to obtain a substantially improved algorithm for closest product state learning. In particular we give an algorithm that takes in $\widetilde{O}\big((nd)^2\big)\, 2^{\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon^8)}$ copies of the unknown state and produces an $\varepsilon$-approximately optimal product state. The key technical components of this learner are a qudit variant of the Bakshi et al. high-fidelity product state learning algorithm and a sampling technique based on Werner's optimal cloning channel.

AI.tldr: This paper studies product-state testing and closest product state learning for unknown n-qudit states. Using random coloring and blockwise spectral projection, it gives a time-efficient, n-independent-copy tolerant tester and a substantially improved closest product state learner.
AI.motivation: Testing whether an unknown n-qudit state is close to or far from any product state, and learning the closest product state, are fundamental quantum learning problems. Prior approaches typically suffer from copy complexity or runtime depending on n, so the goal is to obtain efficient algorithms with n-independent copy requirements and improved sample complexity.
AI.method: The authors introduce a random coloring argument showing that for any unknown state there exists a partition of [n] into q parts such that the squared overlap with the closest product state for that partition exceeds the optimal by at most O(1/q). This reduces the problem to tolerant testing of q parties with possibly growing local dimensions. Combined with blockwise spectral projection, they prove that the natural k-copy generalization of Harrow & Montanaro's product state test is an efficient tolerant tester. For learning, they combine a qudit variant of the Bakshi et al. high-fidelity product state learning algorithm with a sampling technique based on Werner's optimal cloning channel.
AI.result: The paper provides a time-efficient tolerant tester for product-state testing that uses an n-independent number of copies. For closest product state learning, it gives an algorithm using O~((nd)^2) 2^{O~(1/eps^8)} copies of the unknown state to produce an eps-approximately optimal product state.
AI.conclusion: Random coloring and blockwise spectral projection are powerful tools for product-state property testing and learning, yielding n-independent-copy tolerant testing and substantially improved closest product state learning with near-quadratic dependence on nd and subpolynomial dependence on 1/eps.

title: On the Metastability of the Mean-Field Interchange Model for Local Dimension $\geq 3$
summary: Many quantum systems are believed to thermalize slowly at low temperatures due to the existence of metastable phases. However, there are cases where further cooling can restore polynomial-time thermalization: we demonstrate that the Davies dynamics of the mean-field interchange model with local dimension $d\geq 3$ and single-site generalized Pauli couplings exhibits this behavior. The dynamical phase diagram is beholden to two distinguished inverse temperatures, $β_{\mathrm{min}}(d)$ and $β=d$, with the static first-order phase transition lying between them. At low and high temperatures surrounding the interval $(β_{\mathrm{min}}(d),d)$, the spectral gap of the Davies generator is bounded below by an inverse polynomial in system size $n$. Meanwhile, in this interval, the gap vanishes exponentially in $n$, indicating metastability. The proof uses Schur-Weyl duality to decompose the Davies generator into a classical Markov generator on Young diagrams, and the restriction to the remaining symmetry sectors whose gap is $Ω(n^{-1})$. Thus, exponential slowdown arises entirely from the Young diagram chain.

AI.tldr: The Davies dynamics of the mean-field interchange model (local dimension d≥3, single-site generalized Pauli couplings) thermalizes in polynomial time both below β_min(d) and above β=d, but exhibits exponentially vanishing spectral gap (metastability) in the intermediate interval enclosing the static first-order transition.
AI.motivation: Quantum systems are widely believed to thermalize slowly at low temperatures because of metastable phases. Yet there exist cases where further cooling restores polynomial-time thermalization, and the authors aim to exhibit and characterize such a non-monotonic dynamical behavior rigorously.
AI.method: Analyze the Davies generator of the mean-field interchange model using Schur-Weyl duality to decompose it into a classical Markov generator on Young diagrams plus remaining symmetry sectors; bound the spectral gap via this decomposition.
AI.result: A dynamical phase diagram governed by two distinguished inverse temperatures, β_min(d) and β=d, with the static first-order phase transition lying between them. Outside the interval (β_min(d), d) the Davies generator's spectral gap is bounded below by an inverse polynomial in system size n; inside the interval the gap vanishes exponentially in n.
AI.conclusion: Exponential slowdown of thermalization arises entirely from the Young diagram chain; the remaining symmetry sectors have gap Ω(n^{-1}). Cooling past β=d restores polynomial-time thermalization despite the intervening metastable regime.

title: Geometry of Knill-Laflamme Coefficients for Pauli Error Detection
summary: Knill-Laflamme coefficients characterize exact quantum error detection through scalar compressions of error operators to the code space. For prescribed Pauli observables and a fixed code dimension, attainable coefficient vectors form a joint higher-rank numerical range, whose Euclidean norm image is the signature spectrum. We study how operator representation, code dimension, and detection constraints govern this geometry. Our main theorem identifies representation multiplicity as sufficient to lift active expectation data to exact scalar compressions: a lift exists whenever each occupied block has multiplicity at least the code dimension times the rank of the corresponding active state. When multiplicity suffices to realize all active states, the coefficient range is the full active expectation body and is therefore convex and connected, with a closed interval as its signature spectrum. This framework unifies commuting Pauli families, where sufficient common-eigenspace degeneracy yields polytopes, and subsystem stabilizer codes, where protected logical subsystems supply multiplicity spaces for noncommuting gauge observables. Explicit examples show how increasing the code dimension can make a range shrink, collapse, or become empty, while increasing multiplicity can turn a Bloch sphere into a filled ball. In the subsystem setting, parent-Hamiltonian constructions realize exact detecting codes as degenerate ground spaces, selecting distinguished vectors and continuous paths within these ranges. A final three-qubit example shows additional noncommuting detection constraints reduce a tetrahedral range to its barycenter and four vertices, producing a disconnected signature spectrum. The results provide a structural framework for Knill-Laflamme coefficient geometry and motivate sharper criteria for connected coefficient ranges and interval signature spectra under structured error models.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a structural framework for the geometry of Knill-Laflamme coefficients, showing that representation multiplicity can lift active expectation data to exact scalar compressions, yielding convex coefficient ranges and interval signature spectra, with counterexamples from noncommuting constraints producing disconnected spectra.
AI.motivation: Knill-Laflamme coefficients characterize exact quantum error detection via scalar compressions of error operators onto the code space. For fixed Pauli observables and code dimension, attainable coefficient vectors form a joint higher-rank numerical range whose Euclidean norm image is the signature spectrum, but how operator representation, code dimension, and detection constraints govern this geometry is not well understood.
AI.method: The main theorem identifies representation multiplicity as a sufficient condition to lift active expectation data to exact scalar compressions, requiring each occupied block to have multiplicity at least the code dimension times the rank of the corresponding active state. The framework is applied to commuting Pauli families and subsystem stabilizer codes, supported by explicit examples and parent-Hamiltonian constructions.
AI.result: When multiplicity suffices to realize all active states, the coefficient range equals the full active expectation body, hence is convex and connected with a closed interval signature spectrum. Sufficient common-eigenspace degeneracy yields polytopes for commuting Pauli families, while protected logical subsystems supply multiplicity spaces for noncommuting gauge observables. Examples show that increasing code dimension can shrink, collapse, or empty a range, increasing multiplicity can turn a Bloch sphere into a filled ball, and noncommuting detection constraints can reduce a tetrahedral range to its barycenter and four vertices, giving a disconnected signature spectrum.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a structural framework for Knill-Laflamme coefficient geometry, unifying commuting Pauli families and subsystem stabilizer codes, and motivate sharper criteria for connected coefficient ranges and interval signature spectra under structured error models.

title: Operational transformation rates of quantum states
summary: Typically, multiple copies of a quantum state are described by a tensor power of that state. However, from an operational point of view, an experimentalist cannot, in general, rule out imperfections at unknown positions or correlations between copies, so assuming independent and identically distributed (iid) copies is not justified a priori. In the following, we relax the iid assumption by considering a whole set of resource states that are fundamentally indistinguishable from a tensor power state, and in that sense look like many copies of the quantum state to the experimentalist. Using a de Finetti-type argument, we show that this operational set of states can asymptotically be represented by almost-iid states. As an application, we introduce operational analogues of asymptotic transformation rates, such as entanglement cost and distillation. This raises the question of whether these rates coincide with their iid counterparts.

AI.tldr: The paper relaxes the iid assumption for quantum state copies by defining an operational set of resource states indistinguishable from a tensor power state, shows via a de Finetti-type argument that this set is asymptotically almost-iid, and introduces operational analogues of asymptotic transformation rates like entanglement cost and distillation.
AI.motivation: In practice, an experimentalist cannot rule out imperfections at unknown positions or correlations between copies of a quantum state, so the standard assumption of independent and identically distributed (iid) copies is not a priori justified. The work aims to place quantum resource theories on a more operationally realistic footing by relaxing this iid assumption.
AI.method: The authors relax the iid assumption by considering a whole set of resource states that are fundamentally indistinguishable from a tensor power state from the experimentalist's perspective. They employ a de Finetti-type argument to characterize this operational set of states.
AI.result: Using the de Finetti-type argument, the paper shows that this operational set of states can asymptotically be represented by almost-iid states. As an application, the authors introduce operational analogues of asymptotic transformation rates, including entanglement cost and distillation.
AI.conclusion: The operational framework yields new analogues of asymptotic transformation rates whose relationship to their iid counterparts remains an open question, namely whether these operational rates coincide with the standard iid rates.

title: (A Variant of) Clifford Circuit Synthesis is NP-Complete
summary:
Optimal circuit synthesis is the problem of finding the shortest-depth circuit representation of a given functionality with respect to a pre-specified elementary gate set. This is a central problem in both quantum and classical hardware design. While the classical version is very well understood -- both in terms of heuristics and rigorous hardness assertions -- much less is known about optimal quantum circuit synthesis.
  We focus on optimal Clifford circuit synthesis, for which various heuristics are known, e.g. via reduction to 3-SAT. Our main result supplies a matching hardness result: a variant of optimal Clifford synthesis is NP-hard. The proof proceeds in two parts: (i) reduce 3-edge colorability on 3-regular graphs to a circuit synthesis problem that only involves CZ gates, (ii) prove that the availability of additional elementary Clifford gates -- most notably: Hadamard, phase and CNOT -- cannot lead to further improvements of the optimal circuit depth. Our work sharpens the complexity-theoretic understanding of Clifford circuits: simulation and equivalence checking are in P, whereas deciding whether a Clifford unitary admits an implementation within a prescribed depth is NP-complete.

AI.tldr: Optimal Clifford circuit synthesis is NP-hard, complementing known 3-SAT-based heuristics; the paper proves this via reduction from 3-edge colorability and shows extra Clifford gates give no depth improvement.
AI.motivation: Optimal circuit synthesis (finding shortest-depth circuits for a given functionality) is central to quantum and classical hardware design. The classical version is well understood regarding heuristics and hardness, but optimal quantum circuit synthesis is far less understood.
AI.method: Focus on optimal Clifford circuit synthesis. The hardness proof has two parts: (i) reduce 3-edge colorability on 3-regular graphs to a circuit synthesis problem involving only CZ gates; (ii) prove that additional elementary Clifford gates (Hadamard, phase, CNOT) cannot yield further improvements in optimal circuit depth.
AI.result: A variant of optimal Clifford synthesis is NP-hard. The matching hardness result complements existing heuristics (e.g., reduction to 3-SAT).
AI.conclusion: The complexity-theoretic picture of Clifford circuits is sharpened: simulation and equivalence checking are in P, whereas deciding whether a Clifford unitary admits an implementation within a prescribed depth is NP-complete.

title: Sparse Hamiltonian simulation with optimal dependence on the maximum column Euclidean norm
summary:
We give a quantum algorithm for simulating a $d$-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$, assuming a known upper bound $Λ$ on its maximum column Euclidean norm $\|H\|_{1\to2}$. For $tΛ\ge1/2$, simulation with operator-norm error $ε$ uses \[
  O\!\left(tΛ\sqrt d+\sqrt d\log(2/ε)\right) \] sparse-oracle queries. This removes the subpolynomial overhead in Low's algorithm [STOC 2019], replacing it with an additive logarithmic precision term. For $d>1$ and $tΛ\ge\log(2/ε)$, the bound matches the worst-case lower bound. A known spectral-norm upper bound may also be used in place of $Λ$. The number of 1- and 2-qubit gates is linear in the query scale, up to oracle costs and polynomial overhead in the input bit lengths and logarithmic precision parameters.
  As applications, we obtain $O(κ\sqrt d\,\mathrm{polylog}(κ/ε))$ queries for solving $d$-sparse quantum linear systems with $\|A\|\le1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|\leκ$, under standard sparse and state-preparation access. We also give a gate-efficient implementation of black-box unitaries with at most $d$ nonzero entries per row and column using $O(\sqrt d\log(2/ε))$ queries, given sparse access to the unitary and its adjoint. At constant error, the query bound is optimal and yields $Θ(\sqrt N)$ queries for arbitrary $N\times N$ unitaries, resolving the open question on black-box unitary implementation posed by Berry and Childs [QIC 2012].

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm simulates d-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonians using O(tΛ√d + √d log(2/ε)) sparse-oracle queries, removing the subpolynomial overhead of Low's algorithm and matching worst-case lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Prior quantum simulation algorithms for d-sparse Hamiltonians, notably Low's [STOC 2019], carried a subpolynomial overhead. The paper aims to eliminate this overhead and achieve query complexity that matches known worst-case lower bounds, while also resolving open questions in quantum linear systems and black-box unitary implementation.
AI.method: The algorithm simulates a d-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian H assuming a known upper bound Λ on the maximum column Euclidean norm ‖H‖₁→₂. It uses sparse-oracle queries and achieves operator-norm error ε. The technique replaces subpolynomial overhead with an additive logarithmic precision term and can also use a spectral-norm upper bound in place of Λ. It leverages gate-efficient implementation with linear 1- and 2-qubit gate counts up to oracle costs and polynomial overhead.
AI.result: For tΛ≥1/2, simulation uses O(tΛ√d + √d log(2/ε)) queries; for d>1 and tΛ≥log(2/ε), the bound matches the worst-case lower bound. Applications: O(κ√d polylog(κ/ε)) queries for d-sparse quantum linear systems with ‖A‖≤1 and ‖A⁻¹‖≤κ; and O(√d log(2/ε)) queries for black-box unitaries with ≤d nonzero entries per row/column, giving Θ(√N) queries for arbitrary N×N unitaries at constant error.
AI.conclusion: The work removes the subpolynomial overhead in prior sparse Hamiltonian simulation, achieves optimal query complexity matching lower bounds, and resolves the open question on black-box unitary implementation posed by Berry and Childs [QIC 2012].

title: Adaptivity is all you need: Optimal stabilizer learning using just single-copy measurements
summary: Stabilizer states are central to quantum computing, underlying quantum error correction, benchmarking, and efficient classical simulation. Yet their learnability exhibits a striking gap: an $n$-qubit stabilizer state can be learned from $Θ(n)$ copies using two-copy Bell measurements, whereas non-adaptive single-copy measurements require $Ω(n^2)$ copies. Here we show that adaptivity completely closes this gap. We give a polynomial-time adaptive algorithm that learns an arbitrary $n$-qubit stabilizer state from $Θ(n)$ single-copy Clifford measurements, matching the optimal sample complexity of Bell sampling without any multi-copy measurements. The same ideas yield a sample-optimal single-copy tolerant tester and, with $k$ qubits of quantum memory, the optimal testing tradeoff $Θ(n-k+1/\varepsilon)$ at infidelity $\varepsilon$. Finally, we show that this adaptive mechanism extends beyond exact stabilizer states: states of stabilizer nullity at most $r$, including states prepared by Clifford circuits with a bounded number of $T$ gates, can be learned using $O(n2^{r})$ single-copy measurements.

AI.tldr: Adaptive single-copy Clifford measurements achieve the optimal Θ(n) sample complexity for learning stabilizer states, closing the gap with multi-copy Bell sampling, and extend to tolerant testing and low-stabilizer-nullity states.
AI.motivation: Stabilizer states are central to quantum computing, but their learnability shows a gap: two-copy Bell measurements need Θ(n) copies while non-adaptive single-copy measurements require Ω(n²). The paper asks whether adaptivity can close this gap.
AI.method: A polynomial-time adaptive algorithm using single-copy Clifford measurements to learn arbitrary n-qubit stabilizer states. The approach is extended to a tolerant tester and to states with stabilizer nullity at most r under limited quantum memory.
AI.result: Learning uses Θ(n) single-copy Clifford measurements, matching Bell sampling's optimal sample complexity without multi-copy measurements. Optimal testing tradeoff Θ(n - k + 1/ε) with k qubits of quantum memory at infidelity ε. States of stabilizer nullity at most r, including Clifford circuits with bounded T gates, are learned with O(n2^r) single-copy measurements.
AI.conclusion: Adaptivity fully closes the sample-complexity gap between single-copy and multi-copy stabilizer-state learning and generalizes to tolerant testing and low-stabilizer-nullity states.

title: Nonlocality without entanglement for multipartite quantum measurements
summary: We show that a pair of two-qubit product measurements can be perfectly distinguished when accessed jointly, yet cannot be perfectly distinguished when their local components are distributed between distant parties restricted to local quantum operations and classical communication (LOCC). This establishes a measurement analogue of nonlocality without entanglement that, unlike its state-based counterpart, emerges in a remarkably simple setting. We further uncover a hierarchy of LOCC discrimination strategies: adaptive protocols, in which the probe used at one site may depend on classical information obtained from another, can strictly outperform restricted non-adaptive protocols, as demonstrated by a set of six bipartite qutrit product measurements. We also show that LOCC distinguishability of bipartite measurements can be intrinsically directional, depending on which party initiates the protocol. More generally, we construct pairs of $n$-qubit product measurements that are globally perfectly distinguishable but cannot be perfectly distinguished across any bipartition, even when all parties on either side of the bipartition are allowed arbitrary joint quantum operations. Finally, we show how quantum data hiding based on quantum-process nonlocality without entanglement can be realized using elementary optical components.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a measurement analogue of nonlocality without entanglement: certain product measurements are perfectly distinguishable when accessed jointly but not under LOCC, exhibiting hierarchies between adaptive and non-adaptive protocols, directional distinguishability, and optical implementations for quantum data hiding.
AI.motivation: Nonlocality without entanglement is well known for quantum states, where globally orthogonal product states cannot be perfectly discriminated by LOCC. The authors ask whether an analogous phenomenon exists for measurements, and whether it can arise in simpler settings than the state-based counterpart.
AI.method: The authors construct explicit examples of product measurements: a pair of two-qubit product measurements, a set of six bipartite qutrit product measurements, and general families of n-qubit product measurements. They analyze their distinguishability under joint access versus LOCC, compare adaptive and non-adaptive LOCC protocols, examine the directional dependence on the initiating party, and propose an optical realization.
AI.result: A pair of two-qubit product measurements is perfectly distinguishable jointly but not via LOCC. Adaptive LOCC protocols strictly outperform restricted non-adaptive ones, shown with six bipartite qutrit product measurements. LOCC distinguishability can be intrinsically directional. Pairs of n-qubit product measurements are globally perfectly distinguishable but not across any bipartition, even allowing arbitrary joint quantum operations on each side. Data hiding based on quantum-process nonlocality without entanglement is realized with elementary optical components.
AI.conclusion: Measurement nonlocality without entanglement emerges in remarkably simple settings, unlike the state-based case, and exhibits richer structure including adaptive advantages and directionality. These findings enable practical quantum data hiding using basic optical elements.

title: Complexity and Applications of Nearest Stabilizer Product State Problems
summary: Consider the following optimization problem over stabilizer product states: given an $n$-qubit stabilizer state $\left|ψ\right\rangle$ and a set of single-qubit stabilizer states $S$, maximize $\left|\langle ψ| φ_1, \ldots, φ_n \rangle\right|^2$ over single-qubit stabilizer states $\left|φ_i\right\rangle \in S$. By varying the set $S$, we show that solutions to this problem can be useful in a variety of settings: tighter runtime bounds for certain classical simulation algorithms; measures of entanglement; and the complexity of low-rank matrix completion. Moreover, we give a complete complexity classification of this nearest stabilizer product state problem. After accounting for the symmetries in the Clifford group, there are $9$ distinct possible sets $S$, and we show that all but the two simplest of these are $\NP$-complete.

AI.tldr: The paper studies maximizing the overlap between a given n-qubit stabilizer state and stabilizer product states drawn from a set S, shows applications in simulation runtime bounds, entanglement measures, and low-rank matrix completion, and gives a full complexity classification: modulo Clifford symmetries there are 9 distinct sets S, all but the two simplest being NP-complete.
AI.motivation: The nearest stabilizer product state problem is motivated by its relevance across multiple settings—tighter runtime bounds for classical simulation algorithms, entanglement measures, and the complexity of low-rank matrix completion—and by the need for a systematic complexity understanding of the problem as the allowed single-qubit stabilizer set varies.
AI.method: Formulate the optimization: given an n-qubit stabilizer state |ψ⟩ and a set S of single-qubit stabilizer states, maximize |⟨ψ|φ_1,…,φ_n⟩|² over |φ_i⟩ ∈ S. Classify the problem by varying S, accounting for Clifford group symmetries to reduce to 9 distinct possible sets, and analyze the computational complexity of each case.
AI.result: There are 9 distinct possible sets S after accounting for Clifford group symmetries. All but the two simplest of these cases are NP-complete. Solutions to the problem yield useful consequences in tighter runtime bounds for certain classical simulation algorithms, measures of entanglement, and the complexity of low-rank matrix completion.
AI.conclusion: The nearest stabilizer product state problem admits a complete complexity classification, being NP-complete for all but the two simplest of the 9 symmetry-distinct choices of S, and its solutions have applications to classical simulation, entanglement quantification, and low-rank matrix completion.

title: Fermionic Gaussianity can be tested with mode-independent sample-complexity
summary: Deciding whether an unknown quantum state either belongs to, or is far from, a given family of states is a natural question of quantum information theory. In many such cases, there is a natural 2-copy test which always accepts whenever the state indeed belongs to the target family; it is often much more difficult, however, to bound the probability of acceptance for states that are far from the family. Here we develop a simple new technique for upper bounding this probability for general families, and therefore upper bounding the sample-complexity of the decision problem itself. As a particularly striking example of this framework, we show that deciding whether an unknown pure $n$-mode state is fermionic Gaussian, or at least $\varepsilon$-far in trace distance from all Gaussian states, can be accomplished using the optimal number $Θ(\varepsilon^{-2})$ of copies. Remarkably, our analysis applies to the well-known Bell sampling procedure for testing fermionic Gaussianity, which we therefore show to be optimal, even compared to protocols making arbitrary collective and adaptive measurements. As a second example, we show that the analogous decision problem for the family of Slater determinant states can also be solved with mode-independent sample-complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general technique for upper-bounding the acceptance probability of 2-copy tests for states far from a target family, yielding optimal sample-complexity bounds; as key applications, it shows that testing fermionic Gaussianity and Slater-determinant states requires Θ(ε⁻²) copies, and that Bell sampling is optimal even against arbitrary collective/adaptive measurements.
AI.motivation: Deciding whether an unknown quantum state belongs to, or is far from, a given family of states is a fundamental question in quantum information theory. While natural 2-copy tests often always accept states in the target family, bounding the acceptance probability for far-from-family states—and hence the sample complexity—is typically much harder. The paper aims to provide a general tool to overcome this difficulty.
AI.method: The authors develop a simple new technique for upper-bounding the acceptance probability of general 2-copy tests on states that are far from the target family, which in turn upper-bounds the sample complexity of the corresponding decision problem. They apply this framework to Bell sampling for testing fermionic Gaussianity and to the family of Slater determinant states.
AI.result: For pure n-mode states, deciding whether a state is fermionic Gaussian or at least ε-far in trace distance from all Gaussian states can be done with the optimal Θ(ε⁻²) number of copies. The analysis applies to Bell sampling, proving it optimal even compared to protocols using arbitrary collective and adaptive measurements. For Slater determinant states, the analogous decision problem is solvable with mode-independent sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a general and simple method to bound sample complexity of state-discrimination/decision problems for structured families. It establishes the optimality of Bell sampling for fermionic Gaussianity testing and extends tractability to Slater determinant states with mode-independent sample complexity.

title: Sequential Capacity of Quantum Processes with Finite Memory
summary: How complex can the responses of a quantum device become as it runs longer with a fixed internal memory? We quantify this complexity through sequential response capacity: how many adaptive testing stages, each using a fresh run, can continue to separate possible processes by a prescribed gap in response probabilities. For fixed system and memory sizes, we establish a tight law relating this capacity to run length and probability resolution. At fixed resolution, the capacity grows on the order of $K\log K$, where $K$ is the number of time steps in each run. Our construction attains this growth using time-dependent phase rotations on a single visible qubit with no additional internal memory; its tests give response probabilities exactly zero or one. Under the same tests, classical stochastic processes that measure in a fixed basis at every step have only linear capacity at fixed sizes and resolution. For phase sequences selected by a stored classical label, we then quantify how known independent Pauli noise changes this logarithmic enhancement. With ideal controls and weak residual phase noise after correction, we prove matching capacity bounds at a fixed small probability gap. These bounds identify the inverse residual phase-flip probability as the coherence timescale that limits the extra logarithmic growth.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "sequential response capacity" to quantify how many adaptive testing stages (each with a fresh run) can separate quantum processes by a fixed probability gap, and derives a tight law linking this capacity to run length and probability resolution, showing quantum advantage over classical processes and how noise affects it.
AI.motivation: Quantum devices with fixed internal memory run for longer times, and the question arises of how complex their responses can become and how many distinguishable testing stages they support. Understanding the fundamental scaling of this complexity, and how it compares to classical stochastic processes, motivates a precise complexity measure tied to run length and probability resolution.
AI.method: The authors define sequential response capacity as the number of adaptive testing stages, each using a fresh run, that can separate possible processes by a prescribed gap in response probabilities. They establish a tight law relating capacity to run length and probability resolution for fixed system and memory sizes, and construct schemes using time-dependent phase rotations on a single visible qubit with no extra internal memory, yielding response probabilities of exactly zero or one. They compare against classical stochastic processes measuring in a fixed basis each step, and analyze phase sequences selected by a stored classical label under known independent Pauli noise with ideal controls and weak residual phase noise after correction.
AI.result: At fixed resolution, capacity grows on the order of K log K where K is the number of time steps per run, achieved without additional internal memory. Classical stochastic processes with fixed-basis measurements achieve only linear capacity at fixed sizes and resolution. For label-selected phase sequences under independent Pauli noise, matching capacity bounds are proven at a fixed small probability gap with ideal controls and weak residual phase noise, identifying the inverse residual phase-flip probability as the coherence timescale limiting the extra logarithmic growth.
AI.conclusion: Quantum sequential response capacity can grow as K log K, exponentially outperforming the linear capacity of classical fixed-basis processes. This logarithmic enhancement is governed by a coherence timescale given by the inverse residual phase-flip probability, so noise places a quantitative limit on the achievable quantum advantage.

title: Universal Bound and Phase Transition in Many-Body Fermionic Non-Gaussianity
summary: Fermionic non-Gaussianity is a resource for universal quantum computation that can be generated by interactions in quantum many-body systems. Using the magic Rényi entropy (MRE) as a measure of non-Gaussianity, we derive its universal upper bound and Haar mean, proving that typical Haar-random states attain the maximal MRE density of $\ln(4/3)$ per Majorana in the large-system limit. We also show that the MRE can differ extensively between states with identical covariance matrices. To investigate how non-Gaussianity grows toward this maximal density, we evolve a Gaussian state in imaginary and real time under the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Hamiltonian. By varying the imaginary- and real-time durations, we identify a first-order transition marked by a kink in the MRE density and spontaneous breaking of the permutation symmetry among the four copies used to evaluate the MRE. This transition represents a qualitative change in the non-Gaussianity of the state that is not reflected in the thermal free energy.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a universal upper bound and Haar-average value for the magic Rényi entropy (MRE) as a measure of fermionic non-Gaussianity, showing typical Haar-random states reach maximal MRE density ln(4/3) per Majorana, and identifies a first-order transition in non-Gaussianity growth during Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev evolution.
AI.motivation: Fermionic non-Gaussianity is a resource for universal quantum computation, yet a rigorous characterization of how much non-Gaussianity typical states can possess and how it dynamically grows toward its maximum remained unclear.
AI.method: Using magic Rényi entropy (MRE) as a non-Gaussianity measure, the authors derive a universal upper bound and Haar mean, compare states with identical covariance matrices, and evolve a Gaussian state in imaginary and real time under the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev Hamiltonian, varying the imaginary- and real-time durations.
AI.result: Typical Haar-random states attain the maximal MRE density of ln(4/3) per Majorana in the large-system limit. MRE can differ extensively between states sharing identical covariance matrices. During Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev evolution, a first-order transition appears, marked by a kink in the MRE density and spontaneous breaking of the permutation symmetry among the four copies used to evaluate the MRE.
AI.conclusion: The identified transition represents a qualitative change in the non-Gaussianity of the state that is not reflected in the thermal free energy, revealing non-Gaussianity as a distinct resource not captured by conventional thermodynamic quantities.

title: A computational phase diagram for the transverse field Ising model
summary: We study the transverse field Ising model, defined by the Hamiltonian $H =\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i, j\in [n]} J_{ij} Z_i Z_j +\sum_{i=1}^n h_i^z Z_i + η\sum_{i} X_i$ where $J $ is the symmetric interaction matrix, and $η$ is the transverse field strength. Let $Δ(J)=λ_{\max}(J)-λ_{\min}(J)$ be the spectral width of $J.$ When the inverse temperature $β\geq0$ satisfies $Δ(J)\cdot\frac{\tanh(βη)}η\leq1$, we give a randomized classical algorithm that approximates the partition function $Z(β)=\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-βH})$ to a given relative error $ε\in(0,1)$ in time polynomial in $n$, $β$, the model parameters, and $ε^{-1}$. When $ Δ(J) \cdot \frac{\tanh(βη)}η > 1 ,$ we show that approximating $ Z(β)$ within an $\exp(o(n))$-multiplicative factor is $\textbf{NP}$-hard, and thus unlikely to admit an efficient classical or quantum algorithms under standard complexity theoretic assumptions. Furthermore, in the regime $Δ(J)\cdot \frac{\tanh(βη)}η\leq 1,$ we provide an efficient randomized classical algorithm that approximates Pauli string observables of the Gibbs state $ ρ_β= \frac{e^{-βH}}{\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-βH})}$ within an arbitrarily small additive error. In the special case when the observable is also diagonal in the $X$-basis, i.e. $P \in \{I, X\}^{\otimes n}$, the algorithm further achieves arbitrarily small relative error.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the transverse field Ising model (TFIM) and identifies a phase-transition-like threshold governed by Δ(J)·tanh(βη)/η. Below this threshold (≤1), the partition function Z(β) and Gibbs-state observables can be efficiently approximated classically; above it (>1), approximating Z(β) within exp(o(n)) is NP-hard.
AI.motivation: Approximating partition functions of quantum many-body systems, such as the TFIM, is a central problem in quantum and classical complexity theory. A key open question is to precisely characterize for which regimes of the model parameters (interaction spectrum, temperature, transverse field) an efficient classical approximation is possible, and where it becomes intractable. The paper aims to establish such a sharp computational threshold.
AI.method: The authors consider the TFIM Hamiltonian with symmetric interaction matrix J and transverse field strength η, with spectral width Δ(J)=λmax(J)−λmin(J). They design randomized classical algorithms that approximate the partition function Z(β)=Tr(e^{−βH}) and Pauli string observables of the Gibbs state ρ_β. The algorithms operate in the regime Δ(J)·tanh(βη)/η ≤ 1, and complexity is analyzed in terms of n, β, model parameters, and ε^{−1}. Hardness is established via NP-hardness reductions for the complementary regime.
AI.result: When Δ(J)·tanh(βη)/η ≤ 1, a randomized classical algorithm approximates Z(β) to relative error ε∈(0,1) in time polynomial in n, β, model parameters, and ε^{−1}; in the same regime, an efficient randomized classical algorithm approximates Pauli string observables of the Gibbs state within arbitrarily small additive error, and within arbitrarily small relative error when the observable is diagonal in the X-basis (P∈{I,X}^{⊗n}). When Δ(J)·tanh(βη)/η > 1, approximating Z(β) within an exp(o(n))-multiplicative factor is NP-hard, implying no efficient classical or quantum algorithm is likely under standard assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The quantity Δ(J)·tanh(βη)/η acts as a sharp computational threshold for the TFIM: below it, efficient classical simulation of the partition function and Gibbs observables is possible; above it, the problem becomes NP-hard and intractable even for quantum algorithms under standard complexity assumptions.

title: Strong Simulation of 1D Quantum Circuits via Reduced Transition Matrices
summary: Tensor networks are powerful tools for simulating quantum many-body systems, but the growth of spatial entanglement severely limits the direct evolution of pure states under chaotic unitary circuits. Here we consider a more targeted task: the approximate strong simulation of a specified output probability of a 1D chaotic brick-wall circuit at finite relative precision. Given input and output bit strings $\by$ and $\bx$, we evaluate $p(\bx|\by)=|\bra{\bx}U(T)\ket{\by}|^2$ using the Sweeping RTM algorithm, a transverse tensor-network contraction based on reduced transition matrices (RTMs). The algorithm compresses the left and right temporal boundary states jointly, seeking an output probability that converges across spatial cuts and as the bond dimension is increased. For chaotic one-dimensional brick-wall circuits at a fixed relative target precision, we find numerical evidence that the bond dimension required to obtain stable estimates grows subexponentially over the accessible time window. Our findings open a direct route to classical probability queries for chaotic quantum circuits, with potential applications to benchmarking and learning tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Sweeping RTM algorithm, a transverse tensor-network contraction using reduced transition matrices, to approximately strong-simulate a specified output probability of 1D chaotic brick-wall circuits at finite relative precision, finding numerical evidence that the required bond dimension grows subexponentially over the accessible time window.
AI.motivation: Direct evolution of pure states under chaotic unitary circuits is severely limited by the growth of spatial entanglement. The authors target a more tractable task: approximate strong simulation of a single specified output probability p(x|y) at finite relative precision rather than full-state simulation.
AI.method: They evaluate p(x|y) = |<x|U(T)|y>|^2 using the Sweeping RTM algorithm, a transverse tensor-network contraction based on reduced transition matrices (RTMs) that jointly compresses the left and right temporal boundary states, seeking an output probability that converges across spatial cuts as the bond dimension increases.
AI.result: For chaotic 1D brick-wall circuits at a fixed relative target precision, numerical evidence shows that the bond dimension required for stable estimates grows subexponentially over the accessible time window.
AI.conclusion: The findings open a direct route to classical probability queries for chaotic quantum circuits, with potential applications to benchmarking and learning tasks.

title: Stationarity as a One-Mode Constraint on Quantum Correlation
summary: A stationary quantum state has one dynamical phase factor and one scalar energy even when its internal response spans a large Hilbert space. Our argument concerns not the value or observability of an absolute phase, but the one-ness of stationary time evolution. In regularized Hartree--Fock (reg-HF), the connection to the stationary mean field is established before any one-mode reduction: the primitive-product relative-coordinate Gaussian measure induced by the Gaussian HF representation fixes a covariance and, at that covariance, is simultaneously the minimum-Fisher-information and maximum-Shannon-differential-entropy distribution and the equality case of the Stam bound. The Coulomb operator admits a compatible Gaussian scale resolution, and virial completion converts the resulting regularized pair displacement into a stationary-compatible response. Stationarity motivates a one-mode constraint on the terminal scalar correlation response. The decisive reg-HF hypothesis is a one-mode exclusion axiom: covariance carried by response components orthogonal to the retained pair mode is excluded from the terminal scalar energy property, without asserting that the unrestricted response is one dimensional. Helium provides the minimal nontrivial test. The parameter-free retained Coulomb carrier $-δ/e$ and finite-$Z$ insertion $8δ/9$ closely reproduce independent He-like coefficients and energies, while an explicit Bethe--Goldstone calculation displays a broad non-single-denominator return spectrum even though its scalar energy is exactly moment-compressible. The result separates microscopic spectral complexity from one-mode energetic sufficiency.

AI.tldr: A stationary quantum state carries a single dynamical phase and scalar energy even with a large internal Hilbert space. Using regularized Hartree-Fock (reg-HF), the authors show that a one-mode exclusion axiom on the terminal scalar correlation response makes stationary energy moment-compressible, separating microscopic spectral complexity from one-mode energetic sufficiency, validated on helium.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses why a stationary quantum state, despite its internal response spanning a large Hilbert space, exhibits a single dynamical phase factor and one scalar energy. The goal is not the value or observability of an absolute phase but the "one-ness" of stationary time evolution, motivating a framework that connects stationary mean-field evolution to the terminal scalar energy property.
AI.method: Regularized Hartree-Fock (reg-HF) is used, establishing the connection to the stationary mean field before any one-mode reduction. A primitive-product relative-coordinate Gaussian measure fixed by the Gaussian HF representation sets a covariance that simultaneously minimizes Fisher information, maximizes Shannon differential entropy, and saturates the Stam bound. A compatible Gaussian scale resolution of the Coulomb operator and virial completion convert the regularized pair displacement into a stationary-compatible response. A one-mode exclusion axiom excludes covariance carried by response components orthogonal to the retained pair mode from the terminal scalar energy property, and Helium is used as the minimal test case.
AI.result: The parameter-free retained Coulomb carrier $-δ/e$ and finite-$Z$ insertion $8δ/9$ closely reproduce independent He-like coefficients and energies. An explicit Bethe-Goldstone calculation shows a broad non-single-denominator return spectrum, yet its scalar energy is exactly moment-compressible, demonstrating separability of spectral complexity from energetic one-mode sufficiency.
AI.conclusion: The results separate microscopic spectral complexity from one-mode energetic sufficiency: a stationary state's rich internal response can coexist with a single dynamical phase and scalar energy under the one-mode exclusion axiom, without asserting the unrestricted response is one dimensional.

title: One-Way Quantum Symmetric Private Information Retrieval Protocol From A Single Database Server Using NISQ Devices
summary: Symmetric private information retrieval (SPIR) lets an inquirer obtain one specific bit only, without leaking any information about its index to the database owner. With a single server, this is impossible for parties with unrestricted quantum power. We show that it becomes possible, with information-theoretic security, when the server and the user hold only noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices without long-term quantum memory and measure each qubit on arrival, while the eavesdropper remains all-powerful; this is a stricter form of the memory restriction of the bounded- and noisy-quantum-storage models. The server sends BB84 states one way; the user discriminates them unambiguously and so knows a random subset of the bits. After a joint random permutation into blocks, the user announces the conclusive locations of one privately chosen block, and the server hashes and takes a random parity of these locations in every block; the permutation makes it exponentially unlikely that one set of locations fits two blocks. We prove secrecy against the eavesdropper, database privacy through an explicit size rule for the announced set, and user privacy against a server who prepares the prescribed BB84 states and announces truthfully, exactly for single photons and up to a small multi-photon term over a tolerated noise channel. The only addition to BB84 equipment is a passive linear-optical measurement with one ancillary mode. For a $10^{4}$-bit database and database privacy $10^{-6}$, blocks of about a thousand qubits suffice over a tolerated noise channel for a user who applies the prescribed measurement; certifying an arbitrary memoryless user and committing to the permutation need larger auxiliary transmissions, which we quantify with finite keys. Database privacy extends to decoy-state weak coherent pulses, and simulations show that the bound is nearly tight.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that information-theoretic Symmetric Private Information Retrieval (SPIR) becomes possible with a single server when both server and user are restricted to NISQ devices that measure qubits on arrival and lack long-term quantum memory, while the eavesdropper remains all-powerful. Using one-way BB84 states, unambiguous discrimination, joint random permutation into blocks, and a passive linear-optical measurement, the protocol achieves database privacy, user privacy, and eavesdropper secrecy, with quantified finite-key overheads.
AI.motivation: Single-server SPIR is impossible under unrestricted quantum power with information-theoretic security. The authors seek a feasible relaxation: rather than assuming bounded or noisy quantum storage, they impose a stricter operational memory restriction — server and user are NISQ devices with no long-term quantum memory that measure each qubit on arrival — while keeping the eavesdropper all-powerful. This targets hardware-realistic security for practical quantum SPIR.
AI.method: The server sends BB84 states one way. The user performs unambiguous state discrimination, learning a random subset of bits, then a joint random permutation arranges bits into blocks. The user announces the conclusive locations of one privately chosen block; the server hashes and takes a random parity over those locations in every block. Exponential unlikelihood that one location set fits two blocks gives security. The protocol adds only a passive linear-optical measurement with one ancillary mode to standard BB84 equipment. Proofs cover eavesdropper secrecy, database privacy via an explicit size rule for the announced set, and user privacy against a server that prepares prescribed BB84 states and announces truthfully. Analysis handles single photons exactly and includes a small multi-photon term over a tolerated noise channel; decoy-state weak coherent pulses extend database privacy, and finite-key quantification addresses certifying an arbitrary memoryless user and committing to the permutation.
AI.result: For a 10^4-bit database and database privacy 10^-6, blocks of about one thousand qubits suffice over a tolerated noise channel for a user applying the prescribed measurement. Certifying an arbitrary memoryless user and committing to the permutation require larger auxiliary transmissions, quantified with finite keys. Database privacy extends to decoy-state weak coherent pulses, and simulations show the bound is nearly tight. Secrecy against an all-powerful eavesdropper, database privacy, and user privacy are proven for single photons exactly and up to a small multi-photon term.
AI.conclusion: Information-theoretic single-server SPIR is achievable under a stricter, hardware-realistic memory restriction where server and user are NISQ devices without long-term quantum memory and measure on arrival, even against an all-powerful eavesdropper. The construction needs only minimal additions to BB84 equipment, and the finite-key analysis quantifies the overhead for certifying arbitrary memoryless users and committing to the permutation, with simulations indicating near-tight bounds.

title: Quantum state preparation for weighted d-DNNF
summary: The quantum state preparation problem is to, given a description of a quantum state, efficiently generate a quantum circuit computing the state. We show that for quantum states described by weighted d-DNNF (deterministic, decomposable pseudo-Boolean circuits) a quantum circuit computing the state can be obtained in linear time up to complex arithmetic.

AI.tldr: Quantum states specified by weighted d-DNNF circuits can be compiled into a state-preparing quantum circuit in linear time (up to complex arithmetic).
AI.motivation: Quantum state preparation asks for an efficient procedure that, given a classical description of a quantum state, outputs a circuit that prepares it. Finding broad classes of state descriptions admitting efficient preparation is a central problem, since general state preparation is expensive.
AI.method: The paper considers states described by weighted d-DNNF (deterministic, decomposable pseudo-Boolean circuits) and gives a constructive algorithm producing a quantum circuit that prepares the state, running in linear time up to complex arithmetic.
AI.result: For any quantum state described by a weighted d-DNNF, a computing quantum circuit can be obtained in linear time (up to complex arithmetic).
AI.conclusion: Weighted d-DNNF is a tractable specification language for quantum state preparation, extending efficient preparable state classes and linking knowledge compilation with quantum circuit synthesis.

title: A No-Go Theorem for Order-Two Clifford Electric-Magnetic Duality
summary: Electromagnetic duality in the toric code has order two at the level of anyon types and acts as a Hadamard-type logical transformation on the encoded quantum information. Here, we ask whether it can likewise be realized microscopically as an order-two Clifford operation. For the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, we prove that any locality-preserving Clifford realization of electric-magnetic exchange cannot have order two. Our proof is fully general and requires neither translation symmetry with restricted families of system sizes nor a fixed pairing between vertex and plaquette stabilizers. Geometrically, the proof locally emulates the unavoidable crossing between electric and magnetic strings, similar to a cross-cap in a non-orientable manifold. Extending the problem to the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ toric code, we find that an order-two Clifford realization exists for odd $N$, whereas it is impossible for even $N$. Our results show that the group law of an emergent electromagnetic duality need not lift faithfully to its microscopic Clifford realization.

AI.tldr: Electromagnetic duality (EMD) acts as order-two on anyon types in the toric code. The authors prove that no locality-preserving Clifford realization of electric-magnetic exchange can have order two for the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code, generalizing to $\mathbb{Z}_N$ where an order-two Clifford realization exists for odd $N$ but is impossible for even $N$.
AI.motivation: EMD in the toric code has order two at the anyon-type level and acts as a Hadamard-type logical transformation on encoded quantum information. The question is whether this order-two symmetry can be realized microscopically as an order-two Clifford operation—i.e., whether the group law of the emergent duality lifts faithfully to its microscopic realization.
AI.method: A fully general proof for the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ toric code showing any locality-preserving Clifford realization of electric-magnetic exchange cannot have order two. The proof requires neither translation symmetry with restricted system sizes nor a fixed vertex-plaquette stabilizer pairing. Geometrically, it locally emulates the unavoidable crossing between electric and magnetic strings, analogous to a cross-cap in a non-orientable manifold. The analysis is extended to the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ toric code.
AI.result: For $\mathbb{Z}_2$: no locality-preserving Clifford realization of electric-magnetic exchange has order two. For $\mathbb{Z}_N$: an order-two Clifford realization exists for odd $N$, whereas it is impossible for even $N$.
AI.conclusion: The group law of an emergent electromagnetic duality need not lift faithfully to its microscopic Clifford realization. The obstruction is tied to the crossing of electric and magnetic strings, resembling a cross-cap in a non-orientable manifold, and is sensitive to the parity of $N$.

title: An exponential separation between entanglement-assisted and unassisted one-way quantum communication
summary: A longstanding question in quantum communication complexity is whether some task can be accomplished with a small amount of communication in the presence of entanglement, yet require much more quantum communication in the absence of entanglement. Separations of this nature were previously known for relational problems and, in the simultaneous message passing model, for partial functions. But it has remained unresolved whether any such separation exists for a total Boolean function. We resolve this question with an exponential separation in the one-way setting: we exhibit a family of total Boolean functions $f_n\colon \{0,1\}^n \times \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ that can be computed with $O(\log n)$ bits of one-way classical communication given prior entanglement, but that require $Ω(n^{1/3})$ qubits of one-way quantum communication without entanglement. Our function is a special case of the subgroup membership problem, first studied in the communication setting by Aaronson, Le Gall, Russell, and Tani.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves a longstanding open question in quantum communication complexity by proving an exponential separation: a family of total Boolean functions computable with O(log n) bits of one-way classical communication given prior entanglement, yet requiring Ω(n^{1/3}) qubits of one-way quantum communication without entanglement.
AI.motivation: A longstanding question in quantum communication complexity is whether some task can be accomplished with little communication in the presence of entanglement but requires much more quantum communication in the absence of entanglement. While such separations were known for relational problems and, in the simultaneous message passing model, for partial functions, it remained unresolved whether any such separation exists for a total Boolean function.
AI.method: The authors construct a family of total Boolean functions f_n: {0,1}^n × {0,1}^n → {0,1} that is a special case of the subgroup membership problem, first studied in the communication setting by Aaronson, Le Gall, Russell, and Tani. They analyze its communication complexity in the one-way setting, comparing classical communication with prior entanglement against quantum communication without entanglement.
AI.result: The constructed functions can be computed with O(log n) bits of one-way classical communication given prior entanglement, but require Ω(n^{1/3}) qubits of one-way quantum communication without entanglement. This yields an exponential separation for a total Boolean function.
AI.conclusion: The paper resolves the open question by exhibiting the first exponential separation for a total Boolean function in the one-way setting, demonstrating that prior entanglement can provide an exponential advantage over quantum communication without entanglement even for total Boolean functions.

title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes
summary:
Can simple processes appear highly complex? Gowers (Comb. Prob. Comp. '96) conjectured that repeatedly composing local random reversible operations can yield global permutations that are indistinguishable from random. In this work, we study the unitary quantum analog of this question, in an attempt to make new progress on this longstanding conjecture.
  Our first result shows that statistical moment matching in the form of unitary designs does not generically lead to pseudorandomness---even for the simplest quantum processes: for every fixed $t$, we give an efficiently samplable family $\{ν_n\}_n$ of distributions on one- and two-qubit gates such that, after $T=O_t(n^2\log^2 n)$ independent steps, the resulting $n$-qubit ensemble is an approximate unitary $t$-design with negligible error $\exp(-Ω(\log^2 n))$, yet an efficient quantum algorithm distinguishes it from random using only $O_t(\log^2 n)$ queries. This refutes the unitary analog of the Hoory--Magen--Myers--Rackoff conjecture (ICALP '04) for permutations.
  Our second result is a stronger separation between unitary designs and pseudorandom unitaries at polynomially bounded moments; our counterexample, however, requires highly structured ensembles, in contrast with the simple local walks from before. This suggests caution when using unitary designs to model information scrambling in black-hole physics, as even maximally scrambled systems can exhibit structure which is accessible to efficient experiments. Motivated by these findings, we then propose new conjectures for how pseudorandomness can plausibly emerge within simple quantum processes, such as random quantum circuits.

AI.tldr: This work shows that statistical moment matching (unitary designs) does not generically imply pseudorandomness for simple local quantum processes, refuting the unitary analog of the Hoory–Magen–Myers–Rackoff conjecture and proposing refined conjectures for how pseudorandomness emerges in random quantum circuits.
AI.motivation: Gowers conjectured that repeatedly composing local random reversible operations can produce global permutations indistinguishable from random. This paper studies the unitary quantum analog to make progress on that longstanding conjecture, and questions whether low-degree statistical moment matching (unitary designs) suffices to guarantee pseudorandomness.
AI.method: The authors construct efficiently samplable families of distributions on one- and two-qubit gates. They analyze the resulting n-qubit ensembles after T = O_t(n^2 log^2 n) independent steps, showing they form approximate unitary t-designs with negligible error exp(-Ω(log^2 n)) while remaining distinguishable from random by an efficient quantum algorithm using only O_t(log^2 n) queries. They also build a stronger counterexample separating unitary designs from pseudorandom unitaries at polynomially bounded moments, though requiring highly structured ensembles.
AI.result: Local random walks can be approximate unitary t-designs yet efficiently distinguishable from Haar-random, refuting the unitary analog of the Hoory–Magen–Myers–Rackoff conjecture. A stronger separation between unitary designs and pseudorandom unitaries holds at polynomially bounded moments but needs highly structured ensembles.
AI.conclusion: Unitary designs do not generically imply pseudorandomness, so they are unreliable for modeling information scrambling in black-hole physics: even maximally scrambled systems may retain structure accessible to efficient experiments. The authors propose new conjectures on how pseudorandomness can plausibly emerge in simple quantum processes such as random quantum circuits.

title: Time-space lower bounds for breaking quantum cryptography
summary: We prove near-optimal time-space lower bounds for breaking quantum cryptography in the random oracle model. Specifically, we show that a $T$-query adversary with $S$ qubits of non-uniform advice can recover a random key $k$ from the $n$-qubit binary phase state $|ψ_k\rangle \propto \sum_{x} R(k,x) |x\rangle$ with probability at most $O(\frac{T^2 + \sqrt{ST}}{N})$ for $N=2^n$. In contrast, the best known bound for post-quantum one-way functions is $O(\frac{T^2 + ST}{N})$, with a trivial attack at $S = N$. This demonstrates a new advantage of quantum cryptography over classical cryptography: $n$ qubits of communication suffice for security against preprocessing attacks with space up to $N^2$ rather than $N$. Our methodology is simple: express the optimal preprocessing attack as the operator norm of a random matrix, and bound this value in expectation over the random oracle via the trace-moment method. These trace moments have a natural interpretation using compressed oracles [Zhandry, Crypto 2019], which we then analyze. This can be viewed as a simplification and generalization of the approach of Liu [Eurocrypt 2023] for proving time-space tradeoffs for breaking post-quantum cryptography. We also prove the following results: (1) We tighten Liu's analysis of post-quantum PRGs in QROM, achieving a distinguishing advantage bound of $O(\frac{T^2}N + \sqrt{\frac{ST}N})$. (2) For unitary synthesis, we extend the one-query lower bound of Lombardi-Ma-Wright [STOC 2024] to hold against adversaries that can make one arbitrary function query along with polynomially many (adaptive) queries to the random oracle, either before or after the function query. This also interprets the original LMW24 result in terms of compressed oracles. (3) Finally, we prove a tight $O(\frac{\sqrt{S}}N)$ bound for the pseudorandomness of random binary phase states against space $S$ distinguishers.

AI.tldr: Near-optimal time-space lower bounds for breaking quantum cryptography in the random oracle model.
AI.motivation: Demonstrate a new advantage of quantum over classical cryptography: security against preprocessing attacks with larger space.
AI.method: Express the optimal preprocessing attack as the operator norm of a random matrix, bound its expectation via the trace-moment method, and interpret the trace moments using compressed oracles.
AI.result: Recovery probability at most O((T² + √(ST))/N); tightened post-quantum PRG bound O(T²/N + √(ST/N)); extended unitary synthesis lower bound; tight O(√S/N) pseudorandomness bound.
AI.conclusion: n qubits of communication suffice for security against preprocessing attacks with space up to N² rather than N.

title: Unitary Schur Sampling of Qudits via Random SWAP Tests: Hunt for Antisymmetry
comment: 19 pages + 29 pages of Appendices, 2 Figures, Preliminary version
summary: Schur sampling is a fundamental primitive for extracting permutation-invariant information from many-body quantum systems and has broad applications in quantum information science. Circuit-based implementations typically rely on coherent representation-theoretic operations such as Clebsch-Gordan transforms, generalized phase estimation, or quantum Fourier transforms over the symmetric group. We show that unitary Schur sampling of arbitrary permutation-invariant mixed states on $n$ $d$-dimensional qudits can instead be implemented using only pairwise SWAP tests, namely, two-qudit projective measurements onto the symmetric and antisymmetric subspaces. Our protocol achieves error $ε$ in diamond distance using $O(n\min\{n,d\}^{3}\log^2(n/ε))$ random SWAP tests. The central idea is to repeatedly identify and extract the largest antisymmetric subsystem. This turns unitary Schur sampling into a search for antisymmetry and gives the algorithm a natural interpretation as a stochastic traversal of a Young diagram. The protocol preserves the $\mathrm{SU}(d)$-irrep state while preparing a canonical pure state in the multiplicity subsystem. As an application, we consider quantum purity amplification (QPA), in which multiple noisy copies of a pure quantum state are combined to produce a state of higher purity. We show that the optimal purified state can be obtained by retaining a single designated output qudit and discarding the rest.

AI.tldr: Unitary Schur sampling of arbitrary permutation-invariant mixed states on n qudits can be implemented using only pairwise SWAP tests, requiring O(n min{n,d}^3 log^2(n/ε)) random SWAP tests to reach error ε in diamond distance.
AI.motivation: Schur sampling is a fundamental primitive for extracting permutation-invariant information from many-body quantum systems, with broad applications in quantum information science. Existing circuit-based implementations rely on coherent representation-theoretic operations such as Clebsch-Gordan transforms, generalized phase estimation, or quantum Fourier transforms over the symmetric group, which are complex to implement.
AI.method: The protocol uses only pairwise SWAP tests—two-qudit projective measurements onto the symmetric and antisymmetric subspaces. Its central idea is to repeatedly identify and extract the largest antisymmetric subsystem, turning unitary Schur sampling into a search for antisymmetry and giving the algorithm a natural interpretation as a stochastic traversal of a Young diagram. The protocol preserves the SU(d)-irrep state while preparing a canonical pure state in the multiplicity subsystem.
AI.result: The protocol achieves error ε in diamond distance using O(n min{n,d}^3 log^2(n/ε)) random SWAP tests. As an application to quantum purity amplification (QPA), the optimal purified state can be obtained by retaining a single designated output qudit and discarding the rest.
AI.conclusion: Unitary Schur sampling can be performed with simple pairwise SWAP tests, avoiding coherent representation-theoretic operations. This simplifies the primitive and yields a novel interpretation via Young diagram traversal, with implications for quantum purity amplification.

title: Quantum Advantage for Two-Party Differential Privacy
summary:
We introduce information-theoretically private quantum protocols for two-party Hamming distance when both parties must output the same estimate. Classically, for input length $n$, information-theoretic protocols require $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ error under pure differential privacy and $Ω(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ error under strong approximate differential privacy, whereas computational security permits $O(1)$ error. In Klauck's honest, nonpreemptive, message-preserving model, we give an $O(n)$-communication quantum protocol with pure $\varepsilon$ quantum differential privacy (QDP) and expected error at most $\frac{2}{\sinh \varepsilon}+γ$, for every $γ>0$. For approximate $(\varepsilon, δ)$ QDP, an exact hockey-stick divergence calculation yields strictly smaller error, while preserving the $O(1)$-versus-$Ω(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ separation for $δ=o(1/n)$. Thus, quantum communication achieves $O(1)$ information-theoretic error, matching the accuracy available classically only under computational assumptions.
  The main construction uses a guarded coherent round trip and an equal-Gram rigidity principle that prevents an honest player from retaining input-dependent complementary information. We separate this model from weaker prescribed-channel privacy, which already admits an exact classical realization, and from fully retention-robust security, against which measurement-and-abort attacks remain possible. Therefore, we identify preservation of non-orthogonal quantum messages as a resource for privacy.

AI.tldr: The paper presents information-theoretically private quantum protocols for two-party Hamming distance estimation, achieving O(1) error with O(n) quantum communication, matching classical accuracy only attainable under computational assumptions.
AI.motivation: Classical information-theoretic protocols for Hamming distance suffer inherent error lower bounds (Ω(√n) under pure DP, Ω(√n/log n) under approximate DP), whereas O(1) error is achievable only with computational assumptions. The paper seeks to overcome this accuracy barrier using quantum communication.
AI.method: The authors work in Klauck's honest, nonpreemptive, message-preserving model. Their main construction employs a guarded coherent round trip and an equal-Gram rigidity principle that prevents an honest player from retaining input-dependent complementary information. They analyze privacy via pure ε quantum differential privacy (QDP) and approximate (ε, δ) QDP with an exact hockey-stick divergence calculation.
AI.result: An O(n)-communication quantum protocol achieves pure ε QDP with expected error at most 2/sinh ε + γ for every γ > 0. For approximate (ε, δ) QDP, the divergence calculation yields strictly smaller error while preserving the O(1)-versus-Ω(√n/log n) separation for δ = o(1/n). Thus quantum communication attains O(1) information-theoretic error.
AI.conclusion: Quantum communication enables O(1) information-theoretic error for two-party Hamming distance, matching classical accuracy previously available only under computational assumptions. The work separates this model from weaker prescribed-channel privacy (which has an exact classical realization) and from fully retention-robust security (vulnerable to measurement-and-abort attacks), identifying the preservation of non-orthogonal quantum messages as a privacy resource.

title: Local random quantum circuits converge to the Porter-Thomas distribution in polynomial depth
summary: Porter-Thomas statistics are a characteristic feature of the output distribution of random quantum states and, more broadly, chaotic quantum many-body systems. Convergence to Porter-Thomas plays a central role in random circuit sampling and experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage, where the output statistics of low-depth random quantum circuits are expected to be approximately Porter-Thomas, despite the absence of a rigorous proof of convergence. We show that the output distribution of polynomial-depth brickwork random circuits converges inverse-polynomially in total variation distance to the Porter-Thomas distribution. Specifically, consider the output probability distribution over a fixed bitstring of a local random quantum circuit, constructed from nearest-neighbor Haar random gates. Then, for any $m \geq 0$, the distribution corresponding to circuits of depth $O(n^{2m+1}\log(n))$ is at most $O(1/n^m)$ far in total variation distance from the Porter-Thomas distribution. Our proof uses moment bounds from approximate designs, analytic estimates for characteristic functions, and a local anticoncentration property for inverse moments.

AI.tldr: The output distribution of polynomial-depth brickwork random quantum circuits converges inverse-polynomially in total variation distance to the Porter-Thomas distribution; specifically, depth O(n^{2m+1}log n) yields distance O(1/n^m).
AI.motivation: Convergence to Porter-Thomas statistics underlies random circuit sampling and experimental demonstrations of quantum advantage, yet prior work assumed approximately Porter-Thomas output statistics without a rigorous proof of convergence.
AI.method: The proof combines moment bounds derived from approximate designs, analytic estimates for characteristic functions, and a local anticoncentration property for inverse moments, applied to local random circuits built from nearest-neighbor Haar random gates.
AI.result: For any m >= 0, the distribution over a fixed bitstring produced by circuits of depth O(n^{2m+1}log(n)) is at most O(1/n^m) far in total variation distance from the Porter-Thomas distribution.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial-depth brickwork random circuits rigorously converge inverse-polynomially to Porter-Thomas statistics, providing a proof of convergence that was previously absent in the context of random circuit sampling.

title: Spiking neural networks for streaming qubit readout
summary: Fast and accurate qubit-state assignment is essential for feedback, calibration, and error correction in quantum processors. In superconducting platforms, frequency-multiplexed readout makes this task intrinsically multivariate as measured traces can encode crosstalk, qubit-state relaxation events, and other transient nonidealities that are not fully captured by conventional matched filtering. Here, we introduce spiking neural network (SNN) discriminators for superconducting qubit readout. By processing the measurement window in successive time chunks, the networks exploit temporal structure and update classification scores as data arrive, rather than waiting until the end of the readout window. The spiking networks outperform matched-filter discrimination and approach the accuracy of a full-trace artificial neural network. Beyond reaching the performance of artificial neural networks, the key advantage of SNNs is that they provide a streaming, time-resolved estimate of the qubit state that evolves as the readout signal is acquired. Using quantisation-aware training and hls4ml synthesis, we further demonstrate that each FPGA inference update can be completed before the next readout chunk arrives. These results establish spiking neural networks as a promising route to low-latency, real-time qubit readout on FPGA hardware, with broader implications for time-critical quantum-control and scientific-inference applications.

AI.tldr: Spiking neural network discriminators process qubit readout traces in successive time chunks, delivering streaming, time-resolved state estimates that beat matched filtering and approach full-trace ANN accuracy, with FPGA inference fast enough for real-time use.
AI.motivation: Fast, accurate qubit-state assignment is essential for feedback, calibration, and error correction. Frequency-multiplexed superconducting readout is intrinsically multivariate, and measured traces encode crosstalk, relaxation events, and transient nonidealities not fully captured by conventional matched filtering. A latency-efficient, temporally aware discriminator is needed.
AI.method: The authors introduce spiking neural network (SNN) discriminators for superconducting qubit readout. The networks process the measurement window in successive time chunks, exploiting temporal structure and updating classification scores as data arrive instead of waiting until the end of the window. Quantisation-aware training and hls4ml synthesis are used to map the SNNs onto FPGA hardware.
AI.result: SNNs outperform matched-filter discrimination and approach the accuracy of a full-trace artificial neural network. They additionally provide a streaming, time-resolved state estimate that evolves as the readout signal is acquired. Each FPGA inference update completes before the next readout chunk arrives.
